making nominations ; 

(b) the 9th January 1969, as the date for the 
scrutiny of nominations; 

(c) the 11107 January 1969, as the last date for 
the withdrawal of candidatures;

power conferred by section 506 of the said Act to 
confirm the following rules, namely:— 


Rules Regarding Appointment of Municipal Officers 
and Servants 


1, These rules shall apply to all municipal officers 
and servants other than menials, 


2. No person above 25 years of age shall ordi- 
narily be appointed to a permanent post without the 
Sanction of the Commissioners at a meeting: 

Provided that a person whose age does not exceed 
28 years may be appointed to the post of medical 
officer without such sanction. 


3. No person shall be substantively appointed to 
a permanent pogt without a medical certificate of 
health in such form and signed by such medical 
officer as may be required by the Commissioners at 
a meeting. 


4. A ministerial officer may be required to retire 
at any time after attaining the age of 58 years, and 
may not in any case be retained in service after 
attaining the age of 60 ycars except in very special 
circumstances which shall be recorded in writing 
and with the sanction of the Commissioners at a 
meeting. All other municipal officers and servants 
except primary school teachers shall ordinarily 
retire on attaining the age of 58 years but, with the 
sanction of the Commissioners at a mecting, and for 
reasons which shall be recorded in writing, they 
may, if considered by the Commissioners at a 
mecting to be fit for duty, be retained in service 
till they attain the age of 60, by the grant of exten- 


. sion of service by periods of one year at a time.. 


4A. Primary school teachers shall ordinarily retire 
at the age of 60 years: 


Provided that a teacher who is otherwise fit for 
duty may, for sufficient reasons to be recorded in, 
writing and with the sanction of the Commissioners 
at a meeting, be retained in service up to the age 
of 65 years, by granting extension of service by one 
year at a time, 


5. No Government pensioner may be appointed 
to a post without the previous sanction of the Local 
Government and each appointment of a Govern- 
ment pensioner shall be on a contract the terms of 
which are approved by the Local Self-Government. 


Note.—It shall be an invariable condition of 
such contract that the pensioner shall not 
be retained in service after he has attained 
the age of 60 years except for special reasons 
and with previous sanction of the Local 
Government. 


By order of the Governor, 


H. DAS GUPTA, Asstt. Secy,

mal working day inclusive of a period of interval of 
rest, the day of weekly rest, the rate of payment for 
work on the day of weckly rest and the overtime rate, 
as specified in the Schedule below: 


The Schedule 


1. Hours of work constituting a normal working 
day.—Eight and half hours of work including half an 
hour’s interval of rest shall constitute a normal work- 
ing day. 


2. Day of weekly rest.—Sunday or such other day 
in any period of scven days as may suit the local 
convenience shall be the day of weekly rest. 


3. Payment for work on the day of weekly rcst— 
All employees shall be paid for work on the day of 
weekly rest at the overtime rate. 


4. Overtime rate——For work beyond normal 
working hours, the employees shall be paid at couble 
the ordinary rates of wages.

3. The functions of the Board of Vcterinary 
Education, West Bengal, will be— 


(a) To prescribe, subject to approval of Govern- 
ment, the syllabi of studies for the P.G. 
Course in Physio-pathology of Reproduc- 
tion and Artificial Insemination, Veterinary 
Compounders’ Course, etc., at the Bengal 
Veterinary College. 

(b) To prescribe, subject to approval of Govern- 
ment, the syllabi of studies for the training 
‘course of Veterinary Field Assistants at the 
Veterinary Field Assistants’ Training Insti- 
tute, Midnapore. 

(c) To frame rules for examinations in the above 
courses, to appoint paper-setters and 
examiners and to moderate the results of 
examinations as well as to award diplomas| 
certificates to candidates who have success- 
fully complcted the courses. 

(d) To advise Government on any other matter 
referred to them, and to undertake any 
Other function that Government may 
specifically entrust on them. 


4. The Board shall meet in Calcutta as often as 
may be necessary. Meetings of the Board shall be 
convened by the Secretary with the prior approval of 
the Chairman. For ordinary meetings of the Board 
ut least seven days’ notice shall be given to the 
Members. The Chairman shall, however, has power 
to convene an emergent meeting of the Board with 
at least 24 hours’ notice to the Membcrs. 


5. Four Members will form a quorum. 


6. In the unavoidable absence of the Chairman, 
any other Member, other than the Secretary, may be 
elected to preside over the meeting. | 


7. The Board shall have powers of constituting 
ad hoc standing sub-committees for specific purposes 
and to delegate to such sub-committees any of the 
functions of the Board, other than— 


(a) final approval of syllabus or course of studies, 
or rules of examination, 

(b) appointment of paper-setters and examiners, 
and 


(c) moderation of the results of examinations. 


8. A sub-committee constituted by the Board 
may include persons who are not Members of the 
Board, but the number of Such persons shall not 
exceed half the total number of members of sub- 
committee. 


9. The Chairman shall have powers of inviting 
any person, whose presence he may _ consider 
necessary, to attend and participate in the delibera- 
tion of a mecting of the Board. 


10. The Secretary of the Board shall forward 
copies of the minutes of proceedings of each meeting 
of the Board to (1) the Director of Veterinary 
Services, and (2) the Government.

Ordered that this Resolution be published in the 
“Calcutta Gazette” and copies of it be forwarded to 
the Members of the Board.

exercise of the powers conferred upon me under 
proviso (1) of section 12(1) of the West Bengal ’ 
Panchayat Act, 1957, as ammended by section 3 of 
the West Bengal Panchayat (Amendment) Act, 1964, 
read with item 7 of the schedule published by 
Notification No. 11160|Panch.|2A-28|66, dated 1 
September 1967, I do hereby extend the terms of

COVERNMENT OF WEST BENCAL

ORDERS 


No.  8830-I.R./IR/13L-18/68. — 12th | December 
1968.—Whereas under the Government of West 
Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 5717-I.R./ 
IR/13L-18/68, dated the 29th July 1968, the 
industrial dispute between Messrs. Manashi 
Press, 73 Manicktalla Street, Calcutta-6, and 
their workmen represented by Press Employees’ 
Association, 249/8 Bepin Behari Ganguli Street, 
Calcutta-12, regarding the issue mentioned in the 
said order being a matter specified in the Second 
Schedule to the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
(XIV of 1947), was referred for adjudication to 
the Second Industrial Tribunal; 


And whereas the said Second Industrial Tribu- 
nal has submitted to the State Government its 
award on the said industrial dispute; 


Now, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions 
of section 17 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
(XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased hereby to 
publish the said award as shown in the annexure 
hereto. 


ANNEXURE 


In the matter of an Industrial dispute between 
Messrs. Manashi Press, 73 Manicktalla Street, 
Calcutta-6, and thelr workmen represented 
by Press Employees Association, 2491 
Bepin Behari Ganguli Street, Calcutta-12. 
(Case No. VIII-279/68.) 


BEFORE THE SECOND INDUSTRIAL 
TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL 


Present : 


Shri H. N. SEN, Judge, 
Second Industrial Tribunal. 


Government of West Bengal, Labour Depart- 
ment, by its order No. 5717-].R./I.R./13L-18/68, 
dated the 29th July 1968, referred an industrial 
dispute between Messrs. Manashi Press and _ their 
workmen represented by Press Employees’ Asso- 
ciation to this Tribunal for adjudication on the 
following: 


Issue 


Whether refusal of employment to Shri Sudhai 
Chandra Sarker with effect from 18th April 
1968 is justified? To what relief, if any, is 
he entitled? 


After service of usual notices the Union entered 
appearance and filed written statement on 24th 
September 1968. The Company however did not 
enter appearance even after service of notice. 
The Tribunal suo motu waited till 13th Novem- 
ber 1968 for the Company to file written state- 
ment, with the direction that if no step was taken 
by that date the ‘case will be heard ex-parte. 


On 13th November 1968 the Company took no 
step. The case was accordingly fixed on 3rd 
December 1968 for ex-parte hearing. The 


2 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 2, 1969 


Or পা oe‏ 2 اٹ ০ RTE a‏ جج ےس شس شش ش9 


SS ৯১০২৯ ২৩-০০-৯০১০ সত পপ TE 


Company being found absent on 3rd December 
1968, the case was taken up for ex-parte hearing. 


Appearances of the parties are as follows:— 


For the Union: Shri Anil Das Chowdhury, 


Advocate. 


For the Company: None. 


On behalf of the applicant, the applicant-work- 
man examined himself. 


The applicant's case, in short, is that he 
received intimation of serious illness of his father 
on 14th April 1968. On 15th April 1968 he resumed 
duty and approached the Company for two days’ 
leave and obtained such leave. On the expiry of 
his leave he came to resume his duty on 18th 
April 1968. He was however refused employment by 
the Opposite-party-Company. His case is further 
that he was never charge-sheeted طز‎ the 
Company, as such refusal of employment by the 
Opposite-party-Company was unjustified and in 
violation of the principles of natural justice. He 
then approached the Union which took 0) 1713 
case and on the Unions move conciliation was 
called for but no settlement was arrived at. The 
workman examined himself as P.W. 1, to reiterate 
his case mooted in the written statement filed by 
him. Since the Company did not enter appea- 
rance I see so reason why the statement of fact 
made by the workman concerned (P.W. 1.) should 
not be believed and accepted. Accepting the said 
statement of P.W. 1. this Tribunal therefore’ holds 
that the refusal of employment of Shri Sudhai 
Chandra Sarkar with effect from 18th April 1968 
is wholly unjustified. The workman concerned 
is therefore entitled to be reinstated to his former 
job with full back wages from the date of refusal 
of employment till his reinstatement, and it is 
awarded accordingly. This award is to take 
effect on the expiry of 30 days from the date of 
publication of the award in the “Calcutta Gazette”. 


Dictated and corrected by me. 


H. N. SEN, 
Judge. 


H. N. SEN, Judge, 
Second Industrial Tribunal. 
4-12-68, 


By order of the Governor,

AWARD 


The Government of West Bengal, Labour Depart- 
ment, by its order No. 3240-1.R./IR/11L-200/68, dated 
3lst May 1968, referred to this Court under section 10 
of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), 
an Industrial Dispute relating to the undermentioned 
issue existing between Md. Nur Islam Mahalder, Pro- 
prietor of a Bidi Factory, P.O. and district Jalpaiguri, 
and his workmen represented by Zilla Bidi Mazdoor 
Samity, P.O. and district Jalpaiguri, for adjudication. 


Issue 


Whether termination of employment of Shri Suren 
Biswas is justified ? To what relief, if any, is 
he entitled ? 


Notices of this proceeding were duly served upon the 
parties. The Company sent a copy of the written state- 
ment by post, without there being a direction from this 
court and it was received in this court on 26th July 
1968. On 26th July 1968, on the application of the 
Union concerned, 14th August 1968, was fixed as the 
date for filing its written statement. On 14th August 
1968, however, the Union did neither take any step in 
connection with the present reference, nor file its 
written statement as directed. A chance was givén and 
30th August 1968, was fixed suo motu by this court for 
filing written statement by the Union. On 30th 
August 1968, the Union again took no step whatever in 
connection with this case and so the case was directed 
to be put up for orders on 19th September 1968. On 
19th September 1968, the parties again were found 
absent and no step whatever was taken by the Union in 
connection with this case. No written statement was 
also filed. The case therefore was directed to be put 
up for orders on 15th October 1968. On 15th Octo- 
ber 1968, again the parties were found absent and no 
step ‘whatever was taken by either of them in connec- 
tion with this case. Accordingly 19th November 1968 
came to be fixed for orders. The parties also did not 
care to take any step whatever even on 19th November 


Parr IC] 


প্রি 


79068. And so the case was directed to be put up for 
orders on 28th November 1968. Even on this day 
that is 28th November 1968, the parties are again 
absent nnd they do not take any step whatever in 
cunnection with this case. In such circumstance, I am 
inclined to think that the parties are no longer interest- 
৪61 in the instant reference and that the dispute under 
reference is no longer in existence. I accordingly pass 


a ‘no-di«pute’ award. The instant reference is accord- 
ingly disposed of.

By the Government of West Bengal, Labour Depart- 
ment, order No. 3677-1.R./IR/11L-316(A)/67, dated 
the 2nd August 1967, an industrial dispute existing 
between Messrs. Gladstone Lyall & Co. Ltd., 4 Fairlie 
Place, Calcutta-1, and their workmen represented by 
General Workers’ Union of Gladstone Lyall & Co. Ltd., 
3 Joy Krishna Paul Road, Calcutta-23, was referred to 
this Tribunal, under section 10 of the Industrial Dis- 
putes Act, 1947, for adjudication, in respect of the 
following issues :— 


Issues 


1, Working hours of Drivers and Lorry Mazdoors. 


2. Grades and Scales of Pay of the Drivers 
and Lorry Mazdoors. 


3. Tiffin Allowance 
Mazdoors. 


of Drivers and_ Lorry 


4. Dock Allowance of Drivers and Lorry Mazdoors.

Lorry Mazdoors. 


6. Travelling Allowance of Drivers and Lorry 
Mazdoors. 


7. House Rent Allowance of Drivers and Lorry 
Mazdoors. 


It appears from the aforesaid issues sent to this 
Tribunal for adjudication that cases of drivers and 
lorry mazdoors are involved in this order of refer- 
ence. At the time of hearing, P.W. 1, the only witness 
examined on behalf of the Union, stated before me that 
they press for demands in this order of reference, for 
lorry mazdoors. According to him; all the drivers of 
this Company are members of the Union and _ no 
driver is a member of the other Union of the Com- 
pany. According to P. W. 1 further, there are in 
all, 21 drivers including one lorry driver employed in 
this Company. So, we are concerned in this case as 
regards 21 drivers including one lorry driver employ- 
ed in this Company. 


The Union of the drivers of the Company, being 
“General Workers’ Union of Gladstone Lyall & Co. 
Ltd.” in its written statement contended that the Com- 
pany is mainly Engineering and a private commercial 
concern, having multifarious business such as roofiing 
and water proofiing, shipping and banking and the work- 
men connected with the terms of this reference, are their 
motor drivers and lorry mazdoors (I have already 
mentioned above that the case of the lorry mazdoors 
has been given up at the time of hearing). The 
drivers were formely members of Gladstone Lyall & 
Co. Ltd. Employees’ Union, which Union entered into 
aQ agreement on certain terms, not covering all of the 
present items of reference. On 15th April 1957, this 
agreement however brought some improvement in the 
conditions of the clerks, but in fact it brought no bene- 
fit to the drivers. Accordingly, they formed their new 
Union, being “General Workers’ Union” and they sub- 
mitted a charter of demands. There were conciliation 
proceedings before the Labour Commissioner, but no 
decision could be arrived at and the meeting ended in 
a failure. All negotiations came to a close, and the 
instant order of reference was sent to this Tribunal for 
adjudication in respect of the issues as mentioned

above. The Union demanded an increased scale of 
pay than the existing scale of pay of the drivers. As 
the Head Office is closed on Saturday and as_ the 
drivers are Head Office Staff, they also pray for 5 
days work in a week. The Union demands further 
raising the tiffin allowance of 0.37 P. per diem to 
Rs. 1-50 per working day. The Union also demands 
dock allowance of Rs. 45 for the drivers when posted 
in-the docks. They also pray for enhancement of 
Travelling Allowance from Rs. 4 to Rs. 6 per diem 
because of the fact that in the conditions of present 
high price of things, the existing rate does in no way 
come near to compensating the additional expenses 
incurred at outstations or when on travel away from 
the headquarters. The Union further demands 20 per 
cent. of the basic pay or a fixed sum of Rs. 30 per 
month, as house rent allowance for the drivers per 
month. They also demand shoes and shocks to be 
supplied to the drivers. 


The Company in their written statement contended 
inter-alia that the present scale of pay of drivers is 
justified, legal and proper and the Company has no 
capacity to give any further increase in basic wages 
and other allowances due to financial difficulties. 
According to the Company, the working hours from 
Monday to Friday are from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m., i.e., in all 
48 hours a week, which working hours are quite 
reasonable and well within the limits imposed by law. 
The present tiffin allowance of 0.37 P for full work- 
ing day is also just fair and legal, according to the 
Company. ‘The present rate of Rs. 20 per month as 
dock allowance is also stated to be fair. The existing 
travelling allowance of Rs. 4 per diem is according to 
the Company just. Further, according to the Com- 
pany, the drivers are not entitled to any house rent 
allowance as claimed. I have already mentioned above 
that undisputedly 21 drivers including one lorry driver 
employed in the Company, who are now all members 
to the ‘General Workers’ Union of Messrs. Gladstone 
Lyall and Co. Ltd.”, are concerned in this order of 
reference. In January 1967, another Union in which 
the clerical staff and sub-staff are involved, entered into 
an agreement with the Company authorities, by which 
their scales of pay and other allowances and amenities 
were enhanced and increased. Ext. C is a copy of such 
settlement, dated 25th January 1967. But this settle- 
ment, the drivers of the Company did not get any 
benefit. None of their demands was met by that 
agreement, 


On behalf of the Union, Ext. ] (0) has been filed 
to show the present scales of pay and other amenities, 
enjoyed by the drivers of different companies, being 
Messrs. James Finlay, Turner Morison, Kilburn & 
Macneil Barry, Shaw Wallace & Co., Balmer Lawries, 
Andrew Yule & Co. and Messrs. Jardine Henderson. 
On the other hand, on behalf of the Company, a docu- 
ment Ext. B has been filed to show the existing scales 
of pay and other amentities enjoyed by the drivers of 
3 Companies—Bird & Co., Duncan Brothers 204 
Macneil Barry & Co., while fixing new scales of pay 
and other allowances and amenities, to be enjoyed by 
the drivers of Messrs. Gladstone Lyall & Co. Ltd., as 
covered by the aforesaid issues, we are to compare the 
scales of pay and other amenities enjoyed by the drivers 
of the aforesaid Companies as appearing in Exts. 1 (O) 
and B. In this connection, we should also consider the 
present financial capacity of Messrs. Gladstone Lyall 
& Co. and as to whether the Company would be able

to bear the additional financial burden as per the 
claim of the Union. On this question, the evidence of 
D.W. 1, the Secretary-cum-Accountant of the Com- 
pany, the sole witness examined on behalf of the Com- 
pany and also Ext, G., a statement of the Company’s 
financial position from the year 1963-1964 till 1967- 
1968 (up to 30th June 1968) and again the balance- 
sheets of the Company Ext. F series from 1963 till 
1967 (the financial accounting year of the Company 
is from November of a year till the 30th October of 
the next year), are to be considered. It appears from 
the aforesaid documents and also from the evidences 
of D.W. 1 that the Company incurred a loss of 
Rs. 5,69,195 in the year 1963-64, During the next 
two years, the Company earned profits to a total sum 
of Rs. 6,77,000 approximately. Again in the year 
1966-67, the Company incurred loss to the extent of 
Rs. 6,15,943 for the accounting year 1967-68. There 
is also evidence on record of D.W. 1 in his chief that 
they were secretaries and _ treasurers of Messrs. 
Carew & Co., which ceased in September 1964. 
They were also the managing agents of Messrs. 
Calcutta Landing and Shipping Co. Ltd., and that 
their managing agency ceased from March 1966. In 
the year ending 3151 October 1963, Messrs. Gladstone 
Lyall & Co. Ltd., got from the aforesaid two 
managed Companies Rs. 3,98,576 as commission. In 
the next year, they also got such commission at 
Rs. 4,29,278. Next year, they got only from Messrs. 
Calcutta Landing and Shipping Co. Ltd., Rs. 26,367 
as commission and for a portion of the year of 1966, 
they got only Rs. 6,250 as commission from the said 
Company. Balance-sheets, Ext. G and also Ext. A 
and the evidence of D.W. 1 disclosed a very sad 
financial position of the Company in question. But 
even then, it is to be remembered that only in January 
1967, the Company entered into an agreement with 
another Union enhancing the scales of pay and revis- 
ing other amenities of the clerks as well as the sub- 
staff of the Company whose number is much larger 
than 21 of the drivers employed in the Head Office 
of the Company who are only interested in this order 
of reference. 


I first take up issue No. 3 regarding tiffin allowance 
of drivers. It is admitted that by the settlement of 
January 1967, the tiffin allowance of sub-staff except- 
ing the drivers was enhanced from 0.37P. per diem 
to 0.60P. per diem. By that settlement, rate of 
tiffin allowance of the clerical staff was also enhanced. 
Drivers are al present getting 0.37P. per diem as 
tiffin allowance, for each full working day. One of 
the drivers employed in the Company has been exa- 
mined in this case as the sole witness on behalf of the 
Union. He (P.W. 1) in his evidence claimed such 
tiffin allowance at Re. 1 per diem per working day. 
It of course appears from Ext, B that the drivers of 
the three Companies’ as mentioned therein are getting 
0.75P. per day as tiffin allowance. Ext. 1 (0) 
filed on behalf of the Union shows that the drivers 
of the Companies mentioned above are getting 
tiffin allowance varying from 0.62P. per diem 
till 0۰,75۲. per diem. As tiffin allowance of the 
sub-staff of the Company in question has been 
enhanced to 0.60 P. per diem for each full work- 
ing day, Shri D. Basu Thakur at the time of argu- 
ments conceded that 1119 tiffin allowance of the 
drivers might be enhanced to 0.60P. per diem 
for each full working day. Accordingly, it is held 
that the tiffin allowance of each driver should be 
0.60 P. per diem for each full working day. 


[Part IC 


Now coming to issue No. 7, regarding house rent 
allowance of the drivers, it is undisputed that by the 
agreement of January 1967, the sub-staff of the 
Company was not allowed any house rent allowance. 
It also appears from Ext. B that the drivers of the 
three Company's mentioned therein being Messrs. Bird 
& Co., Duncan Brothers and Macneil & Barry are not 
also getting any house rent allowance. Ext. 1 (O) 
filed on behalf of the Union does not also show that 
the drivers of the 7 Companies as mentioned therein 
are allowed any house rent allowance. In the above 
view of the case, I am also inclined not to allow any 
house rent allowance to the drivers. Accordingly, I 
hold that the drivers are not entitled to any house 
rent allowance as claimed. by them. 


As regards the claim of the Union regarding Shoe 
and Socks allowance as covered by Issue No. 5, we 
find that during ‘summer, each of the drivers get two 
coats and two full pants for a year and during winter 
each of the driver get one coat and one pant for a 
year. They are not to return all these uniforms to 
the Company, after the same are torn. But these uni- 
forms, it must be considered as given to the drivers 
for enhancement of the prestige of the Company. 


Now one pair of shoe and one pair of socks would 
not cost much and the Company, in my _ opinion, 
could bear the burden of such additional cost if one 
pair of shoe and one pair of socks be allowed to each 
of the drivers. The number of the drivers is only 
2]. Accordingly, I hold that each of the drivers of 
the Company should get one pair of shoe and one 
pair of socks per annum from the Company ; but the 
quality of such goods would depend on the choice of 
the Company authorities. Issue Number 5 is thus 
disposed of. 


Issue No.6: As regards the claim of the drivers 
regarding travelling allowance, we find from the 
written statement of the Union as.well as the evidence 
of P. W. 1 that this claim of travelling allowance is 
the same as the claim of outstation allowance. It is 
admitted that previously these drivers used to get 
Rs. 4 per diem as outstation allowance, for outstation 
duties. From this year of 1968, it is admitted that 
such allowance was enhanced to Rs. 6 per diem. It 
appears from Exts. B and 1(0) that such outstation 
allowance varies from Rs. 5 per diem to Rs. 8 per diem 
but in most cases drivers are allowed Rs. 5 per diem 
as outstation allowance. On a consideration of this 
fact, I hold that the drivers of the Company in ques- 
tion are entitled to outstation allowance or travelling 
allowance at the rate of Rs. 6 per diem, which amount 
now being given to the drivers, since this year of 

68. 


Issue No.4: From amongst the drivers of the 
Company some are posted at the dock for dock duties 
in the shipping department. The number of such 
drivers posted at the dock would be about one or 
two. Admittedly for dock duties drivers get Rs. 20 
per month, as dock allowance. Their demand is 
Rs. 45 per month. Now we do not find anything from 
Exts. B and 1(0), as regards any dock allowance 
given to the drivers of the Companies mentioned in 
the said documents, for dock duties. As the number 
of the drivers posted at the dock for dock duties is 
negligible, I hold that the ends of justice will be met 
if this dock allowance to be enhanced to Rs. 30 per

month. This enhancement also does not burden the 
Company too much. In the result, I hold that the 
drivers of the Company in question, who are posted 
in the dock for dock duties in the shipping department, 
should get Rs. 30 per month as dock allowance. 


Now coming to issue No. ] regarding the working 
hours of the drivers we find that admittedly such work- 
ing hours of the drivers are from 8 a.m, to 6 p.m. with 
a recess of one and half hours from 1 p.m. to 2-30 
p.m., from Monday to Friday, and on Saturday's the 
working hours are from 8-30 a.m. to 2 p.m. having no 
recess. Thus the total working hours of the drivers 
come to 48 hours per week. It is to be remembered 
in this connection that for all those hours that driver 
are not to drive their respective cars continuously. 
According to P.W. 1 in his cross-examination they are 
not to drive during the entire working hours and that 
they stay in office and sit idle, during the time when 
they are actually not to drive the car. He further 
admitted that at present there are not 20 cars of the 
Company and about 5 to 8 drivers are sitting idle as 
spare drivers. 


The demand of the drivers regarding their working 
hours has been stated by P.W. I. Demand in this res- 
pect is from 8 a.m. till 5 p.m. with half an hour recess 
on 5 days in a week (Monday to Friday) and they want 
Saturdays and Sundays off. These drivers are head 
office staff. It is admitted that the head office em- 
ployees are now to attend office for 5 days in a week. 
Their demand is that they should not work also on 
Saturdays. Now it appears from Ext. B that out of 
the three Companies mentioned therein, the drivers of 
Macneil Barry get Saturdays off also, whereas from 
Ext. 1(0), it appears that the drivers of Messrs. 
Balmer Lawries, Messrs. Andrew Yule and Co. Ltd. 
and also Messrs. Jardine Henderson get Saturdays off. 


I have also considered the working hours of the 
drivers for different Companies mentioned in Exts. B 
and 1(O). In view of the fact that the drivers of the 
Company, in question are head office staff and also in 
view of the fact that the head office of the Company 
is closed on Saturdays also, I hold the drivers of this 
Company, being Messrs. Gladstone Lyall & Co. Ltd. 
should get Saturdays off, excepting of course, the 
driver or drivers who are posted in the dock for dock 
duties in the shipping department, because work is done 
on Saturdays also in the dock. It is to be remembered 
in this connection that the drivers are posted in the 
dock by rotation. When the drivers are getting Satur- 
days off, we must fix their working hours on the other 
5 days of the week, Monday to Friday, keeping the 
total working hours fixed at 48 hours. So I fixed the 
working hours for the drivers attached to head office 
from 8 a.m. till 6-30 p.m. with a recess to one hour, 
from 1 p.m. to 2. p.m., from @Monday to Friday. I 
further hold that the drivers should get Saturdays off 
excepting the driver or drivers who are posted in the 
dock for dock duties in the shipping department, and 
those driver or drivers, who are to. drive the cars, 
carrying officers to the factory, if required. Issue No. 
1 is thus disposed of. 


Now coming to issue No. 2, regarding grades and 
scales of pay of the drivers. I have considered the 
grades and scales of pay of the drivers of the Com- 
pany's mentioned in Exts. 8 and 100), The present 
scale of the drivers of the Company in question 1s

Rs. 62—2—100—3—136. Their demand regarding

demands. P.W. 1 wanted three additional increments 
in each cases. Now in fixing the grades and scales of 
pay certain benefits admittedly enjoyed by the drivers 
of the Company are to be considered. The drivers get 
4 per cent. bonus on basic pay and D.A. The Com- 
pany reimburses the cost of all the medicines, pur- 
chased by the drivers during their illness. Office doctor 
treats them in between 1 p.m. to 3 p.m. The drivers 
enjoy the benefits of provident fund also. They also

drivers get medical leave for one month per annum 
with full pay, such leave being accumulated up to 3 
months. The drivers also get two months’ medical 
leave per annum on half pay. The drivers also get 
D.A. according to Bengal Chamber of Commerce Scale, 
which is also dependent on the cost of living index. 
If it rises, D.A. is also proportionately increased. 


Upon a consideration of an aforesaid existing bene- 
fits enjoyed by the drivers and also the existing scales 
of pay of the drivers of different Companies and also 
the fact that the existing scale was fixed long ago 
appearing from Exts. B and 1(O). I fixed the grades 
and scales of pay of the drivers of the Company in 
question as follows :— 


“Rs. 76—2—110—4—150". In order to fit in with 
this scale as fixed by me, the existing pay of the drivers 
should be enhanced by one, two or three increments as 
would be necessary. This grade as fixed by me shall 
come into force on and from lst January 1969. 


The above benefits given to the drivers of Messrs. 
Gladstone Lyall and Co. Ltd., shall be operative with 
effect from the Ist January 1969. 


This is my award.

rance on different dates. Thereafter the Union filed

pany after obtaining several adjournments filed written 
statement on 26th July 1968. Thereafter the parties 
entered into a compromise and the compromise

AWARD 


The Government of West Bengal, in its Labour 
Department, order Nos. 472-I.R./IR/8L-30/67, 
dated the 31st January 1968 and 1784-I.R./IR/8L- 
30/67, dated the 27th March 1968, referred under 
section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, 
an industrial dispute between Messrs. Shree Ram 
Silk Mfg. Co., 14 Netaji Subhas Road, Calcutta-1 
(hereinafter be referred as the Company), and their 
workmen employed at the Company's factory at 
Rishra, district Hooghly, as also the workmen em- 
ployed at the Company's factory at Konnagar, 
Hooghly, represented by Shree Ram Silk Mfg. Co. 
Workmen’s Union, 150 C. S, Mukherjee Street, 
Hooghly and Shree Ram Silk Mfg. Mazdoor Union, 
C/o. Shri Sudhangshu Sarkar, P.O. and _ village 
Bara Behara, district Hooghly (hereinafter be re- 
ferred to as the Union), to this Tribunal for ad- 
judication on the following common issues : 


Issues 


Revision of Wages. 

Dearness Allowance. 

Leave Facilities. 

Quarter or House Rent Allowance. 
Working Hours. 

Night Shift Allowance. 

Canteen. 


Bonus for thé year ending March 1967. 


০০ کہ‎ ০৯ یں‎ ৯ ৬১ £১ 7১ 


The Union has filed written statement in both 
the cases. It has alleged that Hastings Jute Mill 
Ltd. has a silk division and a jute division. 
Ram Silk Mfg. Company is the silk unit of that 
Mill. It manufactures Terryline, Terriwool and 
Silk Cloth. About 700 workmen work in this silk 
unit and 6,000 in the jute unit. Previously both the 
units were located at Rishra in the district of 
Hooghly. Subsequently due to expansion of the 
silk unit, the factory was shifted to Konnagar in the 
same district. The running of the silk unit requires 
finer workmanship and consequently the workmen 
are entitled to special consideration relating to fixa- 
tion of wages, dearness allowance and other ameni- 
ties. They: are not paid even the subsistence wages 
and the same are less than that of the workmen 
of the jute division of the parent Company. An 
unskilled jute workman gets Rs. 127 as the minimum 
wages, but a skilled workman of the silk unit gets 
only Rs. per month. The silk unit has a 
separate Profit and Loss Account and is more pros- 
perous than the jute unit. There is no scheme for 
neutralisation for the rise in the cost of living and 
the deatness allowance has not been linked with the 
rise in cost of the living index. The result is that 
the real wages are being lowered compared with the 
rise in the price index number. The leave facilities 
are inadequate because only 4 days’ casual leave 
and 9 days’ festival leave are granted. The jute 
unit provides for free quarters to the workmen, 
whereas the workmen of the silk unit do not get 
any such facilities or house allowance. The work- 
ing hours of the Company are too long. The 
workmen are compelled to work during the night 
shift: Such work affects their health and so they 


Shree — 


Part IC] 


should get night allowance. They should also 
get facilities for proper subsidised cheap 
canteen. For the financial year ended in March 
1967. the Company illegally declared bonus of 4 
per cent. only on the alleged earnings. But con- 
sidering the net profits, gross profits, etc., and 
the relevant records of the Company, bonus at 
the rate of 20 per cent. of the annual earnings 
of each workman should be paid. 


The Company has also put in written statement 
in both the cases. It has been alleged inter alia 
that the issues regarding quarters or house rent 
allowance, canteen facilities and bonus cannot be 
the subject matter of industrial dispute. There 
was a previous award between the Company and 
its workmen with regard to wages, leave facilities, 
holidays and night shift allowance. The 5110 
divisiun is a part and parcel of Hastings Mills 
Lid. Due to shortage of space at Rishra, the 
Company had to shift the factory at Konnagar. 
Due to non-availability of Terene Yarn, the 
Company finds it difficult to face competition. 
Its products have been gradually accumulating 
and in March 1967 the value of such accumulated 
stock was Rs. 20 lacs and in March 1968 Rs. 80 
lacs. The work of the silk unit is much simple. 
No special silk is required to carry out such work. 
On 1111) October 1967 there was a _ tripartite 
settlement by which the principle of payment of 
bonus to the workmen was settled. The Company 
has been paying wages, dearness allowance and 
other amenities which compare favourably with 
that of other similar concern. The accounts of 
the jute division and of the silk division have 
been mingled together by Hastings Mills Ltd., 
which has been running the division with one 
capital and publishing only one balance-sheet for 
the same. The silk division does not maintain 
or publish any separate balance-sheet. The other 
allegations made by the Union have been con- 
troverted. It has been stated that the 059 
made by the Union are not sustainable. With a 
view to purchasing industrial peace, a_ tripartite 
settlement was arrived at on 4th December 1967 
for referring the matters to a Tribunal. 


A preliminary objection has been raised on 
behalf of the, Company regarding the jurisdiclion 
of the Tribunal to try the 4 issues, viz., the issue 
No, (1) regarding revision of wages, the issue No. 
(3) in respect of leave facilities, the issue No. (6) 
for the night shift allowance and the issue No. (8) 
respecting the bonus. There was a_ previous 
award Ext. B between Shree Ram Silk Mfg. 
Company, Rishra, Hooghly and their workmen 
and an award was passed by agreement between 
the parties on 26th November 1963. After that 
award was passed, no notice was served by the 
workmen or by the Union according to the provi- 
sions of the section 19(6) of the Industrial 
Disputes Act. The section 19(2) of the Act lays 
down that a settlement arrived at between the 
‘parties shall be binding for such period as is 
agreed upon by the parties, and if no such period 
is agreed upon, for a period of six months from 
the date of signing the settlement and it shall 
continue to be binding on the parties after the 
expiry of two months from the date on which a

notice in writing of an intention to terminate the 
settlement is given by one of the parties. So 
it has been argued that the Union cannot raise 
those 4 points for adjudication. Reference has 
also been made to the latest case of Bangalore 
Woollen, Cotton and Silk Mills v. Workmen in 
F.L.R. 1968 (16) 242 S.C. to show that the decision 
of the Supreme Court in the case of the workmen 
of Western Indian Matches Company Ltd. v. 
Western Indian Matches Co. Ltd. in 1965 (5) 
F.L.R. 130 has been distinguished. The Union’s 
reply on this point is that on the decision of the 
Supreme Court in the case of Western Indian 
Matches Company Ltd., the Tribunal can take the 
view (hat though no express notice of termination 
was given by the workmen or the Union to the 
Company according to the provisions of the 
section 19(6) of the Act, still from the conduct of 
the parties it can be safely gathered that by impli- 
cation the terms of the award have been given a 
go-by. 


It is common ground that previously there was 
only one Union, viz., Shree Ram Silk Mfg. 
Mazdoor Union. Subsequently that Union and 
another Union, to-wit, Sree Ram Silk Mfg. Co. 
Workers’ Union, have been looking after the 
interest of the workmen. A reference 10 the 
award Ext. B shows that Shree Ram Silk Mfg. 
Mazdoor Union was a_ party to the _ settlement, 
dated 26th November 1963. It is true that no 
notice of termination of that award, according to 
the provisions of the section 19(6) of the Act, 
was given by the Union to the Company. The 
facts of the case of Bangalore Woollen, Cotton and 
Silk Company, ciled on behalf of the Company, 
are distinguishable. The Memorandum of Settle- 
ment Ext. 10, arrived at between the parties on 
4th VWecember 1967 shows that as a gesture of 
goodwill and in order to maintain industrial 
peace, the Company agreed to pay ad-hoc increase 
in wages of Rs. 5 per month to all workmen from 
15th October 1967. The parties also agreed that 
all the 8 issues under reference would be referred 
for adjudication by the Government. So such 
agreement and especially the grant of such 
increase of pay clearly show that by implication 
there was a termination of the terms of the 
aforesaid award Ext. B by such act and conduct 
of the parties. It may be stated here that it 83 
possible (0 waive a notice under the section 80 
C.P.C. Hence in the circumstances the notice 
contemplated by the section 19(6) of the Act has 
been waived. This preliminary objection is not 
accepted and it is held that though no notice 
under the section 19(6) of the Act was issued, this 
Tribunal can adjudicate upon all the aforesaid 
four issues. 


Then about the common Issue No. 3. It has 
been stated on behalf of the Company that no 
charter of demands was submitted by the Union 
regarding leave facilities. Hence existing leave 
facilities, as incorporated in the award 1:01. B, 
should stand. That award will disclose that each 
workman will get 4 days’ casual leave and 9 days 
festival holidays. 


10 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 2, 1969 


০ 
পা ও সপ বাপ سد‎ 


মস জু 


The Union has submitted the Memorandum of 
Settlement Ext. 4 arrived at between the Alkali & 
Chemical Corporation of India Ltd. and _ their 
workmen to show that by an agreement the festival 
holidays were fixed at 10 in a calendar year. Even 
the award Ext. B (1) filed by the Company regard- 
ing Vinar Co. shows the same thing. There is no 
reason why the similar facilities should not be 
granted to the workmen concerned. It is immaterial 
whether or not they submitted a charter of demands 
to the Company. It seems that the existing festival 
holidays of 9 days only are not adequate. Hence 
this Tribunal finds that henceforth the festival 
holiday will be 10 (ten) in a calendar year. It 
will continue to be decided according to the current 
practice and the 2nd October will be observed as 
one of those festival holidays. 


Issue No, 4 


It has been stated on behalf of the Union that 
the workmen of the jute division get almost free 
quarters, vide the evidence of the P. W. 4 Golam 
Mainuddin, General Secretary of Shree Ram Silk 
Mfg. Company's Workers’ Union. The basic wages 
and the dearness allowance are too low. So it 
cannot be stated that the same includes an element 
of the house rent allowance as well. The Tribunal 
should give direction to the Company to give 
quarters facilities and house rent allowance to the 
workmen at the rate of Rs. 25 (Rupees twenty 
five only) per month. 


The evidence of the O. P. W. 1 Vishen Lal 
Sharma, Office Superintendent of the Company, 
shows that the workmen do not get any quarters. 
But some of the workmen of the jute division get 
such facilities. He has clearly stated that the Com- 
pany is not willing to grant such facilities to the 
silk workmen. 


The case of Patna Electric Supply in 1959(2) 
L..L.J., 366 shows that a scheme of wages properly 
fixed necessarily takes into account house rent 
allowance amongst other relevant factors and the 
house accommodation of industrial labour being the 
primary responsibility of the State, in the present 
economic condition of the industries, it would be 
expedient to impose on the employers, the obliga- 
tions to provide house accommodation for their em- 
ployees. The Vishen Lal Sharma 
says that the Company has not been making any 
profits. Once the facilities for house rent allowance 
are granted, the same would become a condition of 
service. Since the Company is not willing to grant 
such ‘facilities, it cannot be compelled by the 
Tribunal to do so and ask it to grant suth extra 
benefit. Hence it is held that the workmen are not 
entitled to any quarters or house rent allowance from 
the Company. 


Issue No. 5 


It has been stated on behalf of the Union that 
the working hours may be reduced. The state- 


ments made on behalf of the Company are that. 


the workmen work in 3 shifts and none of them

works for more than 48 hours per week which 
consists of 6 working days per workman. The 
P. W. 4 Golam Mainuddin stated that the first 
shift of the Company is from 6 a.m. to 2-30 p.m., 
the next shift from 2-30 p.m. to 11 p.m. and the last 
one from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. He has also 20060 
that the working hours of Alkali Company are from 
6 a.m. to 2 p.m. from 2 p.m. to 10 p.m. and then 
from 10p.m. to 6 a.m. and such are the working 
hours of Keshoram Rayon and Fort William 
Engineering. This has not been challenged in cross- 
examination. The O. P. W. 1 Vishen Lal Sharma 
has indicated in his evidence that the working hours 
of their jute concern are not more than 8 hours per 
shift. So considering the circumstances and 
specially when the shifts are rotated thrice, the 
Tribunal finds that the working hours per shift 
should not exceed (eight) hours. 


Common Issue No. 6 


It has been contended on behalf of the Union 
that the workmen have to work in the night shift 
as well which starts at 11 p.m. and ends at 6 a.m. 
Such night shift work tells upon the health of the work- 
men and hence they should get some allowance for 
such night shift. 


It is common ground that the workmen work in 
3 shifts which are rotated. The case of Bombay 
Port Trust in 1956 (2) L.LJ., 197 1085 been 
ceferred to show that where the night shift is 
worked on rotation, the claim for higher wages for 
work in the night shift is not justified. In the 
instant case, when the shifts are rotated, the work- 
men get facilittes to work in the morning _ shift, 
in the afternoon shift and then in the night shift. 
So it is held that the claim for night shift allowance 
is not justihed. 


Common Issue No. 7 


It has been stated on behalf of the Union that 
the Company has not started any canteen. The 
workmen do not get snacks and food at subsidised 
rates. So the Company should be directed to open 
a canteen straightway and grant canteen allowance 
to the workmen. 


The section 46(1) of the Factories Act shows 
that the State Government may make rules requiring 
that in any specified factory where there are more than 
250 workers, a canteen or canteens shall be main- 
tained by the occupier for the workers’ use. It 
has not been pointed out that any such rules have 
been framed by. the State Government. The 
O. P. W. 1 Vishen Lal Sharma has stated that the 
Company has a contemplation to start a canteen 
and plans are being prepared for the purpose. He 
has added that the Company is not willing to grant 
canteen facilities, readily to the workmen. There 
has not been any agreement between the parties to 
grant such facilities. In the circumstances, it is held 
that the Company cannot be directed to start a 
canteen or give canteen facilities to the workmen.

It has been argued on behalf of the Union that 
the Company has separate accounts, documents, etc., 
for the jute division and the silk division. Instead 
of keeping such accounts separate, only one balance- 
sheet Ext. A/4, was published by the Hastings Mills 
Ltd. for the accounting year ended 1966-67. Since 
the separate accounts were not produced, the 
Tribunal should draw an adverse inference against 
the Company. There is a statement in the balance- 
sheet Ext. A/4 that the circumstances of the jute 
concern are unfavourable while the condition of the 
silk unit is favourable. Unless the accounts are 
separate, no such observation of favourable and 
unfavourable business can be made. The Company 
has deducted a sum of Rs. 24,46,182 on the heading 
of depreciation as per 85 Income Tax and Develop- 
ment Rebate Allowance amounting to Rs. 21,82,945 
and Rs. 2.63,237, respectively. But these deduc- 
tions were made fraudulently for the purpose of 
income tax by lump and not according to the pro- 
visions of Income Tax Act. There is no convinc- 
ing evidence to show that there was actually such 
depreciation on the head of the Income Tax. 
Moreover, the Company’s statement regarding the 
capital expenditure and the revenue is not con- 
vincing. Moreover, the Company 1795 stated in 
the list that the reserved and the proposed dividend 
amount to Rs. 1,42,26,000 and 6 per cent. of the 
same works at Rs. 8,53,560. There is no basis for 
making such calculation and deducting that amount. 
It has been argued that the Tribunal should hold 
that even from the figures supplied by the Com- 
pany, more than Rs. 10,000 should be made avail- 
able and bonus for the year ended March 1967 
should be paid at the rate of 20 per cent. of the 
annual earnings of each workman for 1966-67. 


It has been argued on behalf of the Company 
that the calculations were correctly made accord- 
ing to the provisions of the Payment of Bonus Acct, 
1965. The depreciation was allowed as per cal- 
culation according to the Income Tax Act. The 
Balance-sheets will indicate that there were only 
revenue expenses and not capital expenses. It will 
clearly appear from the list Ext. 1 submitted by the 
Company, which was. prepared by their Chief 
Accountant, O.P.W. 2 Ganesh Das Mundra, that 
the available surplus is minus 10 lacs odd. In 
view of such financial position of the Company 
there is no question of granting bonus at the rate 
asked for by the Union, since there is no available 
surplus. Under the section 10 of the Act, the 
Company is bound to grant the minimum 4 per cent. 
bonus and such bonus has been granted at that 
rate. 


The section 23(1) of the Payment of Bonus Act 
raises a presumption of accuracy of the Balance- 
sheet and Profit and Loss Account of the Com- 
pany. There is a _ proviso ا٢‎ that sub-section 
which says that where the authority concerned is 
satished that the statements and particulars con- 
tained in the Balance-sheet or the Profit and Loss 
Account of the Corporation or the Company are 
not accurate, it may take such steps as it thinks 
necessary to find out the accuracy of such state- 


ments and particulars. 


[Parr IC 


— ae oie 


———SS === 


The Company has put in the _Balance-sheets 
Ext. A/4 for the year 1966-67. The accounts 
were duly audited and then published for Hastings 
Mills, under which both the jute unit and the silk 
are attached. The O.P.W. 2 Ganesh Das Mundra 
has given evidence and he prepared the aforesaid 
list, Ext. I. It appears from his evidence as well 
as from the statements of the O.P.W. 1 Vishen 
Lal Sharma that there are no separate accounts for 
the silk unit. The O.P.W. 2 Ganesh Das Mundra 
has stated that the calculation was made _ by him 
according to the Income Tax Act. Of course the 
reserves have been included in the proposed divi- 
dend. This is permissible when we consider the 
provisions of the section 6(d) of the Payment of 
Bonus Act read with the column 3-and the 
explanation at the end of the Schedule 3. None of 
the P.W’.s. says that the figures given by the Com- 
pany are inaccurate. It has not been shown by the 
Union that any of the figures is incorrect. Hence 
there is no scope for saying that the Tribunal is 
satished that the statements and particulars con- 
tained in the Company’s balance-sheet in question, 
Ext. A/4 are not correct. 


Reference may be made to the case of Pakshmi 
Raja Studios in 21 F.L.R., 109, S.C., at pages 110 
and 111 to show that the question whether two or 
more units or business under the same ownership 
form one industrial unit or more, has to be decided 
by applying the test of financial integrality and find- 
ing out whether there was unity of finance, employ- 
ment and labour. When the owner of a_ business 
embarks on more than one business activity, it is 
for him to decide whether he will get the business 
activities separate or mingle them. If he mangles 
them, all the activities will become one unit and he 
cannot be heard to say that the high prices of one 
business should be disregarded in deciding whether 
there was surplus of profits for award of bonus. In 
that case the owners of a film studio carried on busi- 
ness in production of films and two of their businesses 
were mixed up and there was one capital fund, etc. [1 
was held that the business should be treated as a single 
unit for the purpose of bonus, even though separate 
Profit and Loss Account and Balance-sheet had been 
drawn up for the two businesses and the workmen 
would get bonus if the entire business resulted in 
surplus of profits. 


There is no challenge to the Company's assertions 
that there was only one capital of Hastings Mills in 
regard to. the jute unit and the silk unit. Only one 
Balance-sheet Ext. ۸/4 was prepared in respect of 
various concerns of the parent Company, 12. 
Hastings Mills. When the parent Mills decided to 
mingle up the business and prepared a single Balance- 
sheet for its silk unit and other units, it must be held 
that the business should be treated as a single unit for 
the purpose of bonus and that consequently the work- 
men would get bonus if the entire business results in 
surplus of profits. 


It has already been indicated that the presumption 
raised by the section 23(1) of the Payment of Bonus 
Act stands. The Union has not been able to satisfy 
this Tribunal that the statements contained 17) the 
Balance-sheet Ext. A/4 or in the list of calculation 
Ext. I are incorrect. A copy of the order of income- 
tax assessment Ext. K(1) has also been put in.

According to such order of assessment of income-tax, 
the depreciation has been calculated at Rs. 21,82,945. 
So there is no inaccuracy on that score as well. 


The latest case of Metal Box Company of India 
Ltd. versus their workmen in the Civil Appeals Nos. 
2138 and 2169 of 1965 says that the tax liability has 
to be calculated on the notional amount, worked out 
under section 4(6) and the Schedule 2 of the 
Payment of Bonus Act and such liability is to be 
worked out first by calculating gross profits and 
deducting therefrom the prior charges under the 
section 6 but not the bonus payable to the employees. 
In the circumstances, the submissions made on behalf 
of the Union are not accepted. The section 10 of the 
Payment of Bonus Act says that 4 per cent. is the 
minimum bonus which can be granted. The Company's 
list of calculation Ext. I shows that there was no 
available surplus and hence the prayer made on behalf 
of the Union that the workmen should get bonus at 
the rate of 20 per cent. of the annual earnings of 
each workman for 1966-67, cannot be allowed. 


Common issues Nos. 1 and 2 


These issues have been taken together for the sake 
of convenience. It has been agrued on behalf of the 
Union that the Tribunal should fix a wage structure 
and minimum wages must be paid to each workman. 
The dearness allowance has a direct link with the 
question of rise and fall in the price level. A workman 
gets only Rs. 105 per month at present, whereas the 
evidence of the P.W.1 Shri Arun Sen and the list, 
Exts. 2, 3, 6, 7 and 8 will show that in the Jute 
Textile Industry a workman gets Rs. 138.60 P. as 
the minimum wages per month, in the Cotton Textile 
Industry, Rs. 143.10P. per month and in the Engi- 
neering Industry at Rs. 150.80P. per month, These 
amounts include the dearness allowance as well and 
the dearness allowance formula is gencrally linked up 
with the cost of the living index working at 1939-100. 
In the Alkali Chemical Corporation of India a workman 
gets the minimum wages and the dearness allowance at 
Rs. 237.64P., in the Fort William Engineering Works 
at Rs. 150.80P. in the Hasting Jute Mills at 
Rs. 138.60P. and the Jaya Sree Textile at 
Rs. 143.10P. per month. It will appear from the letter 
Ext. 7 of Shaw Wallace and Company 11)81 the 
minimum dearness allowance of a workman is Rs. 123. 
The letter sent by the Distillery Employees Union, 
Ext. 8, will show that a workman gets a minimum dear- 
ness allowance of Rs. 30 and the pay scale varies from 
Rs. 80 to Rs. 196 for each workman according to their 
classification. It is the case of the Company as well 
that a workman of the jute division of the same parent 
Company, viz., Hastings Mills Ltd., gets Rs. 138.60P. 
as the minimum wages including the dearness allow- 
ance, The evidence of the P.W. 1 Arun Sen, the 
P.W. 2, Jadu Gopal Sen and the P.W. 4 Golam Main- 
uddin will indicate that the industries concerns are 
situate in almost contiguous areas. Even according to 
the Company there are only two alleged similar concerns 
in West Bengal, viz., Calcutta Silk Mfg. Company and 
Vinar Company. No employee of those employees has 
deposed on behalf of the Company. Their account 
books and other documents have not been produced 
cither hy the Company. So the Tribunal is not in a posi- 
lion to judge what is the basic pay and the dearness 
allowance paid hy the alleged similar concerns. At any 
rate, since there are only 3 silk units in West Bengal.

the other two alleged similar concerns cannot furnish 
proper data for arriving at a correct solution on the ques- 
tion of wage structure keeping in view the principle of 
industry-cum-region basis. Since the number of the 
alleged similar concerns is very few, emphasis should 
be made on the region basis and not on the industry 
basis of the ‘“‘industry-cum-region formula”. Refer- 
ence has been made to the case of French Motor Car 
Company in 1963 (6) F.L.R., 80 to show that in 
applying the principle of industry-cum-region, the wage 
prevailing in similar concerns in the same region has 
to be considered. Similar concerns would be in the 
same line of business and it would not be proper to 
compare a small struggling concern with ৪ large 
flourishing concern. At any rate, Shree Ram _ Silk 
Mfg. Company is the most flourishing concern because 
Calcutta Silk Mfg. Company and Vinar Company are 
small struggling Companies. It cannot be considered 
as proper comparable units. The Tribunal should 
frame wage structure for the unskilled, semi-skilled, 
skilled and other categories of workmen of the silk unit 
and fix the dearness allowance at Rs. 100 (Rupees One 
hundred only) per month on the cost of living index 
figure of 400 (1939-100). 


It has been contended on behalf of the Company that 
it has no financial capacity to bear the additional eco- 
nomic burden if by revising the pay structure, the 
Tribunal raises the wages and the amount of dearness 
allowance to be paid to the workers. In 1963, there 
was an agreement on the basis of which the award 
Ext. ا‎ was passed and the wages were revised at 
Rs. 70.20P. In 1966 wages were increased 10 
Rs. 105. Then before the Conciliation Officer, a 
concession was granted by the Company by which an 
ad-hoc increase in wages of Rs. 5 per month to all 
workmen from the 15th October 1967 was granted. 
The Company is not in a position to grant any further 
increasc in the wages because the stock has _ been 
accumulating and the number of working Jooms is 
becoming less, vide the evidence of the O.P.W. 1 
Vishen Lal Sharma. He has 8150 stated that ٤6 
profits are gradually dwindling. 


The evidence of the O.P.W. 1 Vishen Lal Sharma 
shows that the stock is gradually accumulating, ۶ 
number of the working looms becoming less and the 
profits are also gradually dwindling. He has also 
stated that there are two other similar silk concerns in 
West. Bengal and they are Calcutta Silk Mfg. Company 
and Vinar Company and their Company (Shree Ram 
Silk) pays the highest wages to the workmen. This 
stalement stands unchallenged. Moreover, it will be 
pertinent to point out that not a single workman has 
heen examined on behalf of the Union to make any 
contrary statement and assert that the wages and the 
dearness allowance paid to them are not satisfactory. 
The 0.۲۰۳۷, 1 Vishen Lal Sharma has also stated that 
the work of the silk industry is a simplier one since 
the fibre used by them is strong. His evidence in this 
regard also is accepted. 


Reference may be made to the cases of Filmstan in 
1966(1) L.L.J., 744 and Mathura Prasad Srivastava 
v. Saugori Company in 1966(2) L.L.J., 307 at 
page 310 to show that regarding the question of revi- 
sion of wages, the Tribunal has to consider whether the 
financial position of the Company is such that it can 
hear the burden of a further wage increase. The wage 
structure prevailing in comparable concerns has to be 


14 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 2, 1969

a 


considered and the  industry-cum-region principle fol- 
lowed. Let us apply these principles of the facts and 
circumstances of the case. 


It has already been seen that the financial position 
of the Company is not at all good. On 0081 ground 
the Tribunal will reject the claim for revision of wages 
because it is not in a position to bear the financial 
burden if the wages and the dearness allowance be 
increased. 


The awards Exts. B(1) and B(2) will show that 16] 
workers and 500 workers worked in the Vinar Com- 
pany and the Calcutta Silk Company respectively. 


It has already been indicated that the O.P.W. 1 
Vishen Lal Sharma says that their Company pays the 
highest wages to the workmen. The award Ext. B(1) 
regarding the Vinar Company and the other 2 awards, 
Exts. 8/2 and 8/3 of Calcutta Silk Mfg. Co., go in 
favour of the Company. The Balance-sheet Ext. A/4 
for the Company has also confirmed the statements 
that the financial position is not at all sound. Of 
course the Union has put in the statement Ext. 6 of 
Keshoram Rayon to show the rate of wages. But in 
that case such fixation was not by an award of the 
Tribunal, but pursuant to an agreement, vide the evid- 
ence of the P.W. 4 Golam Mainuddin. Moreover it is 
not at all a similar concern. The aforesaid Distillery, 
Engineering, Rayon and Alkali Companies are also not 
similar concerns. Vinar Company and Calcutta Silk 
Mfg. Company are not sick or struggling ones. Since 
they are similar concerns, the wage structure prevail- 
ing therein, has to be considered by this Tribunal on 
the footing ‘Industry’ basis and hence the ‘Region’ 
basis of the principle need not be emphasized. This is 
not a case regarding the clerical and subordinate staff 
of the Company. The wages and the dearness allow- 
ance paid by the Company are not at all insufficient. 
So considering the facts and circumstances of the case, 
the extent of business, the capital investment, the 
simple nature of work, the strength of labour, the 
dividend declared and the financial position of the 
Company, it is held that it is not necessary to revise 
the wage structure and increase the amount of the dear- 
ness allowance.

AWARD 


The Labour Department, Government of West 
Bengal, has referred an industrial dispute between 
Messrs. Calcutta Iron & Engineering Co. (Pvt.) Ltd., 
77 Banaras Road, Howrah, and their workmen 
represented by Calcutta Iron & Engineering Workers’ 
Union, 5 Hazzarimal Shah Road, Salkia, Howrah, 
to this court by its order No. 3816-I.R./IR/10L- 
513/67, dated 25th June 1968, under section 10, 


Industrial Disputes Act, on the following issue: 
Issue 


Is the refusal of employment to Shri Provat 
Kumar Prodhan justified? To what relief, 
if any, is he entitled? 


Usual notices were sent to the parties fixing 7th 
October 1968 for appearance and for filing written 
statement by the Union. The parties did not appear 
on that date. By my order No. 2, dated 7th 
October 1968, the record was put up for orders on 
26th October 1968. The parties were absent even on 
that date. It appears from the record that the 
notice sent to the O. P.-Company was received on 


Part IC]

7th October 1968, but the notice sent to the Secre- 
tary of the Union came back with an endorsement 
“unclaimed”. There is also an endorsement that 
the postman went to the addressee on a number of 
days and informed him of the same, but he did 
not remain present for delivery of the letter. The 
record was put up on this date for orders by my 


order No. 3, dated 26th October 1968. 


The O. P.-Company has appeared on this date 
and has filed a petition intimating that the dispute 
has been settled between the parties out of court and 
the petitioner-workman has received money from the 
©. P.-Company in full and final settlement of all 
his dues, claims and disputes with the O. P.-Company. 
A letter written by the petitioner-workman to the 
©. P.-Company, dated 10th November 1968, stating 
such facts has been made annexure to the O. P.- 
Company’s petition as such. 


On the facts of the case, I am inclined to accept 
that the parties have compromised the dispute 
pending between them. It is true that the Union

“‘no-dispute”” award be passed accordingly.

Procedure regarding tending Manuscripts for publication of Advertisements, 
“Calcutta Gazette” (Part 11). 


1. Manuscripts should be properly edited and complete in itself. 


2. Manuscripts should always be typewritten on one side of the paper. The name of signatory shwuld 
be typewriticn below the cignature. 


4. Manuscripts intended for advertisement in The Calcutta Gazette shall be received by Publication Sales 
Offices at New Secretariat Bulicings, 1 Kiran Sankar Boy Road, Caloutta, up to 3-30 p.m. on Tuesday of 
the previous wevk of the Publication date and at Head Office at Allpore up to 3-30 p.m. on Wadnesday of the 
previous week, 

4. All costs shall be paid in advanve and deposited along with the manusoripts. 


6. Manuscripts and postal remittances shall be addressod to SUPERINTENDENT, GOVERNMENT PRINTING 
(PUBLICATION BRANCH), WEST BENGAL GOVERNMENT PRESS, ALIPORE.

COMPANY APPLICATION No. 349 of 1968 


IN THE HIGH COURT AT CALCUTTA 
Original Jurisdiction 
In the Matter of the Companies Act, 1956 
And 
In the Matter of sections 391 and 393 of the said Act. 
And 


In the Matter of Shree Ambica Jute Mills Ltd., an 
existing company under the Companies Act, 1956, 
having its registered office at No. 5, Clive Row— 
Applicant. 


Notice convening a meeting of unsecured creditors 


NOTICE is hereby given that by an order dated the 10th 
day of December 1968 the Court has directed a meeting 
to be held of the unsecured creditors of the said Company 
abovenamed for the purpose of considering and if thought 
fit approved with or without modification the compromise 
or arrangement proposed to be made between the said 
Company and its said unsecured creditors, 


In pursuance of the said order and as directed therein 
further notice is herby given that a meeting of the said 
Company will be held at 5 Clive Row, Calcutta, on 
Saturday. the Ist of February 1969 at 2-30 o'clock in the 
afternoon ut which time and place the said unsecured 
creditors are requested to attend. 


Copies of the said compromise or arrangement and of 
the statement under section 393 can be had free of 
charge at the registered office of the said Company or at 
the office of its Attorneys Messrs. Charu Chundra Bosu 
at 9 Old Post Office Street, Calcutta. 


Porsons entitled to attend and vote at the meeting may 
vote in person or by proty provided that all proxies in 
the prescribed form are deposited at the registered office 
of the said Company at 5۵ Clive Row, Calcutta, not iess 
than 48 hours before the meeting. 


Forms of proxy can be had at the registered office of 
the said Company. 


The Court has appointed Shri Dipak Basu, Barrister-at 
Law and failing him: Shr Arjya Mitra, Barrister-at-Law, 
as Chairman of the said meeting. 


The abovementioned compromise or arrangement if 
approved by the meeting will be subject to the subs: quent 
approval of the Court. 


Dated this 23rd day of December 1968. 


DIPAK BASU, 
Chairman appointed for the meeting.

ACT V OF 1911 


Calcutta, the 16th December 1968, 


Proposed Public Street No. ۷۱ (Tangra-Topsia 
between Debendra Chandra Dey Road and 
Pulin Khatik Road) 


Notice is hereby given under section 63(2) of 
Bengal 4০৮৬ of 1911 as amended by West Bengal 
Act XXXII of 1955 that the Board of Trustees for 
the Improvement of Calcutta have prepared a plan 
of the proposed public street in ward No. 60 of the 
Corporation of Calcutta, known as Tangra-Topsia 
Alignment No. VI (between Debendra Chandra Dey 
Road and Pulin Khatik Road). 


The plan provides for the opening of a 120 ft. wide 
road to the area lying between Debendra Chandra 
Dey Road and Pulin Khatik Road in continuation 
of Trust's sanctioned Alignment No. V—Manicktala, 
which is again in continuation of Dum Dum Super 


Highway.

New Delhi, the 20th December, 1968 


In exercise of the powerg conferred by section 169 of the Representation 
of the People Act, 1951 (43 of 1951), the Central Government, after consulting 
the Election Commiésion, hereby makes the following rules further to amend 
the Conduct of Ele¢tions Rules, 196], namely:— 


1. Short title and commencement: (1) These rules may be called the 
Conduct of Elections (Third Amendment) Rules, 1968. 


(2) They shall come into force on the 1st January, 1969. 


2. Aendment of rule 11: For rule 11 of the Conduct of Elections Rules, 
1961 (hereinafter referred to as the said Rules), the following rule shall be 
substituted, namely: 


“11. Publication of list of contesting candidates and declaration of 
results in uncontested election: (1) The returning officer shall, immediately 
after its preparation, cause a copy of the list of contesting candidates to be 
affixed jn some conspicuous place in his office and where the number of 
contesting candidates is equal to, or less than, the number of seats to be 
filled, be shall, immediately after such affixation, declare under sub- 
section (2) or, as the’ case may be, sub-section (3) of section 53 the result 
of the election in such one of the Forms 2] to 21B as may be appropriate 
and: send signed copies of the declaration to the appropriate authority, 
the Election Commission and the Chief Electoral Officer. 


(2) If a poll becomes necessary under sub-section (1) of section 53, the 
returning officer shall supply a copy of the list of contesting candidates to 
each such candidate or his election agent, and then shall also publish the 
list in the Official Gazette.”. 


3. Amendment of rule 38: In rule 38 of the said Rules, for sub-rule (1), 
the following sub-rule shall be substituted, namely: 
“(1) Every ballot paper shall, before issue to an elector, be— 


(a) stamped with such distinguishing mark as the Election Commission 
may direct; and 


(b) signed in full on its back by the presiding officer.”,

4. Amendment of rule 46: In rule 46 of the said Rules,— 


(i) in sub-rule (1), for clauses (b) and (c), the following clauses shal be 
substituted, namely: 


“(b) the ballot papers signed in full by the presiding officer under sub- 
rule (1) of rule 38 but not issued to the voters; 


(bb) any other ballot papers not issued to the voters; 


(c) the ballot papers cancelled for violation of voting procedure under 
rule 39; 


(cc) any other cancelled ballot papers;”; 


(ii) for sub-rule (2), the following sub-rule shall be substituted, namely: 


“(2) Each such packet shall be sealed with the seals of the 
presiding officer and with the seals either of the candidate or of 
his election agent or of his polling agent who may be present at 
‘the polling station and may desire to affix his seals thereon.”. 


5. Amendment of rule 53: In rule 53 of the said Rules, in clause (a) of 
sub-rule (1), for the words “such persons”,*the words and brackets “such 
persons (to be known as counting supervisors and counting assistants)’ shall 
be substituted. 


6. Amendment of rule 56: In rule 56 of the said Rules,— 


(i) in clause (h) of sub-rule (2), for the words “the mark”, the words 
“both the mark and the signature” shall be substituted; 


(ii) for sub-rule (7), the following sub-rule shall be substituted, namely: 


“(7) After the counting of all ballot papers contained in all the ballot 
boxes used at a polling station has been completed,— 


(a) the counting supervisor shall fill in and sign Part Il—Result of 
counting, in Form 16 which shall also be signed by the 
returning officer; and 


(b) the returning officer shall make the entries in a result sheet in 
Form 20 and announce the particulars.”. 


7. Amendment of rule 59: In rule 59 of the said Rules, in rule 56A, 
applicable in relation to notified polling stations in lieu of rule 56,— 


(i) in clause (e) of sub-rule (2), for the words “the mark”, the words “both 
the mark and the signature” shall be substituted; 


(ii) for sub-rule (7), the following sub-rule shall be substituted, namely: 


“(7) After the counting of all ballot papers contained in الد‎ the 
ballot boxes used at a polling station has been completed,— 


(a) the counting supervisor shall fill in and sign Part II— 
Result of counting, in Form 16 which shal] aleo be 
signed by the returning officer; and 


(b) the returning officer shall make the entries in a result 
Sheet in Form 20 and announce the particulars.”, 


8. Amendment of rule 64: For rule 64 of the said Rules, the following 
rule shall be substituted, namely: 


“64. Declaration of result of election and return of eleetion: The 
returning officer shall, subject to the provisions of section 65, if and go 
far as they apply to any particular case, then— 


(a) declare in Form 21C or Form 21D, as may be appropriate, the 
candidate to whom the largest number of valid votes has been 
given, to be elected under section 66 and send signed copies 
thereof to the appropriate authority, the Election Commission 
and the Chief Electoral Officer; and 


(b) complete and certify the return of election in Form 215 and send 
signed copies thereof to the Election Commission and the 
Chief Electoral Officer.”.

9. Amendment of rule 70: In rule 70 of the said Rules, for sub-rule (1) 
of rule 384৯, applicable in relation to elections by Assembly Members and in 
Council constituencies in lieu of rule 38, the following sub-rule shall be 
substituted, namely: 


“(1) Every ballot paper shall, before issue to an elector, be— 


(a) stamped with such distinguishing mark as the Election Commission 
may direct; and 


(b) signed in full on its back by the presiding officer.”. 


10. Amendment of rule 84: In rule 84 of the said Rules,— 


u) for the heading “Return by returning officers’, the heading 
“Declaration of result and return by returning officers” shall be 
substituted; 


(ii) for sub-rule (1), the following sub-rule shall be substituted, namely: 


401) Upon the completion of counting, the returning officer 
shall, subject to the provisions of sub-rule (3) of rule 81,~ 


(a) declare the result under section 66 in Form 23 or Form 
23A, as may be appropriate, and send signed copies 
thereof to the appropriate authority, the Election 
Commission and the Chief Electoral Officer; 

(b) prepare and certify a return of the election in Form 23B 
and after reporting the result of the election under 
section 67, send signed copies of the said Form to the 
“ie Commission and the Chief Electoral Officer; 
an 


(c) permit any candidate or his election agent or counting 


agent to take a نو‎ of, or extract from, such return 
in Form 23B. 


(iii) sub-rule (3) shall be omitted. 


11. Amendment of Form 16: In Form 16 of the Forms appended to the 
said Rules,—- 


(i) for the brackets, words and figures ‘(See rule 45)", the brackets, 
words, figures and letter “[See rules 45, 56(7) and 56A(7)]” shall 
be substituted: 


(ii) for item 2, the following item shall be substituted, namely: 


“(2) Ballot papers unused— 
(a) with the signature of the presiding officer, if any; and 
(b) without the signature of the presiding officer.”; 


(iii) for item 4, the following item shall be substituted, namely: 


(4) Ballot papers cancelled— 
(a) for violation of voting procedure under rule 39; and 


(9) for any other reason.”;

No. T. & C.P./141 /1H-28 /67(A).—-7th January 1969.—Whereas the Gov- 
ernor is of opinion that the use and development of land in the area described 
in the Schedule below to which the Calcutta Metropolitan Planning Area (Use 
and Development of Land) Control Act, 1965 (West Ben. Act XIV of 1965), 
applies (hereinafter referred to as the scheduled area), requires to be controlled 
under the said Act with a view to securing its orderly development; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 3 of tha 
Calcutta Metropolitan Planning Area (Use and Development of Land) Control 
Act, 1965 (West Ben. Act XIV of 1965), the Governor is pleased hereby to 
declare the scheduled area to be a controlled area for the purposes of the said 
Act. 


2. A map delineating the scheduled area may be inspected at the office of 
the Controller.

All that portion of the Ultadanga-Maniktala area bounded on the west ۷ا‎ 
the Circular Canal, on the south by the Beliaghata Canal, on the east by the.

“No, T. & C.P./142/1H-28/67(A).—7th January 1969.—In exercise of the 
powers conferred by clause (a) of section 4 of the Calcutta Metropolitan Plan- 
ning Area (Use and Development of Land) Control Act, 1965 (West Bengal 
Act XIV of 1965), the Governor is pleased hereby to issue the following direc- 
tions in relation to the area declared to be a controlled area under this depart- 
ment notification No. T. & C.P./141{1H-28/67(A), dated 7th January 1969, 
published at page 73 of the “Calcutta Gazette, Extraordinary”, ap 7th January 
1969 (hereinafter referred to as the said controlled area), namely: 


Directions 


(1) The parcels of land appertaining to the said controlled area described in 
Schedules I, II and III appended hereinbelow shall be used respectively for' 
industrial, commercial and residential purposes, and the same are referred to 
hereinafter as the industrial, commercial and residential areas respectively. 
Maps delineating the parcels of land described in Schedules I, 11 and 111 may be 
inspected at the office of the Controller. 


(2) For all industrial developments or uses in the industrial area including 
compatible uses therein, previous permission in writing of the Controller shall 
be necessary. 


(3) For all commercial developments or uses in the commercial area and fon 
such compatible uses therein for which Schedule IV appended hereinbelow so 
provides, previous permission in writing of the Controller shall be necessary. 


(4) For all residential developments or uses in the residential area including 
compatible uses therein, except such compatible uses for which Schedule ۷ 
provides otherwise, permission of the Controller shall not be necessary. 


(5) Schedule 1۷ contains a list of compatible and incompatible usés within 
each of the industrial, commercial and residential areas. Subject to the pro- 
visions of paragraphs (2), (3) and (4) above, compatible uses in respect of an 
area shall be permissible within the area. Incompatible uses in respect of an. 
area Shall not be permissible or allowed to take place within the area.
