OFFICE OF THE CONTROLLER: 


[Appointed under the Calcutta Metropolitan Planning Area (Use and 
Development of Land) Control Act, 1965} 


NOTIFICATION 


No. T&CP/143/1H-28/67(A).—7th January 1969.—In exercise of the 
powers conferred by clause (c) of sub-section (2) of section 18 of the Calcutta 
Metropolitan Planning Area (Use and Development of Land) Control Act, 
1965 (West Ben. Act XIV of 1965), the Controller hereby makes, 
with the previous approval of the State Government, the following regula- 
tions in relation to the area declared to be a controlled area under 
Government of West Bengal, Development and Planning Department, notifi- 
cation No. T&CP/141/1H-28/67(A), dated 7th January 1969, published at 
page 73 of the “Calcutta Gazette, Extraordinary”, of 7th January 1969, namely: 


Regulations s 


&, Title—These regulations may be called the Ultadanga-Manicktola 
Area Control Regulations, 1968. 


2. Definitions—({1) Unless the context otherwise requires,— 


(a) “Act” means the Calcutta Méetropolitan Planning Area (Use and 


Development of Land) Control Act, 1965 (West Ben. Act XIV 
of 1965); 


(b) “section” means a section of the Act. 


(2) The terms and expressions used in these regulations but not defined 
shall have the same meaning as in the Act. 


3. Principles for granting permission—({1) For granting permission for 
development and use of land for industrial purposes within an area allocated 
to industrial use, the Controller shall be satisfied that the applicant has 
already obtained a requisite sanction for the establishment of the industry 
applied for, that the proposed industry is not one of those specified as 
incompatible uses for the area, that the proposed layout and development 
of the industry shall not go against or be contrary to the industrial use 
thereof, and that any industry coming up on or near the boundary of such 
area shall not be prejudicial to the adjoining use-areas. 


(2) For granting permission for any development or use of land for com- 
mercial purposes within an area allocated to commercial use, the Controller 
shall see that the proposed commercial use is in accordance with the plan 
for development of the central commercial core. 


(3) For granting permission for any development or use of land com- 
patible with the development and use thereof for residential purposes within 
an area allocated to residential use, the Controller shall see that the proposed 
development or use is not prejudicial to the residential use of the area or 


does not cause any nuisance, discomfort or disturbance to the residents of 
the area. 


M. G. KUTTY, Controller.

No. T&CP/147/1H-28/67(A).—7th January 1969.—In exercise of the powers 
conferred by clauses (b), (d) and (e) of sub-section (2) of section 18 of the 
Calcutta Metropolitan Planning Area (Use and Development of Land) 
Control Act, 1965 (West Ben. Act XIV of 1965), the Controller hereby makes, 
-with ne previous approval of the State Government, the following regulations, 
namely: 


Regulations 


1. Title—These regulations may be called the Calcutta Metropolitan 
Planning Area (Use and Development of Land) Control Regulations, 1968. 


2. Definitions.—(1) Unless the context otherwise requires,— 


(a) “Act” means the Calcutta Metropolitan Planning Area (Use and 
Tbe of Land) Control Act, 1965 (West Ben. Act XIV of 
1965); 


(b) “Appendix” means the Appendix to these regulations; 
(c) “section” means a section of the Act. 


(2) The terms and expressions used in these regulations but not defined 
shall have the same meaning as in the Act. 


3. Form of application for permission.—All applications for permission 
under sub-section (1) of section 8 shall be made in Form ‘A’ as specified in 


the Appendix. 


4. Manner of communication of the grant or refusal of permission.—All 
orders either granting permission subject to any condition or refusing permis- 
sion shall together with the grounds for such grant or refusal be communicated 


to the applicant by registered post. 


5. Procedure for filing and hearing of appeals—Al\l appeals shall be 
preferred in Form ‘B’ as specified in the Appendix. Every petition of appeal 
shall be verified and signed by the appellant or the appellants and shall be 
submitted to the Secretary to the Government of West Bengal, Development. 
and Planning (Town and Country Planning) Department, or the Controller, 
as the case may be. A true copy of every petition of appeal shall also be 
filed along with the original petition of appeal. After an appeal is received, 
a date for hearing the appeal should be fixed and notice thereof should be 
siven to‘ the appellant or appellants as well as to the officer who passed the 
order appealed, against, and such officer shall also be provided with a true copy 


of every petition of appeal. 


On the date fixed for hearing, the appeal shall be heard in the presence of 
such parties thereto as may be present. The authority hearing the appeal may 
take such further evidence, oral and documentary, as it thinks necessary for 
the proper determination of the dispute and may for this purpose summon. 
witnesses and call for documents and records. As soon as may be after an 
appeal is heard the decision shall be communicated to the appellant by 


registered post.

AGREEMENT 


MEMORANDUM OF AGREEMENT made this 
Seventh day of January of One Thousand Nine 
Hundred and Sixty-nine between “Ministry of 
Defence, Directorate of Research and Development 
and Defence Production Organisation Staff Co-opera- 
tive Housing Socicty Limited”, a Society registered 
under the Bengal Co-operative Societies Act, 1940 
(Bengal Act XXI of 1940) and having its registered 
office at Inspectorate of General Stores, East India, 
Hastings, Calcutta-22 (hereinafter called “The 
Company”) of the ONE PART, And the GOVERNOR 
of the State of West Bengal (hereinafter called “The 
Governor”) of the OTHER PART. 


WHEREAS for the purpose of the construction of 
some building or work, the Company has applied to 
the Government of West Bengal for the acquisition 
under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 
1894 (hereinafter referred to as the said “Act”), of 
the piece or parcel of land containing 1.2854 acre or 
thereabout situate in the village of Behala in the 
District of 24-Parganas and more particularly 
described in the Schedule hereto and delineated in 
the plan* hereunto annexed; 


AND WHEREAS the said Government of West 
Bengal (hereinafter referred to as the “Government”) 
upon the advice of the Land Acquisition Committee 
constituted under the rule 3 of the Land Acquisition 
(Companies) Rules (hereinafter referred to as the 
said “[২0105”) and after consideration of the 
Collector’s report under rule 4 of the said Rules and 
being satisfied on the report of the Collector under 
section JA, Sub-section (2), of the said Act, that 
such acquisition is needed for the construction of the 
building or work for the Company which is engaged 


36 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, EXTRAORDINARY, JANUARY 8, 1969 [ParT I 


or is taking steps for engaging itself in a work which 
is for a public purpose, has decided to acquire on 
behalf of the company the piece or parcel of land 
hereinbefore described; 


AND WHEREAS the said Government has 
required the Company under the provisions of 
section 41 of the said Act to enter into the agrce- 
ment with the Governor hereinafter contained. 


Witnesseth that, without prejudice to the generality 
of the provisions of the said Act and the said Rules, 
it is hereby agreed and declared as follows:— 


(i) On demand the Company shall and will pay 
to the said Government all and every 
compensation in respect of the said land 
tendered, paid or awarded or to be tendered, 
paid or awarded by the Collector under the 
said Act or by Court to which a reference 
under part III of the said Act may be made 
or by the Court or Courts to which an 
appeal from the award of the said Court 
may be preferred and all costs, charges and 
expenses of the proceedings in the afore- 
said Courts, or otherwise incidental to the 
proposed acquisition or payable in respect 
"۵ under the provisions of the said 

ct; 


Not printed but may be inspected in the office of 
the Collector, 24-Parganas. 


(ii) On demand made by the’ said Collector, the 
obligation of the Company under the last 
proceeding clause not being thereby limited, 
the Company shall and will deposit with the 
said Collector such sum or sums of money 
as in his discretion the said Collector may 
in anticipation estimate to be necessary for 
the purpose or purposes mentioned in the 
last preceding clause; 


(tii) On payment by the Company of all demands 
under the foregoing first clause or in the 
discretion of the said Government (on 
deposit by the Company of all estimated 
amounts as provided in the second clause) 
but not before possession shall have been 
taken under the provisions of the said Act, 
the Governor shall make over possession of 
the said land to the Company and exccute 
and do all such acts and deeds as may be 


necessary and proper for vesting the same 
in the Company; 


(iv) The Company shall not except with the 
previous sanction of the Government, use 


the land for any purpose other than that 
for which it is acquired; 


(v) The building or work shall be constructed or 
executed within a period not exceeding 
three years from the date of transfer of the 
land to the Company; 


(vi) Where, however, the Government is satisfied 
after such enquiry as it may deem necessary 
that the Company was prevented by the 
reasons beyond its control from erecting, 
providing, constructing or executing any

NOTIFICATIONS 


No. 6998-PL/P6R-21 /66.—1!1th December 1968.— 
In exercise of the power conferred by the proviso 
to Article 309 of the Constitution of India, the 
Governor is pleased hereby to make the following 
rules regulating the recruitment to the post of 
Police Prosecutors, Calcutta, under the Home 
(Police) Department, Government of West Bengal, 
namely:—— 

Rules 

1. Short title and commencement.—(]) ‘These 
rules may be called the Rules for the Recruitment 
of Police Prosecutors, Calcutta. 

(2) They shall come into force with effect from 
the date of publication of these rules in the Official 
Gazette. 

2. Method cf Recruitment. -Appointment to the 
posts shall be made by selection (direct recruitment). 
The appointing authority shall be the State 
Goevrnment.

3. Qualification and Experience—A _ candidate 
shall be a graduate in Law and shall have at least 
five years’ experience at the Bar. 


4. Age,—A candidate shall not be more than 40 
years of age on the first day of January of the year 
of recruitment. The limit being relaxable in the 
case of a specially qualified and experienced 
candidate. 


5. Scale of pay.—The scale of pay shall be 
Rs. 300—30—900 with a higher initial starting at 
Rs. 450 (efficiency bar after 8th and 16th stages). 


6. Probation and confirmation,—A candidate on 
appointment shall be on probation for a period of 
two 50215 during which he shall be liable to be dis- 
charged if found unsuitable, On successful comple- 
tion of the probationary period a candidate shall 
be confirmed. 


7. Status——A Police Prosecutor, Calcutta, shall 
have the status of a Gazetted Officer, 


8. Control.—Subject to the over-all control of 
the State Government in the Home (Police) Depart- 
ment a Police Prosecutor, Calcutta, shall be under 
the immediate contro] of the Commissioner of Police, 
Calcutta, who may delegate in writing the power of 
control to any Deputy Commissioner of Police, 
Calcutta.

Planning Cell 


RESOLUTION 


No. 798-P.C.—9th December 1968.—The Governor 
is pleased to re-constitute the Fodder and Grazing 
Committee at State level, constituted in Resolution 
No. 6838-A.H., dated 18th October 1962, for effective 
utilisation of available feed and fodder resources 
and for obtaining increased production through intro- 
duction of better varieties of crops, etc., with the 
following personnel: 


Chairman 


(1) Member, Board of Revenue and Sccretary, 
Land and Land Revenue Department. 


Members 


(2) Secretary, Animal Husbandry and Veterinary 
Services Department. 


(3) Director of Land Records and Surveys. 


(4) Chief Engineer-l, Irrigation and Waterways 
Directorate. 


(5) Chief Conservator of Forests. 
(6) Director of Agriculture. 
(7) Director of Panchayats. 


Member-Secretary 
(8) Director of Animal Husbandry. 


2. The functions of the above Committee will be 
the following: 


(1) to watch the progress of feed and fodder 
Development Schemes; 


(2) to consider various measures that may be 
adopted for fuller utilisation of the available 
fodder and feed resources, forest grazing and 
their improvement; 


(3) to suggest measures that may ০০ taken in 
increasing feed and fodder resources through 
better land utilisation, use of better varie- 
ties of crops, fertilisers, irrigation facilities, 
etc. 


(4) to suggest methods for conservation of 
grasses available in the interior forest areas 
and their utilisation during deficit periods; 


(5) to consider the question of village grazing 
areas, their improvement and control; 


(6) to consider cropping practices in different 
regions in the State and to suggest suitable 
cropping rotations for some fodder crops, 
leguminous and non-leguminous, with a 
view to improving the fertility of soil and 
also increased milk production; 


(7) to watch the progress of action taken by the 
Committee formed in Resolution No. 7228, 
dated the 23rd July 1968, with the specific 
object of recommending cropping sequences 
and fertiliser policies for different areas in 
West Bengal in relation to the cultivation 
of fodder, of assessing the requirement of 
secds and fertilisers and devising ways and 
means of raising and/or procuring these 
materials; 


(8) any other relevant matters that may be 
referred to. 


Part I] 


ee و‎ ee 
a, eee ee oe 


Tbe Committee will meet at least once a quarter 
to review the progress made with regard to the func- 
tions of the Committee. 


The Committee may co-opt additional members 
including specialists on various subjects and _ the 
District Magistrates whenever special circumstances 
will require it. 

Order 


Ordered that the Resolution be published in the 
“Calcutta Gazette’ and copies thereof forwarded to 
the Chairman and other Members of the Committee. 


Ordered also that copies of the Resolution be 
forwarded to the other departments of this Govern- 
ment, Commissioners of Division, the District Magis- 
trates and Deputy Commissioners. 


By order of the Governor, 
A. K. SEN, Secy.

the West Bengal General Service.

Qualifications: I. Essential—(1) A degree of a 
recognised University, (ii) Three years’ ex- 
perience of accounts work in a Government 
office or a Statutory Body or a commercial 
concern of repute. 


Desirable.—(i) Experience in conducting‏ .ا1

Stantive appointment under Government.

Qualifications: I. Essential—{i) A degree of a 
recognised University, (ii) Three years’ expe- 
rience in a responsible capacity in a Govern- 
ment office or a Statutory Body or a commer- 
cial concern of repute. 


II. Desirable—({i) Knowledge of Bengali— 
spoken and written, (ii) Experience in handling

products. 


Age: Not more than 35 years on the Ist July of

ANNEXURE 


In the matter of an industrial dispute existing be- 
tween Messrs. Associated Electronics, 10) 
Princep Street, Caleutta-13, and their work- 
man, Shri Chandra Deo Singh, represented 
by Messrs. Calcutta Motor Workers’ Union, 
19/24 Pitambar Ghatak Lane, Calcutta-27. 
(Case No. 240 of 1968.) 


BEFORE THE FIFTH INDUSTRIAL 
TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL. 


Present : 


Shri T. K. MUTSUDDI, Judge, 
Fifth Industrial Tribunal. 


Present for the Union: 911 Hiralal Roy, 


Advocate. 
Present for the Company: None. 


By the Government of West Bengal, Labour 
Department, order No. 4942-1.R./IR/10L-91/68, 
dated the 15th July 1968, this industrial dispute 
between Messrs. Associated Electronics and their 
workman, Shri Chandra Deo Singh, represented by 
the Calcutta Motor Workers’ Union was referred to 
this Tribunal under section 10 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act for adjudication. The issue for ad- 
judication was as follows :— 


Issue 


Whether the termination of service of Shri 
Chandra Deo Singh, Driver, is justified? To 
what relief, if any, is he entitled? 


The case of Chandra Deo Singh, at whose ins- 
lance the reference has been made, is as follows :— 


Shri Chandra Deo Singh was in the service of the 
Company for about 4 years. On 14th August 
1967 he wrote a letter to the Company নিলা 
overtime allowance, leave facilities, bonus, uniform, 
washing charges, etc. The Company sent a reply 
to this letter but his demands were not fulfilled. 


18 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 9, 1969 


TE cee ny Raa 


کھ ےجس علیہ ھ ہے শপ‏ 


Then at the instance of Shri Singh the Union wrote 
a letter to the Company demanding overtime allow- 
ance, etc. The Company thereafter terminated the 
services of Shri Chandra Deo Singh on the 12th 
September 1967 without assigning any reason what- 
soever. It is alleged by the petitioner that the Com- 
pany acted mala fide and against the principles of 
natural justice in dismissing him from service. The 
petitioner, therefore, prays for reinstatement and all 
back wages. 


On receipt of notice the Joint Receivers of the 
Company authorised Shri Anil Nag, Advocate, to 
represent them in this case. But no written statement 
was filed on behalf of the Company though several 
adjournments were granted by the Tribunal suo 
motu. Ultimately on 28th November 1968 1176 


case was taken up for ex parte hearing. 


Ext. 4 is the letter by which the Company termi- 
nated the services of Shri Chandra Deo Singh. 
This notice is dated the 12th September 1967. By 
this notice the services of Shri Singh were terminated 
with effect from the 13th October 1967. It appears 
that the Company did not assign any reason for 
terminating the services of Shri Chandra Deo Singh. 
It further appears that Shri Singh sent a letter to 
the Company making some demands regarding over- 
time allowance, leave facilities, etc. Ext. 1 is that 
letter. It is seen that on 29th August 1967 the 


Union also wrote a letter to the Company making . 


similar demands. The notice of termination of ser- 
vice is dated the 12th September 1967. It is clear 
that the Company terminated the services of Shri 
Chandra Deo Singh immediately on receipt of the 
letter from the Union. There is not a shadow of 
doubt that the Company acted mala fide and that 
it acted against the principles of natural justice. 
Shri Singh was dismissed from service for no fault 
of his own. He was dismissed simply because of 
the fact that he made some demands to the Com- 
pany through the Union. It is thus clear that thie 
termination of services of Shri Chandra Deo Singh 
by the Company was very very unjustihed. It is 
a case of victimisation and unfair labour practice on 
the part of the Company. 


It is, therefore, directed that the Company should 
reinstate Shri Chandra Deo Singh to his former 
post of employment and pay him all his back wages 
within one month from the date of publication of 
the uward in the ‘Calcutta Gazette”, 


Dictated and corrected by me. 


T. K. MUTSUDDI, 
Judge.

T. K. MUTSUDDI, Judge,

Issue 


Whether termination of services of Sarbasree 
ndu  Bhusan’ Bhattacharjee, رام( مادنا‎ 
Puresh Ch. Banerjee, han, Hari- 
ram Kahar and Anadi Goswami is justified? 
To what relief, if any, are they entitled? 


Usual notices were sent to the parties directing 
them to appear on 24th October 1967 and_ the

Union to file its written statement by that date. The 
O.P.-Company filed a petition praying for exten- 
sion of time for appearance. he Union was 
absent on that date. By my order No. 2, dated

November 1967 for filing written statement by the 


Union. The Union took time for filing written 
statement on that date and ultimately filed its

Company took time for filing written statement on 
two occasions and ultimately filed its written state-

hearing on 27th April 1968. After a few adjourn-

September 1968, when one witness was examined 
on behalf of the Union. At this stage the O. P.- 
Company filed a petition for amending the typogra- 
phical errors in its written statement, which was 
allowed and the case was fixed on 23rd October 
1968 for hearing. This date being declared a 
local holiday, the case was fixed on 6th November 
1968 for hearing by my order No. 15, dated 06 
October 1968/24th October 1968. On that date 
the parties prayed for an adjournment on_ the 
ground of compromise and by my order No. 16, 
dated 6th November 1968, the case was fixed on this 
date for compromise, in default, for hearing. 


The parties have filed a joint petition of compro- 
mise stating the terms of scttlement between the 
parties .entered into and also praying for passing 
an award on the basis of the abovesaid settlement 
as such. The petition is under the signature of

Company and Shri Shib Nath Chatterjee, Organis- 
ing Secretary of the Union and also bears the 
signatures of the Advocates of both the parties. 


On a perusal of the terms of settlement contained 
in the joint petition of compromise, I find these 
to be Jawful, reasonable and fair and that the parties 
have compromised the entire dispute pending be- 
tween them, Under the circumstances, ١ am _ in- 
clined to pass a ‘no-dispute’ award on the basis of 
the joint petition of compromise. A ‘no-dispute’ 
award be passed accordingly, which be made a 
part of this award. 


This is my award.

The Government of West Bengal, Labour Depart- 
ment, by its order No. 129-I.R./IR/10L-58/66, dated 
the 11th January 1968, referred this 10000517181 
dispute between Messrs. Remington Rand of India 
Ltd., 493-C G. T. Road (South), Ramkrishtapur, 
Howrah (hereinafter referred to as the Company), 
and their workman Shri Kashinath Dutta, 6 Madhu 
Gupta Lane, Calcutta-12, to this Tribunal under sec- 
tion 10 read with section 2A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, for adjudication on the following issue : 


Issue 


Whether the termination of service of Shri Kashi- 
nath Dutta is justified ? To what relief, if 
any, he is entitled ? 


After service of notices both the parties appeared 
and filed their written statements. 


The case of the concerned workman as made out in 
his written statement is that he is a permanent work- 
man of the Company since 1961, drawing a monthly 
salary of Rs, 125. He suddenly fell ill on 19th July 
1964, and had been undergoing treatment under the 
Employees State Insurance Corporation being affected 
by Tuberculosis. The Employees State Insurance 
Doctor advised him to take complete’ rest and to 
undergo treatments, and he immediately informed 
about it to the Company on the same day. During 
his illness he duly informed the Company from time to 
time regarding his condition of health and also gave 
reasons for not reporting for duty. It 19 the 
grievance of the workman concerned that during the 
period of his treatment his services were illegally and 
wrongfully terminated by the Company with utter dis- 
regard to the fact that he was then undergoing treat- 
ment under the Employees State Insurance Corpora- 
tion. It is his further complaint that such action of 
the Company is illegal, mala fide and ultra vires, and 
that his services have been terminated by violating the 
principles of natural justice and with a motive of 
victimisation. 


The Company has stated in their written statement 
that they were not at all aware if Kashinath Dutta 
fell ill on 19th July 1964, or was undergoing treat- 
ment under the Employees State Insurance Corpora- 
tion, as alleged. The Company did not receive any 
application for leave on medical ground or any medi- 
cal certificate from him since 20th July 1964, till his 
services were terminated with effect from 19th January 
1965. The Company submits that since 19th July 
1964, the whereabouts of Shri Datta were neither 
known nor reported to the Company till the termina- 
tion of his service in spite of the Company's best 
efforts to trace his whereabouts, which will appear 
from the Company’s letters, dated 24th August 1964 
and 12th November 1964. Shri Datta did not send 
any leave application or medical certificate to the 
Company prior 00 his termination of service ; but 
subsequently he sent several medical certificates from 
various medical chambers after his services were ter- 
minated by the Company's letter, dated 19th January 
1965. The Company submits that according to the 
standing orders of the Company absence without per- 
mission for a period not exceeding 8 consecutive days 
is a major misdemeanour which warrants dismissal 
and that as Shri Datta absented himself for about six 
months without permission, the Company had no other 
alternative but to dismiss him from service with effect 
from 19th January 1965. 


Part IC] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 9, 1969 21 
ডা পা সুর ১ এ اص ہج‎ 


After several adjournments on the prayers of the 
parties, including two for effective compromise, the 
case was fixed for hearing on 14th November 1968. 
On that day the workman filed an application for ad- 
journment supported by a medical certificate while his 
lawyer informed the Tribunal that he had withdrawn 
his representation in this case. In these circumstances 
the case was adjourned to 4th December 1968, for 
hearing. Qn 4th December 1968, the workman did not 
appear but an application for adjournment supported 
by a medical certificate was filed on his behalf along 
with a fresh letter of authority. But none appeared to 
move this application even up to 8 p.m. _ By his petition, 
dated 4th December 1968, the workman has prayed 
for time to file objection; but there is 70 scope for 
filing objection in this stage. I am also not inclined to 
rely on the medical certificate filed along with the said 
application. Jt appears to me that this prayer for ad- 
journment made on behalf of the workman is only a 
dévice to delay the matter. In these circumstances, the 
prayer for adjournment was refused, and the case was 
taken up for ex parte hearing. 


The Company has examined its 1১615017186] Manager, 
Shri Bimal Kumar Chakraborty (P.W. 1), who has 
deposed that Kashinath Dutta, the concerned workman, 
remained absent from duty since 10th July 1964, with- 
out any intimation to the Company, that as the workman 
was absent from duty, he, on behalf of the Company, 
wrote a letter to him on 24th August 1964 (Ext. A) 
and on 12th November 1964, he wrote another letter 
to him (Ext. A/1), that as the said workman did not 
reply to those letters and continued to remain absent 
from duty, the Company dismissed him from service by 
a letter, dated 10th January 1965 (Ext. B), and that 
the workman was dismissed from service for major mis- 
demeanour under section J(2) (vi) of the Standing 
Orders of the Company (Ext. C). The concerned 
workman has not been able to file a single scrap of 
paper to show that he ever informed the Company re- 
garding his alleged illness since 19th July 1964, or 
prayed for leave on medical ground or an any ground 
whatsoever. There is no dispute regarding the fact that 
he was absent from duty since ۱۹۲] July 1964 till the 
date of his dismissal. Letters, Ext. A and Ext. 1۰/ھ‎ 
indicate that the Company wrote these two letters to 
the workman on 24th August 1964 and 12th November 
1964, respectively, asking him to report for duty within 
four days and explain his unauthorised absence to the 
management. By the letter, Ext. ۸/۱۰ dated 12th Nov- 
emher 1964, the Company clearly informed the work- 
man that if he failed to explain his absence to the 
management within the stipulated time then his service 
would summarily dispensed with. There is nothing on 
record to show that the concerned workman replied to 
any of these two letters, Ext. A and Ext. ۸/1. In these 
circumstances I am inclined to believe the Company's 
case that Kashinath Dutta, the concerned workman, 
clid not send any intimation leave application or medi- 
cal certificate to the Company prior to his termiation of 
service on January 19, 1965. By the letter of dismis- 
sal, Ext. B, dated 19th January 1965, the management 
treated him as having left the service of the Company 
on his own as the workman’ concerned was absenting 
from 20th July 1964, till date. Under section J (2) (vi) 
of the Standing Orders of the Company, Ext. C, a work- 
man is liable to dismissal for major misdemeanour, 
viz.. habitual absence without permission, or absence 
without permission not exceeding eight consecutive days. 
In the instant case the concerned workman was absent 
from duty for about six months without permission of 


শশী ee লি 


the Company from 20th July 1964, till January 19, 
1965, when the letter of dismissal was issued. The 
order of dismissal passed by the Company is thus in 
conformity with the Standing Orders of the Company. 
P.W. 1 has stated that after the letter of dismissal was 
issued on January 19, 1965, the workman sent seven 
receipts of Employees State Insurance Corporation to 
the Company which were collectively marked Ext. D. 
One of these receipts bearing serial No. B-134777 alone 
covers the entire period of absence of the concerned 
workman, viz., from 19th July 1964 till Sth February 
1965. No reliance can be placed on this receipt as it 
neither bears any date nor is in conformity with the 
rules inasmuch as the period mentioned in this receipt 
٠ 5805 more than four weeks. ‘his receipt again was 
not sent to the Company prior to the issue of the letter 
of dismissal. 


On the materials in the record and in view of what I 
have slated above. 1 therefore hold that the termination 
of service of Kashinath Dutta, the concerned workman, 
is justified, and that he is not entitled to any relief.

AWARD 


The Governor, by Government of West Bengal, 
Labour Department, order No. 2711-1.R./TR/10L-191/ 
67, dated the 2151 June 1967, was pleased to refer an 
industrial dispute between Messrs. Champion Neon 
Signs and Satal Engineering Works, 16 British Indian 
Street, Calcutta-1 (hereinafter called the Company) 
and their workmen represented by Champion Neon 
Signs and Satal Engineering Works Mazdoor Sabha, 
19/2A Pitambar Ghatak Lane, Calcutta-27, (herein- 
after called the Union), for adjudication to 11113 
Industrial Tribunal. The industrial dispute aforesaid 
centered on the following issues :— 


Issues, 


Grades and Scales of Pay.‏ .ا 

2. Dearness Allowance. 

3. Leave and Holiday (Festival). 
4, Gratuity. 


On receipt of the order of reference, this Tribunal 
registered a case on Ist July 1967 and issued notices 
to the parties fixing 8th August 1967 for their appear- 
ance and filing of written statement by the Union. On 
8th August 1967 the Union filed a petition praying for 
15 days’ time to file its written statement. Shri J. R. 
Jain appeared for the Company, but time being 
granted the Union filed its written statement, a copy 
of which was made over to the Company. The Com- 
pany was then called upon to file its written statement 
which it did on 23rd September 1967. Thereafter, 
various dates were fixed and the case passed through 
usual preparatory stages leading to the peremptory 
hearing. The Tribunal then fixed 25th July 1968 for 


hearing of the case. On 25th July 1968 Shri H. سأ‎ 


Roy, Advocate, appeared for the Union and Shri J. R. 
Jain, Labour Adviser of the Company, appeared for 
the Company. The parties filed a joint petition pray- 
ing for adjournment on the ground that a_ talk 01 
settlement was going on between the parties. After 
hearing both the sides, the prayer for time was granted 
and 9th September 1968 was fixed for hearing of the 
case in case a compromise could not be effected. On 
90) September 1968 Shri S. N. Roy Choudhury, Presi- 
dent, appeared for the Union and Sbri J. R. Jain, 
Labour Adviser, appeared for the Company. They filed 
a joint petition of compromise which bears the signature 
of Shri Kamal Kumar Soi for the Company and of 
Shri S. N. Roy Choudhury, President of the Union, 
for the Union. In the petition the parties have prayed 
that the Tribun§l should be pleased to accept the terms 
of compromise as fair and reasonable and pass an 
award in terms thereof.

have perused the terms of compromise set out in‏ ا

AWARD 


The Government of West Bengal, Labour 
Department, by its order No. 7238-I.R./IR/11L- 
448/68, dated the 25th September 1968 referred to 
this ccurt under section 10 read with 2A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), an 
industrial dispute relating to the undermentioned 
issue existing between Messrs. Sehgal Brothers, 20 
Ganesh Chandra Avenue, Calcutta-13, and_ their 
workman Shri B. B. Sarker, 41/1/2 Biren Roy Road 
(West), Calcutta-8, for adjudication. 


Issue 
Whether the termination of service of Shri ظط‎ 


B. Sarker is justified? To what relief, if 
any, is he entitled? 


Notices of this proceeding were duly issued to 
the parties concerned directing them to appear 
before this court on 28th October 1968. The Com- 
pany, it appears, refused to accept the said notice 
and did not attend court on the date fixed, i.e., 28th 
October 1968. It also did not attend court and 
take any step whatever in connection with this 
reference, thereafter on the several dates fixed in 
the case. he worker concerned, however, was 
present on 28th October 1968 and he was directed 
to file his written statement by 11th November 1968. 
The written statement, however, was not filed by 
the worker concerned as directed within the time 
fixed and he did not care to take any step whatever 
in copuection with this reference, thereafter on the 
several dates fixed. In such circumstance, | am 
incline 1 to think that the parties are no longer in- 
teresterl in the reference and that the dispute under 
‘eference is no longer in existence. | accordingly 
pass a ‘No-dispute’ award. The instant reference 
is accordingly disposed of.

After receipt of the order of reference, usual 
notices were served on the parties and they duly 
appeared before this Tribunal and filed their separate 
written statements. After several stages, the case 
was fixed on 20th September 1968 for hearing. On 
that day (20th September 1968) on prayer of the 
Company, the case was adjourned till today for 
hearing. Today (6th December 1968) the Company 
as well as the workmen mentioned in serial Nos. 5, 
6, 8, 10 and 13 of the order of reference along 
with other employees of the Company, have filed 
the joint petition stating that the issues have been 
settled mutually on the basis of the acceptance of 
service period by the Company authorities. One of 
the workmen mentioned in the order of reference, 
being Shri A. K. Bhattacharjee (serial No. 5 
deposed before me. According to him, the workmen 
of serial No. 1 is dead and the workmen mentioned 
in serial Nos. 2, 3, 4, 7, 9, 11 and 12 as above, 
have all left the Company since the receipt of the 
order of reference. Excepting Shri Bhattacharjee 
(P.W. 1) the workmen mentioned in serial Nos. 6, 8, 
10 and 13 are present before me today 6th December 
1968. I have heard these workmen in person. 
have perused the terms of settlement which appears 
to be fair, reasonable and lawful and I accept the 
same. 


Accordingly, I pass a compromise award, in terms 
of the settlement filed by the parties, which do form 
part of the award and Annexure “A”.

With regard to the housing accommodation 
the Company denies the allegation to the effect 
that there has been any discrimination. It is 
submitted that none of the issues referred 10 
[6101০ this Tribunal is maintainable. That the 
claims made by the Union are _ frivolous and 


vexatious and amount to abuse of the process of 
law. 


I first take up the issue No. 1 which read as 
follows :—Categorisation of the clerks and 
revision of wages, grades and scales of pay. 


The Company raised a preliminary point and 
the matter was heard on 27th September 1968. 
On that day it was ordered “The preliminary ob- 
jection raised by the Company with regard to 
issue No. 1 is however kept open”. The same 
preliminary point has again been taken by the 
Company and argument has been made by the 
learned Advocate Mr. C. L. Ganguli. Mr. Gan- 
guli submits that the present reference is not 
maintainable inasmuch as the issue No. 1 has al- 
ready been settled by different awards and 09০1- 
sions of the Wage Boards and by a tripartite 
seltlement. It is stated that there were awards in 
1948 and 1958. Then there was report of the 
Wage Board in 1959. Then there was tripar- 
tite settlement in 1961 and the report of the 
Second Wage Board is expected to be published 
at any moment. Thus as the existing awards 
and settlement have not been terminated as yet 
the issue No. 1 cannot again be decided by this 
Tribunal. In this connection it is also submit- 
ted that the Union is acting upon the awards 
and sctilement by enjoying benefits. So they 
cannot raise any dispute so long the awards and 
the settlement have not been terminated. Mr. 1). ہا‎ 
Sen Gupta, Advocate, appearing for the Union, 
submits that the existing awards and settlement 
have all been terminated as a Charter of Demands 
was placed by the Union on 29th July 1966. In 
the said Charter of Demands the workers claimed 
revision of grades and scales of pay and catego- 
risation of clerks. Mr. Ganguli contends that the 
said Charter of Demands cannot terminate the 
existing awards and settlement as in the said 
Charter of Demands it has not been stated that 
the awards and settlement have been terminated. 
Mr. Sen Gupta, on the other hand, submits that 
it is not at all necessary to state specifically that 
the awards, settlements have been terminated. 
The awards and settlement will be deemed to 
have been terminated as soon as & Charter of 
Demands is placed. Mr. Ganguli refers to a 
decision reported in 1964-1, LL.J. p.100 (Cochin 
States Power, Light Corporation Ltd. and Its 
workmen). It has been held in this case by 
their Lordships of the Supreme Court—"After 
the expiry of the period of settlement by efflux 
of time, the union submitted a charter of de- 
mands. In the Charter of Demands it was stated 
that the union had resolved to terminate the 
settlement and submit the present demands. 
There was specific statement made therein that 
the settlement was being terminated thereby. In 
the circumstances, it must be held that there was 
sufficient notice as required under section 19(2) of 
the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and hence the

حم شر سس سے جم وو oe‏

tlement must be held valid. There = نایا‎ 
prescribed for terminating settlement under 
section 19(2) of the Act and 911] that has 
to be scen 19 whether the provisions 01 
section 19(2) are complied with and in sub- 
stance a notice is given as required thereunder.” 
"In the case, before their Lordships it was not 
specifically mentioned in so many words that 
the settlement was being terminated thereby. 
Their Lordships were of opinion that the Charter 
of Demands itself showed that the Union termi- 
nated the existing settlement and thereafter sub- 
mitted a charter of demands to the appellant, and 
so in their Lordships’ opinion sufficient notice to 
the appellant in substantial compliance with the 
provisions of section 19(2) was given.” 


The Charter of Demands is Ext. A. In item 
No. 2 under the heading categorisation of clerks 
and revision of grades and scales of pay of Ext. 
A, the Charter of Demands, the Union ventilates 
its dissatisfaction with the existing classification 
of clerks and claims different grades and scales 
of pay for the clerks. Amongst the demands 
that were made in Ext. A three issues including 
issue No 1 has been referred to this Tribunal. In 
the present Charter of Demands Ext. A there is 
no mention that the Union has terminated the 
previous awards and settlements. But relying 
on the observations of their Lordships in the 
cases referred to above I am of opinion that 
placing of Charter of Demands is sufficient to in- 
dicate termination of the award of settlement. Mr. 
Ganguli also refers to another decision reported 
in 1968-1, LLJ. 555 (Bangalore Woollen, Cotton 
and Silk Mills Company, Ltd. and Their work- 
men and another). In this case it was held— 
‘Intimation regarding the termination of an 
award must be fixed with reference to a particu- 
lar date so as to enable a Court to come to the 
conclusion that the party giving that intimation 
has expressed its intention to terminate the 
award. Such a certainty regarding date is abso- 
lutely essential, because the period of two months 
after the expiry of which the award will 0 
to be binding on the parties will have to be 
reckoned, from the date of such clear intimation. 
The facts of the case referred to above are com- 
pletely different from the facts of the present 
case and the observations of their Lordships 
referred to above do not apply to this case. 


The decisions cited by Mr. Ganguli therefore do 
not help him. I am of the opinion that issue No. 
1 is quite maintainable and this Tribunal has jJuris- 
diction to enter into the merits with regard to 
issue No 1. 


One of the main demands of the Union with 
regard to issue No, 1 is that the Company ~ has 
given appointment to some clerical staff by giving 
them a special name as “weekly paid checker 
though they are made to perform clerical job 
and in fact they are doing all clerical jobs of a 
full-fledged clerk by such appointment denying 
them the benefit of permanent f ull-fledged clerks,

Considering all the facts of the case I am of

clean meaning of issue No. 1. I am of opinion 
that issue No. 1 empowers this Tribunal only to 
calegorise the existing clerks of the Company. 
This Tribunal therefore cannot give any relief 
to these persons.

Adniittedly that has not been done. It is the

is nv necessity of classifying the clerks as senior

the Mill numbering about 150 do the same kind

Second Industrial Tribunal. 


By order No. 4728-1.R./IR/7L-36/67, dated Calcutta, 
the 18th September 1967, Government of West Bengal, 
Labour Department, referred an_ industrial dispute 
between Messrs. Northbrook Jute Co. Ltd. and their 
workmen represented by Hooghly Zillah Chatkal 
Mazdoor Union, for adjudication on the following : 


Issues 
% 


1. Is the supersession of Shri Shewnath Singh in 
the matter of promotion to the post of a 
Havilder justified ? To what relief, if any, 
is he entitled? 


2. Is the closure of 150 broad looms with effect 
from 8th May 1967, justified ? To what 
relief, if any, are the workmen entitled ? 


After service of usual notices parties entered appear- 
ances and filed their written statements. 


Appearances of the parties are as follows :— 
For the Company: Shri S. C. Sen, Advocate. 


For the Union; 
the Union. 


Shri Phani Ghosh, representative of 


I propose to discuss the cases of the respective parties 
issuewise. Issue No. 1 is taken up for consideration. 


Issue No. 1: 


The Union's case is that Shew Nath Singh, Durwan 
of Northbrook Jute Mills, had been superseded by a 
much junior hand although there was no charge of 
inefficiency against Shew Nath Singh who was decidedly 
the seniormost and had officiated as Havilder and, in 
doing so, the Company apparently resorted to unfair 
labour practice in refusing the claim of Shew Nath 
Singh. The supersession of Shew Nath Singh being 
thus mala fide and vindictive, he is entitled to be pro- 
moted to the post of Havilder with retrospective effect. 
The Union therefore prayed for an award directing 
the Company to promote Shew Nath Singh to the post 
of Havilder with retrospective effect. 


The Company’s case, in short, is that the security 
staff of the group of jute mills, commonly known as 
Jute Mill of Bird and Heilgers, are appointed in a 
common pool and they are posted to individual mills 
with fiberty to be transferred from one mill to another 

lonying to this group. Such security staff of the 
mills are generally divided into four categories with 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 9, 1969 33 


> পপ EGE 


different rates of wages. Hirearchy of such staff is as 
follows: — 


(1) Jamadar, 
(2) Havilder, 
(3) Line Durwan and 
(4) Durwan. 


It is stated that in Northbrook Jute Mills out of the 
two permanent Havilders, one post fall vacant when 
Tukaram Sattam resigned on 17th December 1965. 
Following the prevalent custom and practice some of 
the Durwans and the line Durwans were put on trial 
for the purpose of finally selecting one out of them 
for the post in question. On completion of the trial 
the manager of the mill sent his report in respect of 
the four persons placed on trial. The said report has 
been دا اھ‎ Annexure ‘A’ to the written statement filed 
by the Company. It appears from that report that in 
the Manager's opinion Probhunath Singh and Ram 
Balak Singh out of the four Durwans were found fit for 
the post of permanent Havilder. The Security Officer 
then requested the manager of the mill to put both these 
persons for a further trial to enable him to make the 
final selection and upon such second trial or re-trial 
the management decided to appoint Ram _ Balak 
Singh, the line Durwan as the permanent Havilder but 
in yiew of the fact that in the meantime dispute had 
already been raised, the management allowed Ram 
Balak Singh to work as the Havilder in the permanent 
vacancy without filling up the post permanently. 
Company’s case is that though Ram Balak is junior in 
service to Shew Nath Singh he was found more efficient 
for the post in question and in fact he was already at 
the material time in a rank higher to that of Shew Nath 
Singh and drawing higher salary as well. In the 
circumstances since the question of promotion to a 
higher rank was the management function and the 
selection was made upon such trial and re-trial in a 
bona fide manner the management's decision in this 
regard should not be interferred with by the Tribunal 
when there was no mala fide on the part of the manage- 
ment. The management further denied that this selec- 
tion either amounted to any supersession ora mala fide 
one. 


Shew Nath Singh examined himself as P.W. 1. He 
tried to maintain in his cross examination that the 
Durwan and the line Durwan were at per on the question 
of pay but he had to admit during cross-examination 
that a line Durwan gets Rs. 2 and odd paise as allow- 
ance and such allowances are treated as included in 
the basic pay. There was, therefore, an apparent 
admission on his part that the line Durwan Ram Balak 
Singh was getting at the material time higher wages 
than what Shew Nath was getting. In the hierarchy of 
the security staff line Durwan Ram Balak Singh was 
placed in a rank higher to that of Shew Nath Singh. 
We have it from the evidence of O.P.W. 1, Security 
Officer Shibaji Roy. Exts. A, B and C would show how 
on consideration of seniority-cum-efficiency four Dur- 
wans were placed on trial and out of them Probhunath 
and Ram Balak Singh were placed on re-trial for final 
selection and we have it from the evidence of O.P.W. 1, 
that Ram Balak Singh was eventually selected for the 
post of Havilder caused by the resignation of Tukaram 
Sattam. Shri Ghosh for the Union argued that when 
there was no rule to put anybody on trial or re-trial 
for the purpose of selection to the higher post, the 
Company should have adopted the rule of universal 
application and selected the seniormost man Shew Nath 


54 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 9, 1969 


গাও ভার. 9 পট 


Singh as the Havilder and not having done that it 
would be an instance of unfair labour practice. In 
support of his above conclusion he relied upon the 
case reported in 1961 (1) L.L.J., at page 686. The 
facts of that case were however altogether different 
and distinguishable as such. There the Labour Court 
found that the superseded employees were not only 
senior but were also better qualified for the promotions 
and it further found that they have been deprived of 
the said promotions because they belonged to a particular 
Union. As such on grounds of unmerited promotions 
and partialities towards one set of workers, it was held 
by the Labour Court that it was an instance of unfair 
labour practice. In the case before us the management 
placed four persons including Shew Nath Singh on 
trial. Two persons were selected for re-trial and finally 
Ram Balak Singh was selected for the post of Havilder. 
Ram Balak Singh being apparently senior in rank or 
hierarchy of the security staff and also drawing higher 
wages, the selection could not be properly described as 
a case of supersession. In any event, no mala fide of 
the management could be imputed in this regard, for 
less victmisation of Shew Nath Singh. Shri Ghosh 
then contended that the service record of Shew Nath 
Singh had not been taken into consideration. The 
management very fairly placed the service record 
before me and I found therefrom that Shew Nath Singh 
had a warning for being careless and inalert while on 
duty on 22nd April 1953. He had a second warning 
for gross neglect of duty on 10th March 1964 and 
finally charge-sheeted on 4th July 1968 for disorderly 
behaviour. The statement made by Shri Shew* Nath 
Singh, P.W. 1, in cross examination in denial of the 
suggestion about being warned on 24th April 1953 and 
10th March 1964 was apparently made tu suppress the 
real facts and Shew Nath Singh was clearly exposed by 
the service record produced by the management before 
this Tribunal for consideration. 


The decision reported in 1957 (II) L.L.J., at page 
559 re-affirmed the position decided in Uttar Pradesh 
Electric Supply case (1952, L.A.C. 346) where it was 
decided that promotion did not depend on the length 
of service only. Other factors, such as efficiency and 
educational qualifications should also be taken into con- 
sideration. The above decision further reaffirmed the 
decision in Assam Oil Company case reported in 1954, 
L.A.C., 543 where it was held that the Tribunals will 
not interfere in matters of promotions unless the power 
has been improperly exercised by the management 
Same view was taken in Brooke Bond's case reported 
in 1966 (I) L.L.J. at page 402. It was held that 
promotion was a management function and only there 
might be occasions for interference where it is felt that 
persons superseded had been so superseded on account 
of mala fides or victimisation. 


Viewing the question before us in the light of facts, 
circumstances and the decisions mentioned above, the 
Tribunal has no hesitation to hold that there was no 
question of any interference with the management 
function when there was no evidence, of mala fides or 
victimisation. In the above view of the matter this 
Tribunal holds that there was really no supersession of 
Shew Nath Singh and the word “‘supersession” used in 
the order of reference was in a sense misconceived. In 
any event even if it be construed as a case of super-: 
sessior, it was fully justified and as such Shew Nath 
Singh is not entitled to any relief. This disposes, issue 
No. 1 


(Parr IC 


Issue No, 2: 


The Union's case is that as a result of the closure of 
150 broad looms with effect from 8th May 1967 about 
650 workers were rendered unemployed in different 
departments and sections, most of whom were members 
of the provident fund and thus became quali- 
fied for lay-off benefits when as a matter of fact 
failure of the Company to employ this number 
of workmen by reason of the recession of orders was 
not covered by section 2 (kkk) of the Industrial Disputes 
Act and when no notice under section 9A of the Indus- 
trial Disputes Act had been given to such workmen 
rendered unemployed. In the circumstances the Union 
submitted that the closure of the 150 broad looms 
resulting in unemployment of 650 workmen was illegal 
and mala fide and the workmen rendered idle are 
therefore entitled to full wages for the period of 
closure. The Union accordingly prayed for an award 
directing the Company to pay full wages to the workers 
for the period they were rendered idle on account of 
the illegal and unjustified closure of 150 broad looms. 


The Company's case is that out of the 195 broad 
looms installed, 192 were in working condition at the 
material time. The closure of 150 broad looms was 
decided after a thorough discussion in the Works Com- 
mittee Meeting and the reasons for such closure had 
heen fully apprised to the members of the Works 
Committee. The decision taken in that Works Commit- 
tec Meeting was maintained and no permanent work- 
men was affected by the closure and the Company 
tried to provide them alternative jobs to the casual 
workers who had been affected and who were members 
of the Provident Fund. Company’s positive case on 
this issue is that the workers who are affected by the 
closure of the looms in question were either Badlee or 
casual workers. The closure being bona fide such 
casual workers were not entitled to any relief. The 
Union's prayer in this regard should therefore be 
rejected. 


The Union examined P.W. 2, Mahabir Prosad, on 
the question in issue. The Company examined its 
Labour and Welfare Officer, Protul Ch. Banerjee, O.P. 
W. 2. We have it from their evidence that the persons 
employed in the broad looms comprised both permanent 
and casual workers. P.W. 2 Mahabir Prosad, who 
happened also to be the Secretary of Hooghly Zilla 
Chatkal Mazdoor Union and Joint Secretary of the 
Works Committee tried hard to maintain that these 
casual workers were working continuously in the mill 
for 5 or 6 years, In  cross-examination he however 
admitted that the date of termination is recorded in Ext. 
G for casual workers. He again admitted that workers 
other than Weavers may have a change in the nature 
of their work and in that contingency cards like Ext. G 
are issued to them. Cards like Ext. G will also be 
issued to casual workers who may have occasion to 
work in broad loom in place of a permanent weaver. 
All this would plainly indicate that the element of con- 
linuity in service was absent in the case of such casual 
workers who are taken in because of their past experi- 
ence for a limited duration and fresh cards like the one 
Ext. G is issued to such workers. Apparently therefore 
such workers cannot corhe within the purview of the 
definition of continuous service as laid down in section 
258 of the Industrial Disputes Act and such workmen 
would have no right for any lay-off compensation under 
section 290 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The 
Union in its written statement, paragraph 8, stated that 


Part IC] 


FOS RS EES TT 
হস 


the looms closed on 8th May 1967 were gradually re- 
opened by the middle of August 1967, ie., within a 
little over three months from the date of the alleged 
closure and full complement of looms were run. In 
other words, there was really no closure under the ordi- 
nary connotation of the said term. It was only so done 
for curtailing production. The written statement filed 
by the Union will further show that justification of the 
closure had never been assailed ; only its legality had 
been challenged on certain grounds such as non-service 
of notice under section 9A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act and non-payment of lay-off benefits. As indicated 
above, the casual workers who had principally been 
affected were such as were not entitled to any lay-off 
compensation under section 25C of the Industrial 
Disputes Act. Section 9A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, also cannot be attracted to the instant case by 
reason of the fourth sechedule to the Industrial 
Disputes Act. 


As observed already, justification of the alleged 
closure for a limited period had not been challenged or 
assailed. Ext. D is the proceeding of the Works Com- 
mittee meeting held on 5th May 1967. The reasons of 
the closure had been indicated therein and there was a 
discussion over the question and the suggestions made 
by the members of the Works Committee had also been 
recorded there and the management assured that no 
permanent workmen would be affected and that the 
casual workers who would be affccted and who were 
also members of the provident fund would be provided 
with alternative employment and as it appears from the 


evidence of O.P.W. 2, the management had actually . 


provided alternative employment to many of the affect- 
ed workers and O.P.W. 2, placed before this Tribunal 
a list of 272 workmen who had been given alternative 
employment between 8th May 1967 to 31st August 
1967. In deciding on the question of justifiability of 
the closure, the question of good faith must be deter- 
mined first and this in turn would largely depend on 
finances of the Company, on the adverse effect that re- 
tention would have on the business and whether reten- 
tion would mean the dead-weight of an uneconomic 
surplus 2170 so-forth. Since it was a_ closure for a 
limited duration and the looms closed had within a 
period of little over three months been re-opened and 
even during this interim period quite a large number of 
the casual workers who had been affected were provided 
with alternative jobs, this Tribunal must hold that the 
closure of 150 broad looms, 50 in each shift, with effect 
from 8th May 1967, was justified. 


The question then arises as to whether the Badlee or 
casual workers who had been affected would still be 
entitled to any benefit during the period they remained 
unemployed. The position of Badlee or casual workers 
was elaborately discussed in the case reported in 1953, 
(11) L.L.J. page 512. There it was clearly held that 
Badlee or casual workers were not Company's workmen 
on the muster rolls and that they had no right to get 
pay or allowance during the period of their unemploy- 
ment. This is so because they are taken on purely 
temporary basis on account of their past experience and 
even under the explanation to section 25C they would 
have no right to claim lay-off compensation when there 
was nothing to show that any of the workers who is a 
member of the provident fund, has his name in the 
muster: roll of the Company. As to the above categori- 
sation of the workers into permanent and casual, we 
have before us the Wage Board recommendation, Ext. 
H. In view of the nature of the specific issue raised in 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 9, 1969 35 


re rn ৯ টস পত্র পল পা পপ 
- ee ہے نمو‎ 


a 


the order of reference, there is no scope for contending 
that the cadre of permanent workers had not been fixed 
with reference to the recommendation of the Wage 
Board Ext. H. Being so and the evidence being that no 
permanent workmen had been affected by the closure, 
all the rest of the workers who had been affected by it, 
must be casual workers and in fact P.W. 2, Mahabir 
Prosad and O.P.W. 2, Protul Chandra Banerjee, also 
affirmed that position. Merely because all the workers 
affected were members of the Provident Fund, they 
cannot elevate them to the status of permanent workers. 
Section 25B of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 read 
with rule 10(1) of the Provident Fund Rules and 
Standing Orders of the mill Company, Ext. E, would 
bear it out. It would further show that there was the 
element of continuity of service in one while it was 
absent in the other. 


In view of what has been indicated above the casual 
workers who had been affected by the alleged closure 
which has been held to be justified would not have any 
benefit under the Industrial Disputes Act, more when 
the closure was a bona fide one and was justified. The 
Tribunal has therefore no hesitation to hold that the 
closure of 150 broad looms with effect from 8th May 
1967 was justified and the workers, to be more precise, 
the Badlees or casual workers who had been affected by 
the closure are not entitled to any relief whatsoever. 


I have given my anxious consideration to the cases 
of the respective parties under different issues and have 
given my adjudication thereon. They will constitute 
my award on such issues.

I then take up Issue No. 1, regarding scales of 
pay, for adjudication. 


Admittedly since 1961 the present scales of 
wages or pay are in existence of the Company. 
Such scales have been described by me _ while 
starting the Union's case in their written state- 
ment. The Union's claim regarding these scales 
of pay have also been stated by me above. 101 
the clerical staff the Union's claim is that there 
should be two scales and for other employees, the 
Union's claim has been stated above. Introduc- 
tion of a new wage structure is to be dealt with 
keeping in mind three primary factors. First, we 
are to decide whether the prevailing wages, rates 
and scales of pay would be required to be changed 
and increased. for this purpose the rule is that 
if the existing wages, rates and scales were fixed 
many years ago and there has been material rise 
in the cost of living in the region, primarily a case 
for increase exists and new wage structure with 
enhanced rates and scales must be determined. 
Similarly, a case for increase in the wage of the 
workmen in any establishment must be deemed 
to exist if the rates and scales of wages in that 
establishment are much lower than the rates and 
scales prevailing in other establishments in the 
same industry in the same region. 


Lastly, we are to be satisfied about the financial 
capacity of the employer to bear the burden of 
the increase in the wage arising from the proposed 
enhancement of the wage structure. Satisfaction 
of the Tribunal about the employer's — financial 


position to bear the additional burden is a condi-, 


tion precedent to the effecting of any upward 
trend in the existing wage structure at the time 
of dealing with the question of fair wage. A case 
for revision of the wage structure merely exists 
from the wage scale when the wage scale re- 
mained most static and unaltered for a long

period of years during which the cost of livin 

has considerably increased. Two important Bib 
vant factors are to be kept in mind when fixing a 
wage structure for incremental wage of sale 

These are (1) the financial capacity of the emplo : 
er to bear the additional burden imposed by the

concerns in the region. In dealing with such a 
problem conflicting considerations, which have 
been reconciled, arise such as, the need to do jus-

city of the employer to bear the burden, wages 
paid in) comparable concerns, ete., under the 
present conditions of the country. A living wage 
is only a dream for the future.

AWARD 


This case arises out of a reference made by the 
Governor of West Bengal under Government of West 
Bengal, Labour Department. order No. 2599-1.R./IR/ 
8L-7 (B)/67, dated the 16th June 1967, in regard to 
an industrial dispute between Messrs. The Bangashri 
Cotton Mills Ltd., P.O. Sukchar, district 24-Parganas 
(hereinafter called the Company), and their workman 
Shri Biswanath Tewari, C/o. Shri N..D. Shrimani, 
Elias Road, Agarpara, P.O. Kamarhati, 24-Parganas. 


The Governor was pleased to refer this dispute to 
this Tribunal in exercise of the powers conferred by 
section 10 read with section 2A of the Industrial Dis- 
putes Act, 1947. 


The issue on which the dispute centred on was— 
whether the termination of service of Shri Biswanath 
Tewari was justified 7 To what relief, if any, was he 
entitled? 


On receipt of the order of reference this case was 
registered on Ist July 1967 and usual notices were 
issned to the parties in dispute fixing 7th August 1967 
for appearance and filing of written statement by the

workman. The _ notice issued to the workman was 
received back unserved with the postal remark ‘not

acknowledgment regarding the notice issued 10 the 
workman was received by the office of the Tribunal. 
In fact the notice itself came back with the postal

Bengal Industrial Disputes Rules, 1958, the Tribunal 
can submit an award on the footing that the industrial 
dispute under reference is no longer in existence. 


Hence holding that the industrial dispute under 
reference is no longer in existence I hereby submit this 
report to the State Government for necessary action. 


This is my award.

Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, by 
ws order No. 6068-I.R./IR/15L-13/67, dated the 2191 
November 1967, referred an industrial dispute between 
Messrs. Ashoka 011 Industries, and their workmen, re- 
presented by North Calcutta Oil Mill Gach Cutta 
Mazdoor Union, to this Tribunal for adjudication on 


the following : 


Issue 


Whether the termination of Sarbasree Kashi 
Mahato, Hariram Koiri, Dhari Ahir, Dalsinger 
Harijan, Banshi Harijan, Baljit Ram Harijan, 
Kalipada Das, Anta Jesswara, Rupan Harijan. 
Phirtoo Harijan, Siddeswar Sadhu Khan, Nanda 
Harijan, Paban Harijan and Badri Narayan 
Singh is justified ? To what relief, if any, are 
they entitled ? 


After service of usual notices the Union entered 
appearance and filed written statement. Thereafter the 
Company filed a petition signed by eight of the fourteen 
concerned workmen under the reference whereunder 
those eight workmen had settled their case with the 
Company out of Court in full and final settlement of 


Part IC] 
a ESE کے‎ 


all claims including the claim for reinstatement and had 
further alleged that they had no further or other claims 
against the Company under the order of reference or 
otherwise. Signed receipts evidencing payment to those 
eight workmen were also affixed to the said petition 
and they prayed for disposing their case by passing a 
‘no-dispute’ award. The Company did not however 
file any written statement. So the case was set down 
for ex-parte hearing as respect of other workmen con- 
cerned under the reference. On the date of ex-parte 
hearing the General Secretary of the Union filed a 
yetition stating that the Union would not proceed with 
the case in respect of Kashi Mahato, Hariram Koiri, 
Baljit Ram Harijan and Paban Harijan and would only 
proceed with the case in respect of Siddheswar Sadhu 
Khan and Badri Narayan Singh. The result is that the 
dispute concerning Kashi Mahato, Hariram Koiri, 
Baljit Ram Harijan and Paban Harijan must be held 
to have ceased to exist and a ‘no-dispute’ award 
should be passed in their case as well. 


As observed already, the case was taken up for ex- 
parte hearing so far as Siddheswar Sadhu Khan and 
Badri Narayan Singh were concerned. In the written 
statement filed the Union set up a case for reinstate- 
ment on the ground that the closure was only a pretence 
and the employer closed down the mill by notice, dated 
30th June 1967, only to victimise the workmen and it 
was further alleged that the employer had not paid any 
compensation or wages in lieu of notice period. 
During trial, however, both these workmen, namely, 
Siddheswar Sadhu Khan and Badri Narayan Singh 
examined themselves to accept the closure and the con- 
sequent retrenchment and they laid their claim only for 
money value of the benefits to which they were entitled 
under the statute. 


Retrenchment following closure being thus accepted, 
the only question that could arise for decision by this 
Tribunal is as to the relief which these two workmen 
would be entitled under the statute. Since the Act was 
amended in 1957 and new section 25FFF was inserted, 
the effect of all previous decisions 1951 their force and 
the effect of the new section is that though the close- 
down is not retrenchment, termination of service as a 
result of the closure of the undertaking is brought once 
again at a par with retrenchment—the language 
heing “close down for any reason whatso- 
ever’. By virtue of the new section 25FFF the work- 
men whose services had been terminated, would be 
entitled to notice pay and compensation in accordance 
with the provisions of section 25F, as if they had been 
retrenched. Under section 25F of the Industrial Dis- 
putes Act, 19-17, as amended, such workmen would be 
entitled to one month's notice ا‎ writing or must be 
paid in lieu of such notice wages for the said period 
together with compensation at the rate of 15 days’ 
average pay for every completed year of continuous 
service or any part thereof in excess of six months. 


Difficulty however arises in making computations of 
such notice pay and the compensation because of the 
absence of any statement in the written statement con- 
cerning the wages of the workmen concerned to the 
knowledge of the employer. The two workmen con- 
cernd only spoke about their length of service and the 
pay which they were getting before the closure here 
before this Tribunal and the Tribunal has no data to 
have them verified. Their statement in this regard can- 
not evidently be accepted as uncontroverted since the 
employer had no opportunity to know from the copy of

— Pa RS সহ AE nr mp eel সস 


the written statement served upon it. In such a contin- 
gency it is desirable that the two workmen concerned, 
namely, Siddheswar Sadhu Khan and Badri Narayan 
Singh should be awarded a lump sum compensation on 
such closure of the business as an equitable relief, more 
when they cannot take recourse to the provisions laid 
down in section 33 of the Act inasmuch as section 33 
of the Act will not be attracted to their termination of 
service upon closure of the establishment or under- 
taking. As many as eight other workmen concerned 
under the reference have settled out of Court their 
dispute with the employer Company by cach of them 
receiving Rs. 40 from the employer Company, In 
view of the difficulties pointed out above this Tribunal 
feels inclined to award compensation 10 each of 
Sidcheswar Sadhu Khan and Badri Narayan Singh at 
the same rate of Rs. 40 when the two concerned work- 
men had not been able to satisfy this Tribunal by docu- 
meniery ev.cence regarding the length of their service 
and their wages at the date of closure. 


The result is that there should be an award in favour 
of the two workmen, namely, Siddheswar Sadhu Khan 
and Badri Narayan Singh and in respect of the other 
workmen under the order of reference there should be 
a ‘no-dispute’ award as eight of them had settled their 
disputes with the employer out of Court and had filed 
an application praying for a ‘no-dispute’ award in their 
case and the Union gave up the cases for the remaining 
four other workmen. This Tribunal accordingly passes 
a ‘no-dispute’ award in respect of the following work- 
men, namely, Kashi Mahato, Hariram Koiri, Dhari 
Ahir, Dalsinger Harijan, Banshi Harijan, Baljit Ram 
Harijan, Kalipada Das, Anta Jesswara, Rupan Harijan, 
Phirtoo Harijan, Nanda Harijan and Paban Harijan, 
named in the order of reference and passes an award 
on the following terms in favour of only two workmen, 
Siddheswar Sadhu Khan and Badri Narayan Singh, 
each of whom will get a lump compensation to the tune 
of Rs. 40 from the employer Company for their termi- 
nation of service following the admitted closure. 


This is the award of the. Tribunal which will come 
into effect on the expiry of 30 days from the date of 
publication of the award in the “Calcutta Gazette.”

In the matter of an industrial dispute between

Second Industrial Tribunal. 


By order No. 5950-I.R./IR/8L-16/66, dated Cal- 
cutta, the 12th August 1968, Government of West 
Bengal, Labour Department, referred an_ industrial 
dispute between Messrs. Central Cotton Mills Ltd., 
and their workmen, represented by Central Cotton 
Mills Workmen’s Union, to this Tribunal for ad- 


judication on the following : 


Issue 


What should be the quantum of bonus for the 
accounting year 1966-67? 


Upon receipt of the reference notices were issued 
to the parties for their appearances. The Union 
entered appearance on 4th September 1968 and 
prayed for time to file written statement. The case 
was adjourned to 26th September 1968 for the 
purpose but on that date the Union did neither file 
the written statement nor showed any sufficient case. 
The Tribunal suo motu adjourned the case to 26th 
October 1968 but even on that date no written 
statement was filed by the Union nor any sufficient 
cause was shown by the Union. The Tribunal suo 
inotu. allowed time till 29th November 1968 for 
the purpose but even on that date the Union did 
neither show any sufficient cause nor file any 
written statement. The Tribunal then passed orders 
to wait till 11th December 1968 for the purpose. 
When inspite of repeated opportunities given to the 
Union no written statement was filed and no suffi- 
cient cause was shown, this Tribunal goresumes that 
the Union was no longer interested in the reference. 
As such due to the absence of both parties the 
Tribunal reserved a ‘no-dispute’ award.

Explanatory notes.—Regarding the amendments 
made, the following code letters have been used to 
indicate the manner in which the particulars of a

PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION, WEST BENGAL 


General information relating to age ooncession, fixation of 
initial pay, etc., in respect of posts advertised by the 
Commission and instructions to candidates applying la 
response thereto. 


General concession in age 


vl) (a) For political suflerers: A candidate who before 
15th August 1947 was detained, imprisoned, interned or 
externed on account of his/her activities in connection with 
the country’s etruggle for independence, not being convict- 
ed of an offence indicating moral turpitude, shall be entitled 
to a concession in respect of the upper age limit. Tha 
concession granted will be equal to the exact perivd of 
detention, imprisonment, interment or externment suffered 
up to a maximum of four years. 


(b) For Scheduled 08519171199 cadidates: The upper 
age limit is relaxable by five years for candidates belonging 
to Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes. 


(c) For Displaced Persons: The upper age limit is 
relaxable up to 45 years for displaced persons who have 
وا‎ a to India from East Pakistan on or after January 
1. 1964. ‘The concession in age shail remain in force up to 
December 31, 1967.

Fixation of Pay 


(2) (a) For persons already in permanent Governmen, 
service: If a permanent Government servant is permitted 
to apply and is selected for a post in open competition with 
outsiders, the initial pay will be fixed under rule 42 or بن‎ 
of the West Bengal Service Rules, Part 1, as the case may 
be. If, however, such a recruit is prepared to resign hy 
appointment under Government, before applying, he will be 
eligible to the grant of higher initial pay on the same basis 
as an outsider. 


(b) For a temporary Government servant having no lien 
on any post under the West Bengal Government when 
appointed to a post carrying higher scale of pay: Such 
an officer shall be eligible to draw as initial pay at the 
stage of the time-scale in the higher post which is equa 
to his pay in the lower post, or if there is no such stage 
the stage next below that pay plus personal pay equal & 
the difference, to be absorbed in future increments in the 
higher scale provided that he has alrendy rendered at least 
three years’ continuous and satisfactory service in the 
lower post. The aforesaid benefit of fixation of pay will 
not however, be available in the following cases: 


(i) when the Commission has made a specifie recom: 
নি regarding the pay to be allowed to the 
thicer ; 


(ii) when under anv specific rule such an officer is 
allowed a higher initial pay. 


(c) For outsiders: Unless otherwise specified in 1 
particular advertisement, higher initial pay on the basis of 
age, qualifications and experience (including experience out 
nide Government service) raay be allowed to a person not 
already in Government service, if the relevant advertise 
ment contains a provision to that effect 


instructions regarding submission of application 


(3) Applications are to be made on the prescribed fori 
which will be available from the office of the Public Service 
Commission, West Bengal, Anderson House (ground floor) 
Alipore, Calentta-27, personally or on sending a large self 
addressed envelope with stamps sufficient to cover the post 
age affixed to it Oandidates who are unable to obtain 
copies of the prescribed form may apply on any similar, 
typed (not handwritten) form showing exactly the working 
and spacing of the sample form published in the “Calcutta 
Gazette” of the lst September 1955, provided the blanks 
are filled up in the candidates’ own handwniting. 


Particulars and certificates required 


(4) Candidates should furnish evidence of their age 
qualifications and previous experience together with ء٥‎ 
ficates written not more than one year prior to the date 
of their applications, from responsible persons, testifying 
to their private character. 


The Commission accepts only the age of a candidate # 
recorded in the Matriculation or the Secondary Schoo! 
Final/Leaving Certificate. In the case of a female cand. 
date whose age is not recorded in the Matriculation of 
School Final Certificate, any of the following evidence of 
age is accepted by the Commission: 


(1) A certificate from the Headmistress of the School 
which she last attended, showing her exact age 4! 
recorded in the school register. 


(2) An affidavit regarding her age sworn by her father 
or mother or some other person in a position 
know by having been present or heard of her birth 
at the time of occurrence. 


(3) A certificate regarding her age, from a Member ot 
the Legislature or a gazetted officer, who must 
have known the candidate and her family, indicat 
ing clearly the evidence on the basis of which 
he/she satisfied himse]f/herself on the point.

of Trust’s sanctioned Alignment No. V—Manicktala,
