BURDWAN. — No.  496-L.A./5C-35/64. — 8th 
January 1969.—The following agreement is published 
under section 42 of the Land Acquisition Act, I of 
1894, for general information: 


AGREEMENT 


MEMORANDUM or AGREEMENT made this 
Eighth day of January of the One Thousand Nine 
Hundred and Sixty-nine between The Aluminium 
Corporation of India Ltd. a company registered under 
Indian Companies Act, 1913 and having its registered 
office at 7, Council House Street, Calcutta-1 (herein- 
after called “The Company” of the ONE PART, And 
the GOVERNOR for the State of West Bengal 
(hereinafter called “The Governor’’) of the OTHER 
PART. 


WHEREAS for the purpose of extension of the said 
Company and construction of labour quarters and 
other amenities connected therewith the Company has 
applied to the Government of West Bengal for the 
acquisition under the provisions of the Land 
Acquisition Act, 1894 (hereinafter referred to as the 
said “Act”), of the piece or parcel of land containing 
37.705 acre or thereabout situate in the village of 
Banali in the district of Burdwan and more particu- 
larly described in the schedule hereto and delineated 
in the plan* hereunto annexed; 


*Not printed but may be inspected in the office of the 
Collector, Burdwan. 


AND WHEREAS the said Government of West 
Bengal (hereinafter referred to as the “Government”) 
upon the advice of the Land Acquisition Committee 
constituted under rule 3 of the Land Acquisition 
(Companies) Rules (hereinafter referred to as the said 
“Rules”) and after consideration of the Collector's 
report under rule 4 of the said Rules and being satis- 
fied on the report of the Collector under section SA, 
sub-section (2), of the said Act, 


(a) that the purpose of the acquisition is to obtain 
land for the erection of dwelling houses for 
workmen employed by the Company or for 
provision of amenities directly connected 
therewith; and 


(b) that such acquisition is needed for the cons- 
truction of the building or work for 1116 
Company which is engaged or is taking steps 
for engaging itself in an industry or work 
which is for a public purpose; 


has given its consent to acquire on behalf of the Com-

cribed; 


AND WHEREAS the said Government has 16- 
quired the Company under the provisions of section 41 
of the said Act to enter into the agreement with the 
Governor hereinafter contained. 


Witnesseth that, without prejudice to the generality 
of the provisions of the said Act and the said Rules, 
it is hereby agreed and declared as follows:— 


(i) On demand the Company shall and will pay to 
the said Government all and every compon- 
sation in respect of the said land tendered, 
paid or awarded or to be tendered, paid or

(Department of Food) 


NOTIFICATION 
New Delhi, the 12th December 1968. 


G.S.R. 2181/Ess.Com./Sugar—In exercise of the powers conferred by 
sub-section (3C) of section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 (10 of 
1955), the Central Government hereby determines the price specified in 
column (2) of Schedule I hereto annexed, as the price payable for the Indian 
Sugar Standard (ISS) D-29 grade of sugar packed in twill new gunny 0885 
and produced in 1968-69 by all vacuum pan sugar factories situated in the 
zone specified in the corresponding entry in column (1) of the said Schedule, 
that is to say, the factories specified in Schedule III hereto annexed and 
required to be sold by the Central Government under clause (f) of sub- 
section (2) of section 3 of the said Act: 


Provided that the price differentials for various grades of sugar higher or 
lower than the ISS D-29 grade shall be as shown in Schedule II hereto annexed: 


Provided further that where a sugar factory is situated at a distance 
exceeding 5 kilometres from the nearest railway station or an out-agency of 
the railway or from the godowns outside the factory not connected by rail, 
the producer may charge an additional one paisa per quintal of sugar per kilo- 
metre beyond 5 kilometres of the distance between the sugar factory and such 
railway station or out-agency of the railway, in case of despatches by rail or 
between the sugar factory and such godowns in case of delivery ex-godowns. 


Ezplanation.—The price determined and specified in column (2) of 
Schedule I aforesaid includes— 


(i) charges on transport from factory godowns and loading of sugar at 
buyer’s option on buyer’s carts, lorries or other means of transport 
or into railway wagons at the railway station or siding generally 
ae by the producer and include siding or wagon hauling charges; 
an 


(ii) all other incidental charges including dunnage charges,

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
HOME DEPARTMENT 


Political 


NOTIFICATION 


No. 285-P.—13th January 1969.—Whereas for the 
prevention of disturbances of the public tranquillity 
and of riots and affrays in the areas mentioned in 
the schedule below, in the town of Calcutta (here- 
inafter referred to as the said areas), the Com- 
missioner of Police, Calcutta, issued an order, dated 
ihe 19th November 1968, under section 144 of the 
Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act 5 of 1898), 
prohibiting, with effect from the 20th November 
1968, until further orders, any assembly of five or 
more pefsons or any procession within the said areas 
or the carrying of any lathis or other dangerous 
weapons or the doing of any act which is likely to 
cause a disturbance of the public tranquillity or a 
riot or an affray, within the said areas; 


And whereas it appears to the State Government 
that there is still a likelihood of disturbances of the 
public tranquillity and of riots and affrays within 
the said areas and it is necessary to continue in force 
the said order of the Commissioner of Police, 
Calcutta, for a period extending up to the 19th 
March 1969; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred 
by sub-section (6) of section 144 of the Code of 
Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act 5 of 1898), the 
Governor is pleased hereby to direct that the said

AGREEMENT 


MEMORANDUM OF AGREEMENT made this 
day the thirteenth January of One Thousand Nine 
Hundred and Sixty-nine between West Bengal State 
Electricity Board a company registered under the 
Indian Companies Act 1882 and having its registered 
Office at 48/1, Diamond Harbour Road, Calcutta-27 
(hereinafter called “The Company”) of the ONE 
PART, And the GOVERNOR of the State of West 
Bengal (hereinafter called *‘The Governor”) of the 
OTHER PART. 


WHEREAS for the purpose of the construction of 
33/11 K. V. Sub-Station and Staff Quarters the Com- 
pany has applied to the Government of West Bengal 
for the acquisition under the provisions of the Land 
Acquisition Act, 1894 (hereinafter referred to as the 
said “Act’’), of the piece or parcel of land containing 
0.013 of an acre or thereabout situate in the village 
of Shaktigarh, police-station Burdwan in the district 
of Burdwan and more particularly described in the 
eee hereto and delineated in the * plan hereunto 
annexed; 


AND WHEREAS the said Government of West 
Bengal (hereinafter referred to as the “Government”) 
upon the advice of the Land Acquisition Committee 
constituted under rule 3 of the Land Acquisition 
(Companies) Rules (hereinafter referred to as the said 
“Rules”) and after consideration of the Collector's 
report under rule 4 of the said Rules and being satis- 
fied on the report of the Collector by an enquiry held 
under section 40 of the said Act— 


(a) that the purpose of the acquisition is to obtain 
land for the erection of Quarters for the 
Staff employed by the Company and 


(b) that such acquisition is needed for the cons- 
truction of the building or work for the 
Company which is engaged in an industry or 
work which is for a public purpose, has 
given its consent to acquire on behalf of the 
Company the piece or parcel of land des- 
cribed hereunder. 


AND WHEREAS the said Government has re- 
quired the Company under the provisions of section 
41 of the said Act to enter into the agreement with 
the Governor hereinafter contained. 


Witnesscth that, without prejudice to the generality 
of the provisions of the said Act and the said Rules, 
it is hereby agrced and declared as follows:— 


(i) On demand the Company shall and will pay to 
the said Government all and every compen- 
sation in respect of the said land tendered,

awarded by the Collector under the said Act

tion or payable in respect thereof under the 
provisions of the said Act.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 


Pursuant to the acceptance by the Government of the 
recommendations of the National Integration Council to 
prevent and remove communal and-regional tensions, it is 
proposed to amend sections 153A and 505 IPC and 
Schedule II of the Code of Criminal Procedure with a 
view to amplifying the scope of these sections, providing 
enhanced punishment for offences under these sections 
committed in a place of worship, and making offences 
under sections 163A IPC and 505 IPC (only offences relat- 
ing to enmity or hatred between communities, ৪০০.) 
cognizable. 


2. <A provision is also being made whereby offences 
under section 163A and provision made in the Bill under 
section 606 IPC would constitute a disqualification under 
section 8 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. 


3. The National Integration Council had also recom- 
mended that powers should be taken to prevent the publica- 
tion of alarming, incorrect or provocative news or views 
likely to promote communal] ill-will or hatred or to disturb 
communal harmony, and had suggested that this may be 
done on the lines of provisions of section 2 of the Punjab 
Special Powers (Press) Act, 1956. A provision has accord- 
ingly been made in this Bill to prohibit the printing or 
publication of any matter for a specified period not exceed- 
ing two months if the Central Government or the State 
Government is satisfied that such action is necessary in the 
interest of maintenance of communal harmony.

Notes on clauses 


Clause 2.—Promoting eninity between different groups 
on grounds of religion, race, language, etc., is made au 
offence under section luda, of the Indian Penal Code. It 1s 
proposed to include therein promoting enmity between 
difterent groups on grounds, such as, place otf birth, or 
residence as well. 1৮ is also proposed to widen the scope 
of the provision so as to make promotion of disharmony or 
feelings of ill-will an offence punishable thereunder. Clause 
(b) of the said section provides fur the punishment for 
doing acts prejudicial to the muintenance of harmony 
between different groups. That provision is also proposed 
tu be widened so as to include acts prejudicial to the 
maintenance of harmony between different regional groups 
as well. It is also proposed to provide for enhanced 
puaishment and a mininwim punishment for any such 
offence committed in place of worship. The section is being 
substituted by this clause to achieve the above purpose. 


Clause 3.—Section 505 of the Indian Penal Code 
penalises the making, publishing or circulation of any 
etatement, rumour or report which 1s conducive to public 
mischief. The section does not deal specifically with 
rumours or alarming news which may create tension or ill- 
will between different communities so long as they are not 
intended or likely to incite commission of an_ offence. 
New sub-section (2) which is being inserted is intended to 
widen the scope of the section so as to include such rumours 
or alarming news with intent to create or promote, on 
rounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, 
unguage, caste or community or any other ground whatso- 
ever, feelings of enmity, hatred or ill-will between 
different religious, racial, 19017678969 or regional groups or 
castes or communities, as well. It is also proposed to 
provide for enhanced punishment and a minimum punish- 
ment for any such offence committed in place of worship. 
Section 505 1s being amended for this purpose. 


Clause 4.—Section 196 of the Criminal Procedure Code 
provides that certain offences including an offence wnder 
section 153A of the Indian Penal Code shall not be taken 
cognizance of by a Court unless upon a complaint made by 
order of, or under authority from the State Government 
or some officer empowered by the State Government in this 
behalf. It is proposed to amend the section so as to 
empower the istrict Magistrate to authorise prosecution. 
Schedule II of the Criminal Procedure Code is also being 
amended with a view to make offences under section 153A 
and section 505 (in so far as they relate to offences relating 
to enmity or hatred between communities, ete.) of the 
Indian Penal Code cognizable and non-bailable. 


Clause 5.—Section 8 of the Representation of the People 
Act deals with the disqualification of a candidate who is 
convicted for certain offences. The section is being 
amended so as to make a conviction for an offence punishable 
under section 153A and section 505 of the Indian Penal 
Code (offences relating to enmity or hatred between 
communities, etc.) a disqualification. The scope of the dis- 
qualification in relation to section 505 would extend also 
to convictions under the above-mentioned sections for making 
objectionable use of places of worship as well,

Clause 6.—This is intended to empower the Central 
Government or a State Government or any authority 
authorised by the Central Government to ourb publications 
prejudicial to the maintenance of communal harmony. It 
18 intended to enable the concerned Government to prohibit, 
for a peniod not exceeding two months, the printing or 
publication of alarming, incorrect or provocative news or 
of views likely to promote communal ill-feeling or hatred or 
to disturb communal harmony. It also provides that the 
person sv affected can make a_ representation within ten 
days to the Central or the State Government, 55 the case 
may be, and that Government after consultation with Press 
Consultative Committee dispose of the matter, modifying, 
confirming or rescinding the order. 


Clause 7 is intended to provide for a penalty of imprison- 
ment of either description which may extend to one year or 
fine up to rupees one thousand or both for an accused who 
contravenes, disobeys or neglects to comply with any order 
passed under clause 6. 

Clause 8 gives broadly the composition of the Press Con- 
sultative Committee which would consist of editors, 
publishers and journalists and empowers the Central 
Government to make rules for the constitution of the 
Committees, the term of office of the members of the 
Committees, the allowances, if any, to be paid to such 
members for attending the meetings of the Committees and 
the manner of filling cawial vacancies among them and for 
all matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. The 
rules would also specify the number of members of each 
Committee, the class or category of persons from whom such 
members are to be appointed, the authority or authorities 
which may make such appointment, the procedure for 
consulting the Committee and the procedure to be followed 
by the Press Consultative Committee. It also provides for 
laying on the Table of each House of Parliament miles so 
made and the rules are subject to the approval of Parlia- 


ment. 
FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM 


Clause 6 of the Criminal and Election Laws Amendment 
Bill, 1968 provides for consultation by the Government with 
ithe Press Consultative Committee. Clause 8 of the Bill 
provides for the constitution of such a Committee the 
members whereof will be appointed by the prescribed 
authority. ‘The expenditure is not expected to be large 
and is not likely to exceed Rs. 18,400 (recurring) anmaally. 


MEMORANDUM 22 DELECATED LECISLA- 
N 


Olause 8 of the Bill empowers the Central Government 
to make rules for the constitution of the Press Consultative 
Committee. The matters in respect of which rules may be 
made relate inter alia to the term of office of the members 
of the Committee, the alluwances, if any, to be paid to such 
members for attending the meetings of the Committee and 
the manner of filling casual vacancies among them and for 
all matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. The 
rules would also specify the number of members of the 
Committee, the class or category of persons from whom 
such members are to be appointed, the anthority or 
authorities which may make such appointment, the proce- 
dure for consulting the Committee and the procedure to be 
followed by the Press Consultative Committee. These 
matters pertaining to procedure or detail are necessary for 
the effective administration of the provisions of this Bill and 
as such the delegation of legislative power is of a normal 


character.

DEPARTMENT OF PANCHAYATS 


RESOLUTION 


No. 7628 Panch.—-28th December 1968.—Various 
measures to ensure the desired participation of the 
Panchayati Raj members in the formulation and im- 
plementation of the Panchayati Raj Training ۰ط‎ 
gramme and to mobilise the available co-operation 
and resources of non-officials in that connection have 
been receiving the consideration of Government for 
sometime past. The Governor has now been pleased 
to decide that henceforth there shall be a Managing 
Committee for each of the Panchayati Raj Training 
Centres in this State run under the management and 
control of the Director of Panchayats, West Bengal. 


[Part I 


بیس ە مس 1 


The composition of the Managing Committee will 
be as follows: 


Chairman 
(i) The Chairman of the Zilla Parishad of the 
District in which the Panchayati Raj Train- 
ing Centre is located. 


Members 


(ii) One President of the Anchalik Parishad from 
the area of Operation of the Panchayati Raj 
Training Centre. 


(111) and (iv) One Pradhan and one Adhyaksha 
from the area of operation of the Panchayati 
Raj Training Centre. 

(v) One woman member from the Zilla Parishad 
of the District where the Panchayati Raj 
Training Centre is located. 


(vi) District Panchayat Officer of the District where 
the Panchayati Raj Training Centre is 


located. 
Secretary 
(vii) The Principal of the Panchayati Raj Training 
Centre. 


The members of the categories (ii) to (v) will be 
selected by the Director of Panchayats, West Bengal 
A formal notification of the composition of the 
Managing Committee will also be issued by him. 


Function of the Managing Committee: 


The function of the Managing Committee of the 
Panchayati Raj Training Centres will be as follows:— 


(i) To review the work done by the Panchayati Raj 
Training Centre and to offer suggestions for improve- 
ment of the Training imparted. The Committee will 
also discuss the quarterly report of the Panchayati Raj 
Training Centre and record its remarks. 


(11) To advise on the Training Schedule and pro- 
gramme keeping in view the local conditions. 


(111) To ensure satisfactory attendance of the 
Trainees and to suggest suitable steps thereon. 


(iv) To advise on the follow up programmes by the 
staff of the Panchayati Raj Training Centres. 


(v) To watch on the progress of expenditure and 
to offer general suggestions. 


(vi) To consider the problems of the Panchayati 
Raj discussed by the participants in the training 
courses and to take appropriate steps in transmitting 
these problems to the appropriate agencies for atten- 
tion and solution. 


(vit) To suggest the problems for study and research 
by the Directorate or by the Panchayati Raj Training 
Centre itself. 


Frequency of the meeting of the Managing Committce: 


The Managing Committce will meet at least once ٠ 
quarter. The Secretary of the Managing Committee 
will be responsible for transmission of all minutes an- 
proceedings of the meeting to all concerned regularly 


Order 


Ordered that the Resolution be published in the 
“Calcutta Gazette” for general information. 


Ordered also that a copy of the Resolution be for- 
warded to the Director of Panchayats, West Bengal. 
for information and communication to the Principals 
of the Panchayati Raj Training Centres under him. 


Part 1] 


০ 


Ordered further that a copy of the resolution be 
forwarded to the— 


(1) Commissioners of Divisions. 

(2) All District Officers. 

(3) Regional Assistant Director of Panchayats. 
(4) Chairman of all Zilla Parishads. 

(5) All District Panchayat Officers. 


By order of the Governor, 
A. K. DUTT, Secy.

pleased to constitute a joint committee to ensure

and Murshidabad, consisting of the following:—

office Dharbabati, police-station Labpur, 
district Birbhum—Member. 


(d) Shri Kaji Rahimuddin Ahmed, village Kaji- 
para, post office Thiba, police-station Lab- 
pur, district Birbhum—Member. 


(০) Shri Saktipada Pal, village Kaichara, post office 
Bamnigram, police-station Labpur, district 
Birbhum—Member. 


(f) Shri Sunil Mohan Ghosh Maulik, post office and 
village Panchthupi, police-station Burdwan, 
district Murshidabad—Member.

dabad district to be nominated by the District 
Magistrate, Murshidabad—Members. 


(i) Block Development Officer, Labpur, 
Birbhum—Member. 


district 


(j) Block Development Officer, Buardwan, district 
Murshidabad—Member. 


(k) Executive Engineer, Mayurakshi South Canals 
Division—Member-Secretary. 


2. The Committee shall,— 


(a) before the commencement of Bore Irrigation 
every year, draw up a programme for opti- 
mum utilisation of irrigation water for the 
cultivation of bore crops in the Langalhata 
Beel area lying in the district of Birbhum 
and Murshidabad; and 


(b) suggest action to be taken to ensure equitable 
and smooth supply of available irrigation 
water so that there may not be any dispute 
between the cultivators of the two districts. 


3. The Member-Secretary will convene the meeting 
of the Committee in consultation with the Chairmen 
and may also invite outsiders to attend the meeting, if 
necessary. Sub-Divisional Officer, Suri, and the Sub- 
Divisional Officer, Kandi, will be the Chairmen of the 
Committee in rotation.

CO-OPERATION DEPARTMENT 


NOTIFICATIONS 


No. 5560-Co-op/2R-45/67.—28th December 1968, 
—The following draft of an amendment which, in 
exercise of the power conferred by section 140 of 
the Bengal Co-operative Societies Act, 1940 (Bengal 
Act XXI of 1940), the Governor proposes to make 
in the Bengal Co-operative Societies Rules, 1942, as 
subsequently amended (hereinafter referred to as the 
said rules), is hereby published, as required by sub- 
section (1) of the said section, for the information 
of persons likely to be affected thereby. 


The draft will be taken into consideration on or 
after the fifteenth day from the date of publication 
of this notification in the “Calcutta Gazette”, and 
any objection or suggestion with respect thereto 
which may be received by the undersigned before 
that day shall be considered. 


Draft Amendment 


In rule 43 of the said rules,— 


(1) in clause (a), after the words “existing 
members” add the words “by the votes of 
three-fourths of the members of _ the 
Managing Committee present and voting at 
a meeting;” | 


(2) for clause (৫), substitute the following clause, 
namely : — 

£(৫) to appoint salaried or non-salaried officers 
and employees for conduct of the business 
of the society and to define their duties 
and responsibilities and also to determine 
the securities to be furnished by them;’’; 
and. 


(3) for clause (f), substitute the following clause, 

namely: — 

“(f) to dispose of application for shares and 
issue shares against rebates as declared 
by the Managing Committce, subject to 
directions given by the general meeting 
from time to time;”’.

FISHERIES DEPARTMENT 
Fish 


NOTIFICATION 


No. 4894F/2R-3 /68.—26th December 1968. — In 
exercise of the power conferred by the proviso to 
Article 309 of the Constitution of India, the 
Governor is pleased hereby to make the following 
amendment in the rules regulating the recruitment 
to the West Bengal Subordinate Fisheries Service, 
Class II, under the Directorate of Fisheries, Govern- 
ment of West Bengal, published with this department 
Notification No. 2061-Fish., dated the 19th April 
1965, at pages 1352 and 1353 of Part I of the 
“Calcutta Gazette”, dated the Ist July 1965 (herein- 
after referred to as the said rules), namely:-— 


- Amendment 


For clause (i) of rule 2 of the said rules, substitute 
the following clause, namely :— 

“(i) a Bachelor’s degree in Science of a recognised 
University with Zoology as one of the 
subjects in the degree course, preference 
being given to a candidate who had Botany 
or Chemistry as another subject in the said 
course;”. 


By order of the Governor,

ORDERS 


No. 9203-I.R./IR/15L-7/68.—27th | December 
1968.—Whereas under the Government of West 
Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 2087-1L.R./ 
IR/15L-7/68, dated the 8th April 1968, the indus- 
trial dispute between Messrs. Esso Standard Eas- 
tern, Inc., 6 Church Lane, P.O. Box No. 146, 
Calcutta-1, and their workmen represented by 
Petroleum Workers’ Union, 3 and 4 Hare Street, 
' Calcutta, regarding the issue mentioned in the 
said order being a matter specified in the Second 
Schedule to the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (৯1৬ 
of 1947), was referred for adjudication to the 
Eighth Industrial Tribunal; 


And whereas the said Eighth Industrial Tri- 
bunal has submitted to the State Government its 
award on the said industrial dispute; 


Now, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions 
of section 17 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
(XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased hereby to 
publish the said award as shown in the annexure 


hereto. 
ANNEXURE 


In the matter of an industrial dispute between 
Messrs. Esso Standard Eastern, Inc., 6 Church 
Lane, P.O. Box No. 146, Calcutta-1, and 
their workmen represented by Petroleum 
Workers’ Union, 3 and 4 Hare Street, 
Calcutta, referred under G.O. No. 87-۰. 
IR/16L-7/68, dated the 8th April 1968. 
(Case No. VIII-118/68.) 


BEFORE THE EIGHTIT INDUSTRIAL 
TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL 


Present: 


Shri B. N. MAITRA, H.J.S., Judge, 
Eighth Industrial Tribunal. 


AWARD 


The Government of West Bengal, in its Labour 
Department, order No. 2087-I.R./IR/15L-7/68, dated 
the 8th April 1968, referred under section 10 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, an industrial dispute 
between Messrs. Esso Standard Eastern, _ Inc.. 
6 Church Lane, P.O. Box No. 146, Calcutta-1, and 
their workmen represented by Petroleum 
Workers’ Union, 3 and 4 Hare Street, Calcutta, to 
this Tribunal for adjudication on the following 
issue: 


Issue 


Whether the Company's order, dated February 
23, 1968, transferring the employees from 
Chitraganj Installation to Budge Budge 
Installation is lawful and justified? To 
what relief, if any, are the workmen 
entitled? 


The parties have not taken any steps. Both 
the sides filed written statements. it seems that 
they have amicably settled their disputes and

AWARD 


The Government of West Bengal, in its Labour 
Department order No. 2451-1.R./IR/11L-131/68, 
dated the 26th April 1968, referred under section 
10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, an indus- 
trial dispute between Messrs. Auto Cars, 53 Free 
School Street, Calcutta, and their workmen represen- 
ted by Automobile Engineering Workers’ Union, 
249-D Bepin Behari Ganguly Street, Calcutta-12, 
to this Tribunal for adjudication on the following 
issues : 


Issues 


1. Whether the closure of the factory with 
effect from 151 April 1968, as per notice of 
the Company, dated 29th February 1968, is 
real and bona fide? 


2. Whether the closure is beyond the control of 
the management and in the circumstances 
justifed? To what relief, if any, are the 
workmen entitled? 


The Union has filed a written statement and 
alleged that Messrs. Auto Cars had two Workshops 
in Calcutta, one at 53 Free School Street and 
another at 94C Rippon Street, Calcutta. The 
Management was the same. 47 workers, listed in 
the Annexure ‘A’ to the written statement, worked 
in the disputed garage in Free School Street. On 
29th February 1968 the Management illegally issued 
a notice stating that the Workshop at 53 Free School 
Street would be closed with effect from 1st April 
1968. The Union made a protest, but the Concern 
paid no heed to such objection. The workers were 
not paid any wages from March 1968. The alleged 
closure of the Workshop is illegal and not at all real 
or bona fide. The matter was referred 10 the 
ce amass Officer and ultimately the reference was 
made. 


A written statement has been put in on behalf of 
the Company, which has alleged inter alia that since 
the undertaking has already been closed, the refe- 
rence is not maintainable in law. It has no other 
branch or undertaking at 94C Rippon Street. The 
Workshop had to be closed due to circumstances 
beyond the control of the Company. So the workers 
cannot get any benefit whatever. 


It has been contended on behalf of the Union 
that the evidence of the P, W. 1, Tarak Nath Bhar, 
the then Head Clerk of the Garage in question, 
shows that 47 workmen were in the employ of the 
Company's Garage at Free School Street. The 
Workshop was closed after the 31st March 1968 
because an ejectment decree was passed regarding 
that Garage. The Company did not take any 
effective steps to get that ejectment decree set aside. 
So the Tribunal should hold that the alleged closure 
is not a real and bona fide one. Moreover the 
evidence of that witness shows that one Narayan 
Chandra Sarkar was an employee of the disputed 
Garage. By an order of that Company, the latter 
was transferred to the Company’s রত at 940 
Rippon Street. So at all events, even if the Tribunal 
holds that the workshop was in fact closed, the 


[১৮710] 


EE EE TS و‎ 


disputed 47 workmen are entitled to compensation 
according to the provisions of the section 25FFF 
read with the section 26F(b) of the Industrial 
Disputes Act. The Tribunal should follow the 
principle of ‘Last come first go’ and ask the 
Company to absorb some of the retrenched workers 
eS the Company’s Workshop at 94C Rippon 
treet. 


It has been submitted on behalf of the Company 
that the closure is a real one and hence there is no 
industrial dispute between the parties. In that view 
of the matter, this Tribunal has no jurisdiction to 
enter into the question of payment of compensation 
or any other incidental relief. Reference has been 
made to the case of Hind Shippers in 1968 .(1) 
L.L.J., 365 to show that where the reference has 
been made to consider the question of closure of a 
Company with effect from 4th August 1963 with 
a direction to determine whether such closure was 
.on account of unavoidable circumstances beyond the 
control of the employers, and if not, what relief the 
workmen were entitled to, it was held that when 
the business had been actually closed, the reference 
was not maintainable and the quantum of compensa- 
tion which the workmen were entitled to had to be 
investigated by the specihed Labour Court under 
the provisions of the section 33002) of the Indus- 
trial Disputes Act. 


The evidence of the P. W.1, Tarak Nath Bhar, 
shows that the Company issued the notice Ext. A 
before the closure. It is common ground that an 
ejectment decree was passed in respect of the 
disputed Garage and after the 31st March 1968, 
that Workshop was closed. 


Reference may be made to the latest case of 
Indian Hume Pipe Company in 1968 (17) L.L. J., 
145 at page 149 (S.C.) to show that if the employer 
has actually closed its factory, the Tribunal is not 
concerned to go into the question as ‘to the motive 
which guided him to do the same and such a 
closure cannot give rise to an industrial dispute. 


As stated before, there is no denial that an 
ejectment decree was passed regarding the disputed 
Garage. Consequently it must be held that the 
Company had to close down the disputed Garage 
at 53 Free School Street since the ejectment decree 
was passed and that fact was beyond the control 
of the Management and that due 10 such 
unavoidable circumstances, the closure of the factory 
with effect from 1st April 1968, as per notice of 
the Company, dated 29th February 1968 (Ext. A), 
is real and bona fide and that in the circumstances, 
such closure is justified. 


There is no satisfactory evidence to show that 
the terms of the employment of the workmen of 
the unit at 94C Rippon Street were the came. It 
is true that the P. W. 1, Tarak Nath Bhar, has stated 
that one Narayan Chandra Sarkar was transferred 
from the disputed Garage to the unit at 94C Rippon 
Street. But he is constrained to admit in his cross- 
examination that Narayan Chandra Sarkar used to 
draw the salary from the previous unit at 53 Free 
School Street. In that view of the matter, the 
principle “Last come first go’ cannot be applied. 


EL ee EE. Obes ee کسہے۔ہ۔‎ 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 16, 1969 55 


The upshot of the aforesaid discussion is that 
there is no industrial dispute between the parties 
regarding the main issue since ز‎ has been 
found that the Workshop has in fact, been closed. 
Since the concern is dead and not a living one and 
as the main issue is decided in favour of the 
Company, consequently the 47 disputed workers are 
not entitled to any compensation. The provisions 
of the sections 33C(1) and (2) of the Industrial 
Disputes Act are clear because the compensation 
payable under the provisions of the Chapter VA of 
the Industrial Disputes Act will have to be deter- 
mined by the Labour Court. It will be pertinent to 
point out that both the sections 25F and 25FFF, 
relied on on behalf of the Union, appear in the 
Chapter VA of the Industrial Disputes Act. In 
that view of the matter, it is held that the workmen 
are not entitled to any relief whatever. The re- 
ference is disposed of accordingly.

AWARD 


The Government of West Bengal, in its Labour 
Department, order No. 2117-1.R./IR/7L-9/67, dated 
the 10th April 1968, referred under section 10 of 
the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, an industrial 
dispute between Messrs. National Company Ltd., 
Banipore, Rajgunj, Howrah (hereinafter referred 
to as the Company), and their workmen repre- 
sented by Jute Textiles Workers’ Union, 34 Joy- 
bibi Road, Ghusury, Howrah (hereinafter describ- 
ed as the Union), to this Tribunal for adjudication 
on the following issues سس‎ 


Issues 


1. Fixation of wage-rates of Inside Sclectors 
of B.L. Section of Mill No. 2. 


2. Permanency of Selectors of B.L. Section 
of Mill No. 2. 


The Union has filed a written statement and 
alleged that the workmen of the Broad Loom 
Selector (B.L. Selector) are paid wages at a very 
low rate. The Jute Wage Board fixed the wages 
of different categories of workers. But it did not 
consider the wages of the Selectors working in the 
Broad Loom. The Selectors are all skilled and ex- 
perienced workmen. Their job is to select the 
quality and the standard of jute from different 
bundle of the jute bale and separate the same 
according to their quality. In 1965 the Manage- 
ment granted an increment of wages as an interim 
measure in pursuance of an agreement. The dis- 
pute regarding the wages of the Broad Loom 
Selectors (Katari Department) and permanency 
of 48 workmen was referred to Mr. B. K. Roy for 
arbitration. On 1st April 1967, he gave his award 
and fixed the rate of wages with effect from 131 
January 1967. It was stated in the award that at 
least 33 per cent. of the workmen of the Broad 
Loom Selection (Katari Department) should be 
made permanent with immediate effect. He also 
fixed the wages of the Selectors at different rates. 
The job of the Bale Selectors is a permanent one. 
But the workmen have been kept temporary for 
years on end and they have’ not been made per- 
manent bv the Management. The Company re- 
fused to implement the award of Mr. B. K. Roy 
regarding the wage-rate and the permanency as

A written statement has been put in on behalf

that the Jute Industry has been facing a crisis for 
the last few years. The Company has implemen- 
ted the recommendations of the Jute Wage Board. 
According to such recommendations, the Selectors 
will get Rs. 3.72 P. per 100 mds., but the Company 
pays at the rate of Rs. 6.25 P. per 100 mds. to 
each workman of the Broad Loom Selectors. 
There are two types of Selectors in the Mill, viz., 
the Inside Selectors and the Outside (Katari) 
Selectors. The Inside Selectors open the jute bales, 
sclect the quality of jute from cach bundle of the 
jute bales and stack them quality-wise. On the

Selectors open the jute bales, select the quality of 
the jute from each bundle of the jute bales and

they have to cut the roots of the sticks and hackle

function of the Inside Selectors. The award of 
Mr. B. K. Roy has been fully implemented regard-

Issue No 1: 


It has been contended on behalf of the Union 
that the Tribunal should accept the evidence of 
the P.Ws. and state that the work done by the 
Inside Selectors of the Broad Loom Section is 
more onerous than that of the Katari Section. So 
a rate of wages should be fixed for the workmen 
of the Inside Selectors. 


The learned Lawyer appearing on behalf of the 
Company has stated that the financial position of 
the Company is not sound. Moreover there is no 
reason to revise the wage structure of the work- 
men of the Inside Selectors. The Union has 
failed to establish their case according to the 
principle of industry-cum-region basis. The evi- 
dence will show that the Company pays wages at 
a rate higher than that fixed by the Jute Wage 
Board. So the Union's claim in this regard should 
be rejected. 


Reference may be made to the cases of Express 
Newspapers Ltd., in .۸ھ‎ 1958, S.C., 578 and 
Kamani Metals and Alloys in 1967 (II) L.L.J., 55, 
(S.C.). It will appear from those cases that in 
xing the wage structure, the Tribunal should 
follow the principle of ‘Industry-cum-Region’ 
basis and consider the capacity of the industry to 
bear the burden of the altered wages. 


It is common ground that the recommendations, 
of the Jute Wage Board came into force from 
July 1963. It will appear therefrom that the 


PART IC] 


Selectors will get Rs. 3.72 P. per 100 mds. while 
the O.P.W. 1 Megharaj Sharma says that the 
workmen of the Inside Selection Group get the 
wages at Rs. 6.25 P. per 100 mds. This has not 
been denied. Moreover, a perusal of those recom- 
mendations shows that the Wage Board consi- 
dered the cases of the Broad Loom Selectors and 
the Narrow Loom Selectors as well. 


The aforesaid case of Express Newspapers Ltd. 
will show that the Wage Board relating to a parti- 
cular trade or industry, is best calculated to arrive 
at the proper fixation of wages of that industry. 


No doubl, the P.W. 1 Ramchandra Singh and 
the P.W. 2 Abdul Sakur state that the Inside 
Selectors) work عز‎ heavier. But they did not 
depose convincingly. It will appear even from the 
evidence of P.W. 2 Sakur, that the workmen of 
the Katari Section have to cut the jute sticks. The 
0.۲۰۷۷۰۰ ۱ Megharaj Sharma has stated that there 
are about 35 or 36 Inside Selectors and in cutting 
the jute sticks, the workers of the Katari Section 
have to use Katari weighing 10 to 15 Kgs. each. 
He deposed quite satisfactorily and hence his evi- 
dence is accepted. So there is no point in the 
submissions made on behalf of the Union that the 
workmen of the Inside Selection Group have to do 
heavier job. 


The onus is on the Union to prove the rate pay- 
able by the other Companies. Only the P.W. 1 
Ramchandra Singh has stated in his evidence that 
the workmen of Alebian Jute Mill, Ludhian Jute 
Mill, Fort Gloster Jute Mill and Ludlow Jute Mill 
get higher wages and in the Ludlow Company, the 
maximum rate is Rs. 21. None of the workmen of 
those Companies deposed as P.Ws. There is no 
documentary evidence to show that in fact the 
workmen of any of the aforesaid Companies get 
wages at any higher rate. The wages paid by the 
Company to the workmen of the Inside Selection 
Group are not in the 10241 ina‘leqvate. It will 
appear from the aforesaid discussion that the 
Union has failed to discharge the aforesaid onus 
and suow the rate of wages of any comyarable 
unit. It has been indicated that the Company 
pays wages to the workers of the Inside Selection 
Group at arate which is not at all inadequate. 
Hence it is: held that there are no good grounds 
to fix a new wage-rate or wage-structure of the 
Inside Selectors of the Broad Loom Section of the 
Mill No. 2.

Disputes Act is a bar to the trial of issue No. 2. 
The award passed by Mr. B. K. Roy on 151 April

The Union's reply 15 that this point was not 
taken in the written statement. At any event, the

when the reference was made to this Tribunal. 
So the Tribunal should hold that the Company has

115 charter of demands, there was termination of

Now, this is purely a question of law which can

in this regard in the written statement will not 
stand in the way of the Company in making such 
submission before the Tribunal. 


Reference may be made to the section 19(6) 
of the Industrial Disputes Act to show that not- 
withstanding the expiry of the period of operation 
under sub-section (3), the award shall continue 
to be binding on the parties until a period of two 
months has clapsed from the date on which notice 
is given by any party bound by the award to the 
other party or parties intimating its intention to 
terminate the award. 


Reference may also be made ا١‎ the latest case 
of Bangalore Woolen Company in 1968, (16) 
F.L.R., 242 (S.C.) to show, that according to the 
provisions of the section 19(6) of the Act, a parti- 
cular date of termination is necessary and such a 
certainty regarding the date of termination is 
essential. Distinguishing the case of the Work- 
men of Western India Match Company in F.U.R., 
1962, (5), 129, S.C., it has been stated that the 
decision in Western Match Company’s case does 
not show that there will be an inference of inten- 
tion to terminate the award from the various cor- 
respondences and in that case a particular 7۴۳ 
was treated as amounting to a notice of termina- 
tion of the settlement. In this case no such letter 
or notice was sent by the workmen or the Union 
to the Management. Hence in the facts of the 
case, there is no scope for applying the principles 
laid: down by the Supreme Court in the aforesaid 
case of Western Match Company. 


It will appear from the award Ext. A of Mr. B. 
K. Roy, Conciliation Officer, Howrah, that it was 
sizmed by him on Ist April 1967. The present re- 
ference is dated the 10th April 1968. Since no 
notice was given by the Union or by the workmen 
to the Company intimating an intention to termi 
nate the award, it must be held that the aforesaid 
award Ext. A is a bar to the trial of the issue No. 
2 regarding the permanency of the Selectors of the 
Broad Loom Section of the Mill No 2. Moreover 
the written statement filed by the Union itself, 
indicates that the award of Mr. B. K. Roy was 
passed in favour of the workmen. There is 7> 
dication in that written statement that such award 
was terminated. So in view of the pleadings of

By the Government of West Bengal, Labour 
Department, order No. 4236-1.R./IR/10L-183/66, 
dated the 4th November 1966, this industrial dispute 
between Messrs. Sinha Bahini Engineering Works and 
Messrs. D. A. Engineering Works on the one 
hand, and their workmen on the other, was referred 
to this Tribunal under section 10 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act for adjudication on the issues men- 
tioned below :— 


Issues 


1. Whether the closure of the 2 factories is 
real and bona (1063 


2. Whether their closure was due to reasons 
beyond the control of the management and, 
in the circumstances, justihed? 8۲۷ا‎ 
relief, if any, are the workmen entitled to? 


On receipt of notice from the Tribunal both the 
parties made their appearance and filed their res- 
peclive written statement. 


The case of the workmen is as follows :— 


Messrs. Sinha Bahini Engineering Works and 
Messrs. R. D. A. Engineering Works are two units 
of one concern. The Company manufactures tank, 
filter, boiler and other engineering products. The 
workmen of the Company were smarting under 
manifold difficulties. They were denied the bare 
minimum wages. The workmen tried to realise 
their economic demands through constitutional trade 
union movements. The Company did not take 
steps for the redress of the grievances of the work- 
men. On the other hand, the Company suddenly 
closed the factory on the 21st May 1966. This 
closure amounted to hasty lockout, and the manage- 
ment was actuated by a motive to crush the trade 
union. A few days after the so-called closure of 
the factory the management engaged new workers 
and continued to run the factory. It is, therefore, 
the prayer of the Union that the workmen should 
be reinstated in service and paid their full back 
wages. 


Messrs. Sinha Bahini Engineering Works and 
Messrs. R. D. A. have filed separate written state- 
ments. Their case is that the two firms have no 
connection with each other and they are separate 
concerns and, as such, the present reference is not 
maintainable. It is also alleged by them that they 
really closed their business. 


Decision with reasons, 


Ext. B is the licence in respect of Messrs. Sinha

Works. Ext. D is the trade licence in respect of

A. Engineering Works. It appears that these two 
Companies have separate entities. Exts. C., C-l 
and C-2 show that these two Companies have got 
separate code numbers for the Provident Fund and 
Employees’ State Insurance schemes in respect of

their workers. It also appears that these two Com- 
panies maintain separate Payment Registers and 
Muster Rolls. On a consideration of the documents 
on record I have not the slightest doubt that these 
two Companies have separate entities and they are 
two separate concerns. However, it cannot be said 
that the reference is not maintainable at all. The 
unchallenged evidence of P. W. 1 Ram Chandra 
Row is that there was one Manager for the Sinha 
Bahini Engineering Works and_ the 
Engineering Works. According ٥ 
Patra was the Manager. Again, the unchallenged 
evidence of P. W.2 Nirmal Chandra Shome is that 
there was one Time Office for both the factories. 
It is clear that by some private arrangement these 
two factories used to be run by one management. 
It is true that the, Sinha Bahini Engineering Works 
is a proprietory concern, and R. A. is a partner- 
ship concern. O. P. W. 1 Ranjit Kumar Khan is 
the proprietor of Sinha Bahini Engineering Works. 
Rathindra Kumar Khan (O.P.W.2) is one of 
the partners of R. D. A. Rathindra is the son of 
Ranjit Kumar Khan, O.P.W.1. The partners of 
Rathindra are his cousins, i.e, the partners of 
Rathindra are nephews of Ranjit Khan, O. P. W. 1. 
In view of the close relationship of the partners of 

D. A. and the proprietor of Sinha Bahini 
Engineering Works, and in view of the fact that 
there was one Time Office and one Manager in 
both the factories, | am inclined to think that by 
some private arrangement these two factories were 
run by the same management. In this view of the 
case I am _ of opinion that the reference 13 
maintainable. 


him Jogin 


According to the workmen these two factories 
were closed on 21st May 1966. Admittedly Sinha 
Bahini Engineering Works was closed on 21st May 
1966. Ext. F is the notice issued by the proprietor 
of Sinha Bahini Engineering Works on 17th May 
1966. By this notice the factory was closed with 
effect from 21st May 1966. Ext. F-1 is the notice 
which was issued by R. D. A. Engineering Works 
on 10th August 1966. By this notice the factory 
of R. D. A. Engineering Works was closed with 
effect from 11th August 1966. It is thus clear that 
the factory of Sinha Bahini was closed on 21st May 
1966 and the factory of R. D. A. was closed on 
11th August 1966. The Union’s case that both 
the factories, viz., Sinha Bahini Engineering Works 
and the R A. Engineering Works, were closed 
on 21st May 1966 seems to be absolutely false. 
O.P.W.1 Ranjit Khan says that he closed the 
business totally since 21st May 1966. He wants to 
‘say that as orders dwindled down he decided to 
close the factory. He does not produce any paper 
to show that orders actually dwindled down. But 
it is clear that he actually closed the factory on 
218 May 1966. The workmen led evidence to 
prove that the Sinha Bahini Engineering Works is 
in working condition. But the evidence on this point 
is hopelessly unsatisfactory. There is no paper to 
indicate that Ranjit Khan of Sinha Bahini has 
started the factory again after the closure. It 
appears that sume of the workers received payment 
tom the proprietor in full and final satisfaction of 
their dues. Ext. J series show this. Had the 
Proprietor of Messrs. Sinha Bahini Engineering 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 16, 1969 59 


SN لج‎ 


= arate, er 


Works not closed the business these workmen 
would not have received payment in full and final 
satisfaction of their dues. So, considering the 
evidence on record I am convinced that the proprietor 
of Messrs. Sinha Bahini Engineering Works really 
closed the business on 21st May 1966. 


It has been proved in this case that the factory of 
R.D.A. Engineering Works was closed on 11th 
August 1966. The question is whether 1116 
management of R.D.A. actually closed the business 
on that date. It is the evidence of O.P.W. 
Rathindra Nath Khan that he closed the business 
with effect from 11th August 1966. It appears that 
immediately on the closure of Sinha Bahini Engine- 
ering Works, the workers of R.D.A. Engineering 
Works resorted to a strike, and that after giving 
opportunity to the workers the management decided 
to close down the factory. In the notice of closure, 
Ext. F-1, the management of R.D.A. Engineering 
Works mentioned that the workers had resorted to 
a strike since 21st May 1966. O.P.W. 2 Rathindra 
Khan also says in his evidence that after the closure 
of Sinha Bahini Engineering Works on 21st May 
1966 there took place a strike by the workers in 
R.D.A. Engineering Works. It appears that the 
management of Engineering Works in- 
formed the Labour Commissioner about the strike. 
Ext. M shows this. There is no evidence on the 
side of the workers that they did not resort to any 
strike. In these circumstances I cannot but conclude 
that immediately after the closure of Sinha Bahini 
Engineering Works, the workers of R.D.A. Engine- 
ering Works resorted to a strike and that they did 
not resume their duties thereafter. ١ am, therefore, 
inclined to thing that the management of R.D.A 
Engineering Works also really closed the business 
on 11th August 1966. In this connection it should 
be mentioned that P.W. 2 Nirmal Chandra Shome 
has not deposed truthfully in this case. He says 
that he was re-employed by ‘the management of 
R.-D. A. Engineering Works, and that after re- 
employment he worked for about 1) years and 
thereafter. he was retrenched. According to him 
the management of R.D.A. Engineering Works re- 
started work one year after it had closed the factory. 
It appears that this witness received payment from 
R. D. A. Engineering Works on 12th October 
1966. Ext. A(2) is the receipt granted by him. 
According to him he received the amount after he 
had been re-employed. But according to him the 
factory was restarted one year after the closure. 
It is clear that the factory of R. D. A. Engineering 
Works was closed on 11th August 1966. The 
receipt granted by him is dated 12th October 1966. 
So it is clear that his evidence that he received the 
amount after he had been reappointed is false. No 
reliance can be placed on his evidence. However, 
‘t is an admitted fact that the management of 
R. D. A. Engineering Works actually restarted the 
business. 0. P. W. 2 Rathindra Khan says in his 
evidence that in March 1967, they have restarted 
the business. As the factory has been restarted by 
R. D. A. Engineering Works, it is submitted on 
behalf of the workers that it should be taken that 
the closure of the factory of R. D. A. Engineering 
Works was not real. I am unable to accept this 
submission. The management of A. En- 
gineering Works had to close the business on 1111 


60 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 16, 1969 


August 1966 as the workers resorted to a_ strike. 
It may be that when the management found the 
almosphere congenial they started the business 
again. Simply because of the fact that the manage- 
ment of R. D. A. Engineering Works started the 
factory again, it cannot be said that they had not 
closed the business on 11th August 1966. The 
evidence on record leads me to think that the 
management of R. D. A. Engineering Works really 
closed the business on 11th August 1966. 


P. W. 1, Ram Chandra Row, says in his evidence 
that after the closure of these two factories the 
Company used to get works done in another factory 
at Daégsnagore. and the said factory was New 
Rajlakshmi & Co. But no paper has been filed by 
the workers to show that either the Sinha Bahini 
Engineering Works or the R. D. A. Engineering 
Works got their works done in the factory of New 
Rajlakshmi & Co. I am of opinion that it has not 
been proved that either of the factories in question 
got their works done in the factory of New 
Rajlakshmi & Co. I find from the evidence that 
both the concerns really closed their business. 


It has not been, however, proved that the two 
concerns in question closed business under circums- 
tances beyond their control. However, these two 
concerns do not seek the aid of proviso to 
section 25FFF(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act. 
They are willing to pay compensation to the work- 
men under the principal part of sub-section of 
section 25FFF read with section 25F of the In- 
dustrial Disputes Act. I think that the workers of 
these two concers, viz.. Messrs. Sinha Bahini En- 
gineering Works and Messrs. R. D. A. Engineering 

orks, are entitled to compensation under the 
principal part of sub-section of section 25FFF read 
with section 25 of the Industrial Disputes Act. 


This is my award.

The Union, in its written statement, contended that 
the Company having been established so far back 
in 1774, is possibly the biggest and most prosperous 
industrial concern in the State of West Bengal. 
About 8,200 workmen including about 926 clerical 
and technical staff and also 325 subordinate staff 


are’ employed in the Company. The Union com- 
prises clerical and technical staff including sirkars 
and checkers and also subordinate staff and since 
its formation in 1946 has been championing the 
cause of the aforesaid workmen. The Company 
though prosperous, is very slow to appreciate the 
genuine grievance of the workmen and even do not 
feel shy to pursue the palpably discriminatory 
treatment between workmen and workmen. The 
Durwans, numbering about 132, belong to the cate- 
gory of subordinate staff are discriminated by way 
of denial of 14 days’ festival holidays in a year, 
though the other categories of subordinate staff and 
other employees enjoy the same. No extra beneft 
ig given to the Durwans by way of compensation 
for denial of the said festival holidays in a year.

Excepting the aforesaid festival holidays, in all

The Company in their written statement con- 
tended, inter alia, that the Order of Reference, dated

(vide Exhibit 1D). As no additional or new facts 
were brought to the notice of the Government by 
the Union, the subsequent reference, i.e., the present 
one is ultra vires, illegal and void. It has been 
contended that the different categories of workmen 
in the Company’s factory have different grades and 
scales of pay and the Watch-and-Ward Durwans 
are governed by a separate set of Standing Orders, 
different from the said Standing Orders governing 
the other categories of workmen mentioned therein.. 
The Durwans also get various extra benefits and 
facilities which the subordinate staff do not get. 
Workmen other than hourly-paid workmen (exclud- 
ing Watch-and-Ward Durwans) enjoy 14 days’ 
holidays in a year according to the provisions of 
the relevant Standing Orders governing them. 
Watch-and-Ward Durwans belong to a_ cetegory, 
separate and different from the subordinate staff as 
regard the scale of pay, provision of free single 
accommodation in quarters, if and when they want 
them, supply of free fuel and electric light, supply

Durwans may express their preference in favour of 
leave and মদন as awarded by the First Omnibus

annual leave and at the same time claim for more

the occasion of 12 holidays of the Factory, there 
should be Durwans in the factory to guard the 
Company’s properties there. The Standing Orders 
applicable to the Durwans only provide for more 
generous leave than under the said awards. Besides, 
30 days’ annual leave with full pay, the Durwans 
get a day off in a week. They also enjoy sick leave 
under the provisions of the E.S.I. Act. Durwans 
enjoy more generous and privilage leave than those 
enjoyed by the factory manual workers. Any in- 
diserimination or injustice as alleged on behalf of 
the Union, is denied.

As regards the contention of the learned Lawyer 
for the Company regarding the maintainability of 
the instant Order of Reference, it is admitted that 
the Union is agitating over the claim of the Durwans 
for 14 days’ festival holidays from the year 1964 
(vide Ext. 1). The Government at first by a 
letter, dated 4th June 1966 (vide Ext. 1D), refused 
lo refer the matter for adjudication to any Tribunal, 
on the grounds mentioned in the said letter, copy 
being Exhibit “‘D’. Subsequently the instant Order 
of Reference was made. According to the learned 
Lawyer for the Company the instant Order of 
Reference is void and illegal and does not confer 
_on this Tribunal to adjudicate upon the same issue. 
But on a consideration of the principle of law 
discussed in the case reported in A. I. R. 1959 
Calcutta, page 339, I cannot but reject this conten- 
tion of the learned Lawyer for the Company and 
I hold that the Government having sent the issue 
for adjudication to this Tribunal, this Tribunal has 
acquired jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the issue. 
Nothing debars the State Government to refer any 
dispute to any Tribunal for adjudication, having 
refused to refer at the first instance, if upon a second 
thought the Government deemed it necessary to 
send the industrial dispute to any Tribunal for 
adjudication. Accordingly ! hold that the instant 
Order of Reference is not void and illegal as alleged 
on behalf of the Company. I hold that this Order 


of Reference is quite maintainable. 


As regards the merits of this case, we find that 
undisputedly 132 Durwans are employed in the 
Howrah Factory of Messrs. Burn & Co. Ltd. 
According to Shri D. N. Sen Gupta, Advocate for 
the Union, the Company made discrimination by 
refusing festival holidays to the Durwans when the 
other subordinate staff, namely, Chaprasis and 
bearers employed in the same factory of the 
Company at Howrah are getting such leave. This 
is a discriminatory treatment on behalf of 1176 
Company's authorities, according to the Union. On 
the other hand, according to the Companys the nature 
and duties of the Durwans are different from the 
nature and duties of Chaprasis and bearers and as 
such the Durwans should not be allowed festival 
holidays. The factory in question, Messrs. Burn & 
Co., at Howrah was established more than 100 
years back. Durwans were never allowed any 
festival holidays. There are also admittedly 3 sets 
of Standing Orders for the factory in question, one 
admittedly is for hourly-rated workmen, the second

AWARD 


On the issue~“Whether the workmen are entitled 
to more bonus over and above the quantum already 
paid by the Management for the year 1965, payable 
in the year 1966 ?” There having existed an industrial 
dispute between Messrs. Scott & Saxby Ltd., 1 Tara- 
talla Road, Calcutta-24 (Registered Office at Charter- 
ed Bank Buildings, Calcutta) (hereinafter called the 
Company) and their workmen represented by Scott & 
Saxby Employees’ Union, 3 Jay Krishna Paul Road, 
Calcutta-23 (hereinafter called the Union), ٥ 
Governor of West Bengal, was pleased under Govern- 
ment of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 
1633-1.R./1R/11L-50/65, dated 22nd April 1967, to 
refer the said dispute for adjudication to the First, In- 
dustrial Tribunal ; but, the Presiding Officer of the said 
First Industrial Tribunal having not joined his office, 
the Governor, by Government of West Bengal, Labour 
Department, order No. 3435-1.R./IR/11L-346/67, 
dated 22nd July 1967, was pleased to withdraw the 
said proceedings from the file of the said First Indus- 
trial Tribunal and transfer the same to this Seventh 
Industrial Tribunal for speedy disposal. 


The parties to the dispute appeared before this 
Tribunal and filed their respective written statements. 
Thereafter, various dates were fixed by this Tribunal 
for @king various necessary steps preparatory to the 
final hearing of the case. 28th October 1968, was 
fixed by this Tribunal for hearing the Union's prayer 
for submission of documents by the Company. The 
Tribunal being on Jeave, the case could not be taken 
up on 28th October 1968. On 30th October 1968, the 
parties filed a joint petition of compromise which was 
placed before the Tribunal on 4th November 1968, on 
his return from leave. The joint petition of compro- 
mise is signed by Shri P. S. Roy, Works Manager of 
Scott & Saxby Ltd., on behalf of the Company. Shri 
Rajani Mukherjee, President, Shri Rahmat Khan and 
the Secretary of the Union have signed the joint peti- 
tion on behalf of the Uni6n. On perusal of the peti- 
lion, it is found that the workmen and their Union 
agreed to accept the bonus of 13.76 per cent. of the 
annual earnings as declared by the Company for the 
financial year ended 31st December 1965, payable in 
1966 in accordance with the Payment. of Bonus Act in 
full and final settlement of their claim for 1965. The 
petition further says that the Union has no further 
claim on the Company for any more bonus for the said 
year. In the opinion of this Tribunal, the agreement 
made by the parties is fair and reasonable and there is 
no reason whatsoever for not accepting the said terms 
of compromise. 


Therefore, accepting the terms of compromise which 
satisfied the parties to the dispute, I hereby pass this 
compromise award and dispose of this case. 


Usual number of copies of this award be sent to the 
State Government for necessary action. The joint

AWARD 


By the Government of West Bengal, Labour 
Department, order No. 468-I.R./IR/8L-2/66, dated 
the 7th February 1966, an industrial dispute between 
Messrs. Ma Kali Ganga Hosiery alias Messrs. 
Gopal Krishna Hosiery, 4B Nayan Sur Lane, 
Calcutta-5, and their workmen represented by 
Hosiery Workingmen’s Union, Sova Bazar 
Street, Calcutta-5, was referred to this Tribunal under 
section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, for 
adjudication in respect of the following issue :— 


Issue 


Whether the refusal of employment to Shri 
Sudhir Chandra Saha is justified? What 
relief, if any, is he entitled to? 


After receipt of the order of reference, notices 
were issued to the Union, as well as the Company. 
In the original order of reference the name of the 
Compnay was mentioned as Messrs. Gopal Kriskina 
Hosiery and notice was accordingly issued to the 
said Company. The union appeared before this 
Tribunal and filed its written statement on 29th 


April 1966. Notice could not be served on the 
said Company named ‘Messrs. Gopal Krishna 
Hosiery". Then on being queried, the Government 


intimated this Tribunal that the above Company had 
changed their name as ‘Messrs. Makali Ganga 
Hosiery,’ the address of the Partners of the Com- 
pany, however, remained the same. The order of 
reference was accordingly amended by naming the 
Company correctly as Messrs. Makali Ganga 
Hosiery alias Messrs. Gopal Krishna Hosiery. That 
was done on 5th July 1968. Notice was then 
issued under registered cover to the said Company 
as Messrs. Makali Ganga Hosiery alias Messrs. 
Gopal Krishna Hosiery. But the registered notice 
was returned back to this Tribunal as ‘‘not claimed” 


by the said addressee on 20th July 1968. This 


[PART [C 


ooo oe eee ey 


service was accepted by this Tribunal as sufficient 
and this case was fixed on 4th December 1968 for 
ex-parte hearing. On the prayer of the Union, the 
case was then finally adjourned to this day, 13th 
December 1968 for ex-parte hearing. 


Today the concerned workman, Shri Sudhir 
Chandra Saha has been examined as the sole witness 
on behalf of the Union. He, in his evidence, proved 
that he was refused employment by the Company 
authorities since 16th May 1968 without any justi- 
fication. He was never charge-sheeted nor any 
enquiry was made against him prior to the said date. 
I accept the evidence of . 1 as correct and 
on his evidence I hold that the refusal of employ- 
ment to Shri Sudhir Chandra Saha since 26th May 
1965 is not justified and accordingly I further hold 
that he is entitled to an order of reinstatement. The 
concerned workman is not entitled to any back 
wages, as admittedly he has been working in 
another concern, though temporarily. 


In the above view of the case the Company is 
directed to reinstate the concerned workman Shri 
Sudhir Chandra Saha within one month from the 
date of publication of this award 17 the “Calcutta 
Gazette”. 


This is my award. 


Dictated and corrected by me. 


G. B. GHOSH, 
Judge. 


G. B. GHOSH, Judge, 
Third Industrial Tribunal.

Short Recital of the Case 


The Management of Calcutta Chromotype Private 
Limited contends that as the workmen absented them- 
selves from their duties on the 16th and 17th May 1968 
and in view of an assault on Mr. ۶. L. Hoogan, 
Personal Secretary to the Managing Director, on 16th 
May 1968 and consequent insecurity of the Management 
Personnel, the Company declared closure on and from 
the 18th May 1968 until further notice. 


The Union on the other hand maintains that 11) 
view of a protest demonstration against mass _ scale 
charge-sheets, suspensions and victimisation the Com- 
pany locked out the factory on and from 16th May 
1968. After protracted negotiations between the 
representatives of the Management and the Union, and 
through the good offices of the Labour Directorate, the 
parties have agreed to the following Terms of Settle- 
ment :— 


Terms of Settlement 


1. It is agreed that the Management of Calcutta 
Chromotype Private Limited shall reopen the factory 
with effect from 12th December 1968. 


2. Ten days time will be given to all workmen, who 
may fail to join on the date of reopening. The work- 
man, who fails to join within this period will be allow- 
ed further time up to five days, provided he can 
explain to the satisfaction of the Company the reason 
for delay in reporting for duties. Any workman, who 
fails to report for his duties within this time shall be 
deemed to have left the Company's services of his own 
accord and shall have no lien on his service in the 
Company. lLowever, a further extension of fifteen 
days may be allowed to a workman only on medical 
grounds, provided the workman informs the Manage- 
ment of his illness within the said period of fifteen 
days and produces a medical certificate from a Regis- 
tered Medica] Practitioner at the time of reporting for 
duties. Maternity cases will be dealt with as per .ہل‎ 
Rules, provided due intimation is sent to the Manage- 
ment requesting for leave within the aforesaid period 
of fifteen days.

as a special case, to allow the workman to enjoy leave 
on the basis of their actual days of working during the 
year 1968 irrespective of the fact that the workmen 
might not have worked for two hundred forty days in 
the year. 


9. It is agreed that the Company will pay Bonus 
for the accounting year 1967-68 to each of its eligible 
workmen at the rate of four per cent. to be calculated 
as prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965. 
This payment will be made before 27th December 
1968.
