The Company was being represented by Shri Atul 
Lahiri, Advocate, from the very beginning. After pass- 
ing through: several stages, the case was taken up for 
hearing on 18th September 1968 One of the concern- 
ed workmen, Shri Debendra Nath Paul was examined on 
that date as P.W. 1, and several documents on both the 
sides were produced and_ exhibited. On 24th October 
1968, the next date of hearing of this case, the Com- 
pany filed a_ petition for an adjournment, and the 
prayer was allowed. The case was then fixed on 25th 
November 1968, for further evidence. On this date 
(25th November 1968) Shri A. Ghosh, Advocate, 
appeared for the Company and filed a petition praying 
for an adjournment on the ground that he had been 
recently engaged and had been suffering from high 
fever. This prayer made on behalf of the Company 
was allowed and the case was adjourned to 10th Decem- 
ber 1968, for hearing. On 9th December 1968, Shri 
A. Ghosh, Advocate, appearing on behalf of the Com- 
pany filed a petition praying for hearing the prelimi- 
nary objections regarding the jurisdiction of this Tri- 
bunal on the ground of maintainability of the order of 
reference first, before entering into the merits of the 
dispute referred for adjudication. This prayer of the 
Company was allowed on 10th December 1968, as the 
objections raised struck to the root of the case, sub- 
ject to payment of Rs. 50 as_ costs to the workmen. 
Such cost of Rs. 50 was paid by the Company to the 
workmen on 19th December 1968, on which date the 
concerned workmen filed an _ objection § against the 
Company’s application filed on 9th December 1968, 
contending that the said Company's application was a 
misconceived one and is a belated attempt on the part 
of the Company to delay the matter. 


I have heard the representatives of both sides re- 
garding the maintainability of the order of reference 
and the jurisdiction of this Tribunal to entertain and 
adjudicate the issue in question referred to by the 
Government, at length on 19th December 1968. 


It has been canvassed from the side of the Company 
that the present order of reference is not maintainable 
in law inasmuch as the case of the five concerned work- 
men has not been espoused by any appreciable number 
of workmen of the Company or by any Union, to cons- 
titute an industrial dispute. The contention of Shri 
A. Ghosh, Advocate on behalf of the Company, is that 
the new section 2A of the Industrial Disputes Act by 
virtue of which the five concerned workmen had 
been made parties, is not retrospective in effect and 
therefore, the termination of services of the five con- 
cerned ‘workmen before the introduction of section 2A 
cannot be a_ subject-matter of the present reference, 
specially when the dispute has not been taken up by a 
number of workmen or by any Union. 


In order to decide the aforesaid question we must 
state first certain admitted facts of this case. Five con- 
cerned workmen Sarbashri Sourendra Mohan Moitra, 
Debendra Nath Paul (P.W. 1), Sk. Kaloo, Sk. Soley 
and Govinda Ch. Kundu, were undisputedly the workers 
of the Company. Charge-sheets, dated 17th February 
1964, were served on them (vide Exts. 1 series). 
There were domestic enquiries against all of them and 
by letters of dismissal, all the workmen were admitted- 
ly dismissed from the service with effect from 16th 
June 1964 (vide Annexure A of the written statement 
filed on behalf of the workmen). Dispute challenging 
the orders of dismissal was first raised before the 
Managing Director of the Company on 17th June 1966, 


[PART IC 


en ey soe + ৮ ১০ 
Se ot ولا چپ ےجو ججےےے‌ےبےموووفووود‎ ie ee সেভ - == 


by the letter Ext. J, written by the five concerned work- 
men. )ا‎ is also admitted that the conciliation proceed- 
ings started over this matter before the Labour Com- 
missjoner on 5th November 1966 (vide Ext. 7, copy 
of the letter of Labour Officer, dated Ist November 
1966), resulting to the instant order of reference of 
the Government, dated 10th April 1967, to the First 
Industrial Tribunal, under section 10 read with section 
2A of the Industrial Disputes Act and was then trans- 
ferred to this Tribunal by an order, dated 10th July 
1967. By the introduction of the Industrial Disputes 
(Amendment) Act of 1965 the new section 2A has been 
inserted. This section 2A runs as follows :— 


“Where any employer discharges, dismisses, re- 
trenches or otherwise terminates the services 
of an individual workman, any dispute or 
difference between that workman and his 
employer connected with, or arising out of, 
such discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or 
termination shall be deemed to be an indus- 
trial dispute notwithstanding that no other 
workman nor any union of workmen is a 
party to the dispute.” 


This Amending Act of 1965 received assent of the Pre- 
sident of India on the 19th November 1967. It was 
published in November 1965, for general information, 
and it came into force by the Central Government Noti- 
fication, dated 27th November 1965, with effect from 
the first day of December 1965. There cannot be any 
dispute that section 2A creates a substantive right and 
cannot be retrospective in operation. It cannot be said 
by any stretch of imagination that section 2A has only 
brought about a change in the procedural law as con- 
tended on behalf of the Union, and, therefore, although 
section 2A is not retrospective 17) effect, the instant 
order of reference is good because the workmen moved 
the Labour Commissioner for conciliation proceedings 
after section 2A had come into force on 1st December 
1965. According to Shri Pathak, when the Government 
has made the reference after the aforesaid date, i.e., 
on 10th April 1967, there cannot be any Jegal flaw over 
the maintainability of the same. It is also admitted 
that the case of the dismissed five workmen was not ‘es- 
poused by a number of workmen or by any Union in 
this case. Under section 2(k) of the Industrial Dis- 
putes Act, “industrial dispute’ means any dispute or 
difference between employers and employers or between 
employers and workmen, or between workmen and 
workmen, which is connected with the employment or 
non-employment or the terms of employment or with 
the conditions of labour of any person. It is now a 
well-settled principle of law that individual dispute, j.e., 
disputes directly concerning workmen individually can ٭‎ 
take up the character of an industrial dispute to which 
the Act applies, only when it is collectively supported 
and taken up by the other workmen or by a section of 
them or a Union representing them, before the date of 
reference. In other words, a dispute between an em- 
ployer and a single workman or some workmen is not 
per se an industrial dispute ; but it may become as such 
if taken by a number of workmen or a Union repre- 
senting the workmen. Collective support by the work- 
men is essential for making an individual dispute and 
industrial dispute. In the instant case it is undisputed 
that the dispute was initiated by the dismissed employees 
only. The services of the concerned workmen were un- 
disputedly terminated nearly 1} years prior to the date, ' 
when the aforesaid added section 2A came into force. 


PART 10] 


আপ সি | SRNR OGRE sO ee ETS OTIS CE 
আতিক 


The dispute challenging the dismissal was, of course, 
raised after section 2A has been inserted. By the intro- 
duction of new section 2A, individual workman ۰ھ‎ 
ed at the termination of service acquire a right to have 
his or their dispute adjudicated by the industrial Tribu- 
nal and to receive relief in appropriate cases. The new 
section has given such right to a dismissed workman. 
This section is not a procedural matter, pure and 
simple. The present dispute, accordingly, I hold, is 
not an industrial dispute as per the provisions of sec- 
tion 2A brought into being by Act XXXV of 1965. It 
can be argued that where a discharge or dismissal or 
retrenchment or termination of service took place prior 
to the date which section 2A came into force and con- 
tinued to exist on that date, the section came into force 
and thereafter, it would fall within the provisions of 
section 2A of the Industrial Disputes Act. But the 
instant case cannot be brought into within the compass 
of this proposition of law. It could not be the inten- 
tion of the Legislature that all dismissed personnel in 
the past could now claim reference after the introduc- 
tion of section 2A, on the ground that such a dismissal 
was an industrial dispute. 


In the above view of the case, I accept the conten- 
tion of Shri A. Ghosh, Advocate, challenging the main- 
tainability of the order of reference and also the juris- 
diction of this Tribunal to entertain and adjudicate 
upon the issue referred for adjudication by the Govern- 
ment first on 10th July 1967. In the result, I hold 
that the dispute under reference is not an industrial 
dispute within the meaning of the Industrial Disputes 
Act. I further hold that this Tribunal, accordingly, has 
no jurisdiction to adjudicate the issue under reference 
or to give any relief-whatsoever to the dismissed work- 
men Sarvashri Sourendra Mohan Moitra, Debendra 
Nath Paul, Sk. Kaloo, Sk. Soley and Govinda Ch. 
Kundu. This case is accordingly disposed of as not 
maintainable. 


This is my award.

Issue 


Whether the termination of service of Shri 
Jyotirmoy Das Gupta is justified? To 
what relief, if any, is he entitled? 


The workman has put in a written statement 
and alleged that Messrs. Sekai Private Ltd. is 
a well-established Advertising Marketing Con-

been seen that the copy of the letter of appointment 
Ext. H shows that Jyotirmoy Das Gupta was 
ت0"‎ 7 on probation for a period of 6 months. 

hat letter was signed by the Manager (O. P. W: 2, 
Mr. U. Joshi). He also says that he made the 
appointment with the concurrence of the Chairman. 
It has already been found that the original letter 
of appointment along with the duplicate was made 
over to the workman concerned by the O. P. W. 3 
Mr. D. Ganguly. The O. P. W. 2 Mr. U. Joshi 
has stated that with the concurrence of the Chairman 
he had terminated the services of the workman. The 
letter of termination Ext. K, dated 8th May 1967, 
was also signed by him and he has aserted therein 
that Jyotirmoy Das Gupta was the production 
assistant on probation and his services were termi- 
nated under clause 3 of the letter of appoint- 


ment, dated 15th March 1967. 


The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of 
the Company has cited the case of Rohtas [ndustries 
Ltd. vs. Brijnandan Pandey in 1956 (II) L.LJ.. 
444, to show that where the Company engages tem- 
porary workman and the appointment contract, inter 
alia, provided that though put on a permanent work, 
the workman would not become permanent unless 
the Works Manager made him _ permanent in 
writing, and when the Company sought to terminate 
his services, in the absence of any suggestion or 
proof of unfair Labour Practice or victimisation, 
permission should be granted to terrhinate his ser- 
vices. He has contended that since Jyotirmoy Das 
Gupta was a temporary workman, his services 
could be terminated by the Management any 
moment at its pleasure. This contention is absolute- 
ly malicious and should not have been advanced for 
the stand of the Company is that he was a 
probationer. The aforesaid case of Rohtas Indus- 
tries Ltd. vs. Brijnandan relates to the employ- 
ment of a temporary worker, whereas in the instant 
case we are dealing with the case of P. W. 1 J. 
Das Gupta, who even according to the Chairman 
of the Company (O. P r. D. Dinanath), 
was appointed probationer for 6 months. Reference 
may be made to the case of Express Newspapers Ltd., 
in 1964 (I) L.L.J., 9 at p. 11(SC) to show that within 
the period of probation, the workman has the same 
rights as a permanent employee and so his services 
cannot be terminated except on the ground of miscon- 
duct or other sufficient reason. 


01 course in this case it has already been indi- 
cated that the workman concerned was guilty of 
seyere misconduct. 


PART IC] 
৩ = =o ee 


The P. W. 1 Jyotirmoy Das’ Gupta has admitted 
that on 11th May 1967, he went to the Company’s 
office and he was shown that letter of termination 
of his services. He also admits that on that date 
he received his salary for 6 days up to 6th May 
1967, vide the voucher, Ext. C. That voucher shows 
that such payment was made in full and final 
settlement. That voucher does not indicate that the 
workman signified his protest when he accepted his 
salary for 6 days. So it appears that the authority 
who issued the letter of appointment (Ext. H) مم‎ 
garding the disputed workman, issued the letter of 
termination, vide Ext. .ا‎ 9০ the appointing 
authority and the dismissing authority was the same. 


Reference may be made to the case of Rohtas 
Industries ‘Ltd., Dalmiah Nagar Vs. Ali Hassan 
in 1963 (1) L.L.J., 253 to show that where the 
workm«n were dismissed without any domestic en- 
quiry, it is open to the Industrial Tribunal to take 
evidence and decide the matter for itself on an 
application for approval of the action taken against 
them. It is common ground that the workman was 
not charge-sheeted and he was not heard before 
his services were terminated on 8th May 1967. ۲ 
has already been found that the workman was 
guilty of severe misconduct because he _ stealthily 
removed his leave application Ext. 2 from the Com- 
pany’s office along with the Manager’s notes thereon 
(Ext. J) and he intentionally enjoyed leave for 3 
days though no leave was sanctioned. The facts 
and circumstances previously discussed, will show 
that there is no infirmity in the evidence adduced by 
the Company against the workman concerned. 
There was no victimisation or punitive measure or 
unfair labour practice. Since a case of gross mis- 
conduct has been proved against him, this Tribunal 
holds that the order of termination of his services, 
dated 8th May 1967, is justified and must, in the 
circumstances, be upheld. That was not a slight 
offence and hence no severe order was_ passed. 
পর the workman is not entitled to any 
relief. 


It has been argued on behalf of the Company 
that the reference is not maintainable in law because 
the Government has stated that there is an industrial 
dispute between Messrs. Sekai Private Ltd. and 
their workman, Shri Jyotirmoy Das Gupta. Re- 
ference has been made to the case of Express 
Newspapers in 1959 (I) L.L.J., 600, to show that 
there will be an industrial dispute if the case of 
any individual workman is taken up by the Union 
to which the majority or a large portion of the 
workmen employed in the particular industry are 
concerned in the dispute. In the instant case the 
dispute is not being pressed by any Union but by 
the workman himself. The new section 2A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act is ultra vires of the Indus- 
trial Disputes Acct. 


The section 2A says that where any employer 
discharges, dismisses, retrenches or otherwise termi- 
nates the services of an individual workman, any 
dispute or difference between that workman and his 
employer connected with, or arising out of, such 
discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or termination 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 23, 1969 87 


পে সস 


shall be deemed to be an industrial dispute notwith- 
standing that no other workman or any Union of 
workmen is a party to the dispute. 


The aforesaid case of Express Newspapers was 
reported long ago, whereas the amending section 
of the Act was inserted in the Act with effect from 
1st December 1965. In order to cover cases where 
an employee is not attached to any Union, that 
section was incorporated in the Act and such incor- 
poration was for the benefit of the workman con- 
cerned مز‎ particular cases and to meet such 
contingencies. 


Reference may be made to the case of Moti Das 
Vs. 9. P. Sahi in ۸.۱... 1959 S.C., 942, to show 
that it is well-established that there is a presump- 
tion in favour of constitutionality of an enactment 
and the onus is on the person who maintains the 
contrary. It will further appear from that case that 
it must be presumed that the legislature understands 
and correctly appreciates the needs of the people 
and its laws are directed to problems made mani- 
fest by experience. It has already been indicated 
that the legislature considered these aspects and in 
order to meet such problems introduced the new 
section 2A to the Act. So this Tribunal is of 
opinion that the new section 2A of the Industrial 
Disputes Act is not ultra vires of the Act. 


The reference is disposed of accordingly. 


Dictated and corrected by me.

AWARD 


On the issue “whether the workmen are entitled 
to any more bonus than that declared by the Com- 
pany on the trading result of the financial year 
ended 31st December 1966, payable in 1967”, there 
having existed an industrial dispute between Messrs. 
Scott & Saxby Ltd., 1 Taratalla Road, Calcutta-24 
(hereinafter called the Company), and their work- 
men represented by Scott & Saxby Employees’ 
Union, 3 Jay Krishna Paul Road, Calcutta-23 
(hereinafter called the Union), the Governor of 
West Bengal was pleased in exercise of the 
powers conferred by section 10 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 1947, on him, to refer the said in- 
dustrial dispute for adjudication to this Tribunal 
under Government of West Bengal, Labour 
Department, order No. 6674-I.R./IR/11L-346/67, 
dated the 20th December 1967. 


On receipt of the aforesaid order, this Tribunal 
started a case on 23rd December 1967 and issued 
usual notices to the parties to the dispute demand- 
ing their appearance before the Tribunal on 27th 
January 1968 and filing of written statement by 
the Union. On 27th January 1968 the Union 
appeared before the Tribunal and filed its written 
statement in triplicate, a copy of which was made 
over to the other side and 27th February 1968 was 
fixed for filing of written statement by the Company. 
On 28th February 1968 the Company appeared 
before the Tribunal and filed its written statement 
in reply a copy of which was made over to the other 
side. Thereafter, the Tribunal fixed various dates 
for taking various steps preparatory to the peremp- 
tory hearing of the case. That over, the case was 
fixed for hearing on 22nd August 1968. On 22nd 
August 1968 the parties appeared before the 
Tribunal and filed a petition praying for adjourn- 
ment on the ground that a talk of settlement was 
going on between the parties. The Tribunal con- 
sidered the petition and granted time till 4th 
November 1968. On 4th November 1968 Shri A. 

۱ Roy, Vice-President of the Union, appeared for 
the Union and Shri D. K. Ghosh, Assistant Legal 
Adviser of I.E. A., appeared for the Company. The 


[PART IC 


parties filed a joint petition of compromise which 
bears the signature of the Works Manager of the 
Company and that of Shri Rajani Mukherjee, 
President, Rahmat Khan Vice-President, amongst 
others of the Union. The Tribunal accepted the 
petition and reserved its award. 


The petition filed by the parties is perused by 
the Tribunal and it finds the Terms of Settlement 
arrived at by the parties to this dispute fair and 
reasonable. The terms of agreement have satished 
the parties to the dispute and there is no reason why 
the Tribunal should not accept the joint petition 
fled by the parties. Therefore, accepting the 
petition of compromise, I hereby pass this compro- 
mise award as prayed for by the parties. The 
petition filed by the parties shall form an integral 
part of this award and be published as Annexure 
‘A’ hereto. 


Let usual number of copies of this award be 
sent to the State Government for necessary action.

AWARD 


By the Government of West Bengal, Labour 
Department, order No. 4619-I.R./IR/10L-257/66, 
dated the 1st December 1966, an’ industrial dispute 
between Messrs. Asia Electric Lamp Co. Private 
Ltd., 45 Durga Charan Mukherjee Street, Calcutta-3, 
and their workmen represented by Asia Electric 
Lamp Mazdoor Congress, 292/7 Rabindra Sarani, 
Calcutta-9, was referred under section 10 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, to this Tribunal for 


adjudication, in respect of the following issue :— 


Issue 


Whether the closure of the factory with effect 
from the 29th August 1966 is real and bona 
fide? Whether the closure was beyond the 
control of the management and in the circums- 
tances justified? What relief, if any, are 
the workmen entitled to? 


Usual notices were served on the Union, as well 
as the Company, from this Tribunal after receipt 
of the order of reference. The Union, being Asia 
Electric Lamp Mazdoor Congress filed its written 
statement on 17th January 1967. . The Company, 
on the other hand, filed their written statement on 
31st March 1967. Then 21st August 1967 was 
fixed for hearing of this order of reference. The 
case was then adjourned either on the application 
of the Company or on the application of the Union, 
on several occasions for hearing. On 19th October 
1967, the Director of the Company filed a petition 
along with a Memorandum of Settlement, with 
several workmen alleging that in pursuance of the 
said Memorandum of Settlement, the factory was 
reopened and all workmen have joined, accepting 
the same. By that petition, the Company prayed 
for passing a ‘no dispute’ award. No action was, 
of course, taken on this petition filed by the Director 
of the Company. Then, on the prayer of either 
party, the case was adjourned on several dates for 
the purpose of hearing. On 30th August 1968, a 
joirft petition for the management of the Company 
and for Asia Electric Lamp Mazdoor Congress 
was filed. This petition, dated 28th August 1968 
and filed before this Tribunal on 30th August 1968 
was signed. by Shri Swapan Kumar Saha, Director 
of the Company and the Vice-President and also 
the General Secretary of Asia Electric Lamp 
Mazdoor Congress. In this petition, it was stated 
that in terms of an agreement entered into, the 
workmen had received payment of their dues and 
have joined the factory which was reopened on 
30th August 1967. By this application, parties 
prayed for passing a ‘no dispute’ award in this case. 
On the same date, i.e., on 30th August 1967, a 
petition signed by 67 workmen of the Company, was 
also filed before this Tribunal alleging that they 
had severed all connections with the Asia Electric 
Lamp Mazdoor Congress and have formed a new 
Union, viz., Asia Electric Lamp Company Private Ltd. 
Workers’ Union, and praying for adding the said 
Union as a party to the order of reference. This 
Tribunal on this petition could not amend the order 
of reference and asked the workmen to approach 
the appropriate Government for the purpose. Then 
those workmen took several adjournments for the 


said purpose, but they lastly on 26th December 
1968, filed a petition before this Tribunal for with- 
drawing the said petition filed on 30th August 
1968 and also prayed for passing a ‘no dispute’ 
award in this case. This petition has been signed 
by the same Director, Shri Swapan Kumar Saha 
of the Company as well as the Secretary and a 
workman of Asia Electric Lamp Company Private 
Limited Workers’ Union. (Registered No. 7950). 
On 26th December 1968 also, the representatives 
of Asia Electric Lamp Mazdoor «Congress, who 
signed the joint petition filed on 30th August 1968, 
before this Tribunal, appeared. I have heard the 
Director and the representatives of Asia Electric 
Lamp Mazdoor Congress and Asia Electric Lamp 
Company Private Limited Workers’ Union ৪৪ 
aforesaid, in person. I am satished that neither 
party of this order of reference nor the applicants, 
ie., the workers of the Company, who signed the 
petition, filed on 30th August 1968, are interested 
in the matter of proceeding with the hearing of this 
order of reference and that there is no dispute 
whatsoever between them, over the issue. sent for 
adjudication. Accordingly, | pass a ‘no dispute’ 
award in this case. 


This is my award.

AWARD 


By the Government of West Bengal, Labourt Depart- 
ment, order No. 1588-I.R./IR/4L-21/66, dated the 22nd 
April 1966, an industrial dispute existing between Shri 
Baldeo Shaw, owner of Bus No. WBR-1075 of Route 
No. 78, 18 Thakurdas Chatterjee Road, P.O. Kamar- 
haty, 24-Parganas, and his workmen represented by 
Barrackpore Bus Employees’ Union, 8. T. Road, 
Khardah, 24-Parganas, was referred under section 10 
of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, to this Tribunal 
for adjudication, in respect of the following issue : 


Issue 


Whether the termination of service of Shri N. 
Krishna Rao, is justified ? To what relief, if 
any, is he entitled ? 


After receipt of the order of reference, usual notices 
were served on the owner of the Bus as well as the 
Union. Both the owner of the Bus, and also the Union 
appeared before this Tribunal. The Union filed its 
written statement on 19th July 1966. The Bus owner 
in turn filed his written statement on 3rd August 1967. 
After several stages, the order of reference was fixed 
on 4th January 1968, for hearing. On an application 
for adjournment filed on behalf of the Union on 4th 
January 1968, this case was adjourned to 2nd April 
1968, for hearing. Then the case was adjourned to 
25th July 1968, for hearing. On this date, i.e., on 25th 
July 1968, the Union as well as the Bus owner filed 
a joint petition for adjournment on the ground that the 
case was likely to be amicably settled. Their prayer 
was allowed and the case was adjourned to 19th August 
1968, for hearing, if talk of compromise fails. On 
19th August 1968, on an application for adjournment 
filed on behalf of the Union, the case was adjourned 
till 3131 August 1968, for hearing. Then on an appli- 
cation filed by Shri Nanda Dulal Srimani, Advocate for 
the Union, on 27th August 1968, the date of hearing 
was shifted to 24th October 1968. Again on 24th 
October 1968, on an application filed by Shri N. D. 
Srimani, Advocate, the case was adjourned to 17th 
December 1968, for hearing. On 17th December 
1968, again, Shri N. D. Srimani, Advocate, appeared 
for the Union and filed a petition for adjournment. 
His prayer was allowed and the case was adjourned till 
today (26th December 1968) for hearing. Today, 
Shri N. D. Srimani, Advocate, and Shri Madan Saha, 
Advocate, appeared before me for the Union as well 
as the Bus owner respectively. According to both of 
them, they have got no further instructions to proceed 
with the hearing of the instant order of reference. 
Shri N. D. Srimani, Advocate for the Union, has 
endorsed in the order-sheet to the above effect. 


In the above view of the case, I am of opinion that 
neither party is interested to proceed with the hearing 
of this order of reference and as such ] pass a “no- 
dispute” award in this case. 


This is my award. 
Dictated and corrected by me. 


G. B. GHOSH, 
Judge. 


G. B. GHOSH, Judge, 
Third Industrial Tribunal. 
26-12-68. 


By order of the Governor, 
N. R. SIRCAR, Asstt. Secy.

following issue : |] 


Issue 


Whether the termination of service of Shri Netai 
Chandra Ganguli is justified? To what 
relief, if any, is he entitled? 


Usual notices were served on the Company as 
well as the Union from this Tribunal after receipt 
of the order of reference. Both the Union as well 
as the Company appeared. The Union filed its 
written statement on 4th November 1967 and the 
Company in turn, filed written statement on 11th 
March 1968. After several stages, the case was 
fixed on 6th September 1968 for hearing of this 
instant order of reference. On 6th کی"‎ 1968,

This is my award.

[PART 16

Issue No. 1 


Regarding closure the case of the Union as made 
out in its written statement is that since prior to 19th 
September 1967, several disputes were pending between 
the workmen and the management over certain matters 
such as implementation of the Wage Board's recom- 
mendations, abolition of the contract system of work, 
imposition of illegal fines and non-payment of wages 
of two days in March 1967. There was also a dispute 
over bonus for the year 1966. During pendency of 
these disputes the Company without any justification 
and without any reason whatsoever declared closure of 
its factory with effect from 19th September 1967 by a 
notice, dated 18th September 1967, purported to be 
under provision of section 25FFF of the Industrial 
Disputes Act. The allegations made in the said notice 
of closure are mala fide, baseless and have been made 
with intent to defeat of the legitimate demands of the 
workers. The Company, however, reopened _ the 
factory on 11:5 December 1967, by a_ notice, dated 
911) December 1967. 


The case of the Company as made out in the written 
statement is that the said closure is a real and 
bona fide one. It is stated further that for various 
subversive and rowdy acts of the workers as stated in 
the notice of closure, the Company was compelled to 
close down the factory for circumstances beyond their 
control. It is submitted on behalf of the Company 
that the workmen are not entitled to get any relief in 
excess of what has been offered to them as compensa- 
tion in accordance with the proviso to section 25FFF 
of the Industrial Disputes Act, as standardised for 
closure due to unavoidable circumstances beyond the 
control of the management. 


On behalf of the Union, its General Secretary Shri 
Pannalal Datta (P.W. 1) has proved three letters, 
Exts. 2, 2/a and 2/b, and a collective petition, Ext. 3, 
to show that some disputes were pending in March and 
April 1967. His letter, dated 4th August 1967, written 
to the Assistant Labour Commissioner (Ext. 4), 
regarding demand of bonus for the trading year 1966, 
shows that a dispute over payment of bonus for the 
year 1966 was also pending at that time. The letters, 
Exts. 5, 5/a and 6, were written after the closure. 
Regarding the conditions prevailing in the factory 
immediately prior to the closure, dated 19th September 
1967, O.P.W. 1, D.C. Chakraborty, the Works 
Manager of the Company, has deposed that the facts 
mentioned in the notice, Ext. 1, are correct. He has 
proved the letters, Exts. F to F/3, written by him to the 
Managing Director of the Company prior 10 the 
closure mentioning about the conditions prevailing in 
the factory at that time. In Ext. F, dated 2nd June 
1967, there is mention of threat of Gherao of the 
Works Manager, The letter, Ext. F/1, dated 23rd 
August 1967, shows that the Works Manager was 
actually Gheraoed on that day. Ext. F/2, dated 16th 
September 1967, speaks about serious acts of indisci- 
pline and threats prevailing in the factory. In Ext. F/3, 
dated 18th September 1967, the Works Manager has 
expressed his apprehension of physical violence on him. 
O.P.W. 2, Shri Ananda Mohan Lahiry, the Factory 
Accountant of the Company, has deposed that on 28th 
April 1967 he was Gheraoed by a batch of workers who 
threatened him and made violent demonstration, and 
that he was ultimately rescued by the police under a 
Search Warrant, Ext. 1/1. O.P.W. 2 has stated further 
that since August 1967, the workmen started violent 
demonstration, abusing the officers and _ inscribing 
abusive language on the factory walls and threatened 
them with dire consequences, and that he was not 


allowed to enter the factory premises since 15th Septem- 
ber 1967. In cross-examination he has stated that 
he was not Gheraoed on any other day subsequent to 
28th April 1967. O.P.W. 3, Shri Sukumar Dey, the 
Secretary of the Company, has deposed that the 
factory reopened on the 11th December 1967, and 
that it started anew as the circumstances had changed. 


It is submitted on behalf of the Union that 
admittedly there was no Gherao inside the factory 
after 28th April 1967, and that the Company's 
case regarding alleged acts of indiscipline and 
threats prevailing in the factory immediately prior 
to the closure cannot be believed inasmuch as no 
paper has been filed relating to the alleged incident 
since August 1967, and no specific instance has also 
been mentioned in the notice of closure, Ext. 1. But 
I find no substance in this contention. There is 
no reason to disbelieve the letters, Exts. F/1, F/2 
and F/3, which give a clear picture of lawlessness, 
indiscipline and chaos prevailing in the factory 
since 23rd August 1967 till 18th of September 
1967. This is corroborated by the evidence of 
O.P.W. 2, Shri Ananda Mohan Lahiri, which has 


already been discussed above. 


On behalf of the Company my attention has been 
drawn to a decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court 
reported in A.I.R., 1968, S C, p.1002 (Messrs. 
Indian Hume Pipe Co. Ltd., Appellant vs. their work- 
men, Respondents) in which it has been held that 
once the Tribunal finds that an employer has closed 
its factory as a matter of fact it is not conceryed to 
go into the question as to the motive which guided 
him and to come to a conclusion that because of the 
previous history of the dispute between the employer 
and the employees the closure was not justified. 
According to their Lordship such a closure cannot 
give rise to an industrial dispute. This view has 
also been subsequently confirmed by the Hon’ble 
Supreme Court in the case of Kalinga Tubes Ltd. 
vs. their workmen. The aforesaid principle of law 
laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court is certainly 
binding on me. In the instant case the factum of 
closure of the factory is not disputed. After con- 
sidering the entire facts and circumstances of the 
present case ] am inclined to hold that the closure 
of the factory was bona fide and_ genuine, and that 
such closure was due to unavoidable circumstances 
beyond the control of the management. There is .no 
dispute that the workmen have not received com- 
pensati' » in accordance with the proviso to section 
25FFF cf the Industrial Disputes Acct. e work- 
men are not, therefore, entitled to any further relief. 
Issue No. 1 is thus disposed .)ہم‎ 


Issue No. 2 

This issue has not been pressed on behalf of the 
Union at the time of hearing. 

This is my award. 
Dictated and corrected by me.

Decision 


With regard to the five issues I give my decision 
as below : 


(a) Classification of the workmen: 


The workmen who have been performing 
manual work only and whose nature of employ- 
ment is as such, do not have to help in operating 
‘machines, shall be placed in the category of un- 
skilled workmen. The new recruits may be kept 
in that category as they are not conversant with 
the production technique. At the moment the 
Company has 21 workmen in that category, i.e., 
about 22 per cent. of the workmen engaged by the 
Company are unskilled workmen. 


The workmen who normally according to the 
job requirements of the Company, help the opera- 
tion of machines and productign processes but 
cannot run the machines independently and cannot 
work independently shall be placed in the category 
of semi-skilled workmen. At present there are 31 
workmen in this category, i.e., about 40 per cent. of 
the workmen engaged by the Company are semi- 
skilled workmen. 


The workmen who are capable of running the 
machines independently and possess knowledge 
about the mechanism of the machines and also are 
in a position to operate, shall be kept in the cate- 
gory of skilled workmen. At present the Company 
has 17 such workmen, i.e., about 20 per cent. of the 
workmen engaged in the factory are skilled work- 
men. 


The Company in their written statement opined 
that they have no highly skilled workmen in their 
foctory. However, on a scrutiny of the detailed

See 


wage statement of the workmen it appears that they | 
have indicated that there are 8 workmen who can 
be termed as highly skilled. According 10 the 
Company they represent about 10 per cent. of thes 
workmen engaged in the factory. 


(b) Placement of the workmen: 


The above paragraphs indicate the current place- 
ment of the workmen of the Company, It appears 
that in the skilled category of workmen there are 5 
workmen who have been drawing more than Rs. 
117 the lowest wage of a skilled workmen. Those 
5 workmen shall be fitted into the category of 
highly skilled workmen and should get such wages 
and allowances fixed for the highly skilled work- 
men. These workmen are : (i) Bania Ram 
Laksman, (ii) Dey Sudhir, (iii) Kori Ram 
Bharosh, (iv) Pal Dhiren, and (v) Sarkar 
Nirapada. 


The vacancies occuring as a result of upgrading 
of above 5 skilled workmen to the category of

hese five workmen are: (i) Bania Ram _ Laks- 
man (2), (ii) Dey Dhiren, (iii) Ghosh Dilip, (iv) 
Sett Mangroo, and (v) Sarkar Hemnath.

পুতি —= 


In view of the above considerations I would not 
award separate D.A. for the workmen. 


(e) Wages of the workmen for the lockout period: 


The Company locked out their factory as a result 
of an unhappy incident which has been characterised as 
‘gherao’. Undoubtedly the Company took resort to 
lockout in view of the indiscipline that prevailed at that 
moment. Much water has flown in the meantime and 
a smooth and peaceful climate has since been restored. 
To avoid further bitterness and controversy I would 
not award any wages to the workmen for the lockout 
period. 


All the issues under reference are disposed of accor- 
dingly.

industrial dispute between Messrs. Cosmo Equip- 
ment Co., 10/19A Deshpran Sasmal Road, Calcutta- 
33, and their workmen. represented by Shri 
Pannalal Dutta, 23 Russa Road South, 2nd Lane, 
Calcutta-33, regarding the issues mentioned in the 
said order being matters specified in the Third 
Schedule to the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
(XIV of 1947), was referred for adjudication to 
the Fifth Industrial Tribunal; . 


And whereas the said Fifth Industrial Tribunal 
has submitted to the State Government its award 
on the said industrial dispute;

of section 17 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
(XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased hereby to 
publish the said award as shown in the annexure 
hereto. | 


98 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 23, 1969 [PART IC 
—— OO ae 
ANNEXURE before the Conciliation Officer by the workmen, 


In the matter of an industrial dispute existing 
between Messrs. Cosmo Equipment Co., 
10/19۸ Deshpran Sasmal Road, Calcutta-33, 
and their workmen represented by Shri 
Pannalal Dutta, 23 Russa Road South, 2nd 
Lane, Calcutta-33. (Case No. 707 of 1967.) 


BEFORE THE FIFTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL,. 


WEST BENGAL 
Present: 


Shri T. K. MUTSUDDI, Judge, 
Fifth Industrial Tribunal. 


Present for the Company: Shri Kiron Mitra and 
Shri Shyam Sundar Choudhury, Advocates. 


Present for the Workmen: Shri Biswanath Ash, 
Advocate. 


By the Government of West Bengal, Labour 
Department, order No. 4654-I.R./IR/10L-303/67, 
dated the 15th September 1967, this industrial 
dispute between Messrs. Cosmo Equipment Co. 
and their workmen was referred to this Tribu- 
nal under scction 10 of the Industrial Disputes 
Act for adjudication on the issues mentioned 
below. 


Issues 
1. Basic Wages—grades and scales. 
2. Dearness Allowance. 


On receipt of the reference usual notices were 
served on the parties, and they made their appear- 
ances and filed their respective written statements. 


The Company takes a preliminary objection as 
to the maintainability of the reference. In the 
first place, it has been submitted on behalf of 
the Company that the issue regarding dearness 
allowance cannot be a subject-matter of a refe- 
rence as the parties entered into an agreement 
before the Conciliation Officer regarding this issue 
in question. 


The Company has adduced evidence to show 
that the workers were given higher dearness 
allowance after the dispute had been raised ما‎ 
fore the Conciliation Officer. It may be that the 
workers accepted higher dearness allowance. 
But it does not necessarily follow (1771 the 
workers and the Company entered into an agree- 
ment regarding dearness allowance. It is the 
case of the Company that the settlement was 
arrived at before the Conciliation Officer. Ext. 
1 is the order-sheet of the conciliation proceed- 
ings, and Ext. 2 is the order passed by the Con- 
ciliation Officer. Ext. 1 does not show that any 
settlement was arrived at between the parties 
before the Conciliation Officer during the pen- 
dency of the conciliation proceedings. Ext. 2 
does not show any such agreement between the 
parties. I, therefore, find that, the Company’s 
assertion that an agreement was reached at re- 
garding dearness allowance is not at all true. So, 
it cannot be said that the issue regarding dear- 
ness allowance is not maintainable. 


It is, however, submitted by the Company that 
the entire reference is invalid and that it is not 
maintainable. It is submitted on behalf of the 
Company that the dispute has not been raised 


according to law. It appears that 13 workers of 
the Company authorised Shri Pannalal Dutta, 
who is said to be the General Secretary of Maya 
‘Engineering Works, to represent them in the con- 
ciliation proceedings. Admittedly, these 13 
workers are not members of any Union. They 
are also not member of the Union of Maya Engi- 
necring Works. Section 36(1) says that a work- 
man who is a party to a dispute shall be entitled 
to be represented in any proceeding under the 
Act by (a) an officer of a registered trade union 
of which he is a member, (b) an officer of a 
federation of trade unions to which the 11806 
union referred to in clause (a) is affiliated ; (c) 
where the worker is not a member of any trade 
union, by an officer of any trade union connec- 
ted with, or by any other workman employed 
in, the industry in which the worker is employed 
and authorised in such manner as may be pres- 
cribed. Admittedly, the workers have got no 
union. The question is whether section 36(1)(c) 
comes to their rescue. When the workers are 
not members of any Trade Union, they may be 
represented by an officer of a Trade Union con- 
nected with similar industry. Now, it is the 
case of the workers that they authorised Shri 
Pannalal Dutta, General Secretary of the Maya 
Engineering Workers Union, to represent them. 
The evidence of O.P.W. 1 Shri Wazir Chand, the 
proprietor of the Company, is that this Company 
is engaged in the manufacture of Loose Leaf 
Binders and other office equipments, and that 
this Company is not similar to Maya Engineering 
Works. His evidence goes unchallenged. There 
has been no cross-examination on this point. 
Pannalal Dutta is the General Secretary of the 
Maya Engineering Workers’ Union. The Cosmo 
Equipment Company is not at all an engineer- 
ing establishment. It is engaged in the manu- 
facture of Loose Leaf Binders and other office 
equipments. So it cannot be said that this 
Company is similar to an engineering establish. 
ment. That being so, the workers are not en- 
titled to be represented by Pannalal Dutta who 
is the General Secretary of an_ Enginecring 
Workers’ Union. I find that the workmen were 
not properly represented before the Conciliation 
Officer. It is not the case of the workers that 
they themselves raised the dispute before the 
Conciliation OMcer. I, therefore, find that the 
dispute was not raised by the workers themselves 
or through any legally represented body. 


In the circumstances, it must be held that there 


_1s no industrial dispute before me and, conse- 


quently, it must be held that this reference is 
not maintainable. 


The reference is, therefore, rejected. 
Dictated and corrected by me. 


T. K. MUTSUDDI, 
Judge. 
2-1-69. T. K. MUTSUDDI, Judge, 

Fifth Industrial Tribunal.

CALCUTTA IMPROVEMENT TRUST 


THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES FOR THE 
IMPROVEMENT OF CALCUTTA 


Notice under section 43 of the Calcutta Improvement 
Act, 1911 (Bengal Act V of 1911) 


Calcutta, the 3150 December 1968. 


Scheme No. XV-M (Supplementary) 


It is hereby notified under section 43 of the Calcutta 

Improvement Act, 1911, that a Rehousing Scheme for 
the construction of flats and shops for providing alter- 
native accommodation mainly to the bustee-dwellers 
and shop-keepers to be displaced due to execution of 
Scheme No. XV-M (Widening of Manicktala Main 
Road between Scheme No. I-M and western flank of 
Railway Bridge) on a block of 19170 in Scheme No. 
VI-M (Narkeldanga Main Road to Manicktala Main 
Road) and Scheme No. VII-M (Manicktala Main 
Road to Ultadanga Main Road), to be hereinafter 
known as Scheme No. XV-M (Supplementary), has 
been framed by the Board of Trustees for the Im- 
provement of Calcutta in constituency No. 32 of the 
Calcutta Corporation. 


2. The area comprised within and ধা for the 
execution of the scheme (shown in yellow verge in 
the plan) measures 1.71 acres, more or less, and is 
more particularly described below:— 


Boundaries of the land 
On the North: Calcutta Improvement Trust 
acquired land in Scheme No. VII-M. 


On the East: 40 feet wide Calcutta Improvement 
Trust Road in Scheme Nos. VI-M and VII-M. 


On the South: 120 feet wide Manicktala Main 
Road. 


°On the West: 
embankment. 


Eastern Railway permanent way 


3. Particulars of the scheme and a map of the 
area comprised in the scheme may be scen at tho 
office of the Calcutta Improvement Trust at 10 Netaji 
Subhas Road, Calcutta-1, on week days between 1 
a.m. and 3 p.m. and on Saturdays between 11 a.m. 
and 12 noon. All the lands required for the execu- 
tion of the scheme have already been acquired in 
connection with Calcutta Improvement Trust Scheme 
Nos. VI-M and VII-M. 


Copies of the above documents will be available on 
payment of the following fees:— 


Particulars of the scheme—Re, 0.25P. 
Plan of the scheme area—Re. 1.00P. 


4. Objection will be received by the Chairman up 
to the 17th March 1969. 
M. ISMAIL, 


Chairman.

NOTICE 


The 3rd January 1969 

Notice is hereby given for information of the public 
that the Corporation of Calcutta in exercise of the 
powers vested in it under section 356 of the Calcutta 
Municipal Act, 1951, has by its resolution, dated the 
22nd November 1968, prescribed a road alignment 
for Ballygunge Store Road, now Gurusaday Road, to 
a width of 60 ft. in Ward No. 59, now 72.

in this office of the Chief Valuer and Surveyor on any, 
working day during the hours of 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. 
On payment of usual fees.

he matter of an igdustrial dispute between 

= রা Fort Gloster Industries Ltd., P.O. Fort

BEFORE THE SECOND LABOUR COURT,

For the Company: Shri S. Sen, Advocate.

AWARD 


The Labour Department, Government of West 
Bengal, has referred to this Labour Court an indus- 
trial dispute between Messrs. Fort Gloster Industries 
Ltd., P.O. Fort Gloster, district Howrah, and their 
workmen represented by Bengal Chatkal Mazdoor 
Union, Bauria Branch, village Radhanagar, P.O. Fort 
Gloster, district Howrah, by its order No. 3374-I.R./ 
IR/7L.-32/67, dated 20th July 1967, under section 
10, Industrial Disputes Act, on the following 
issue :— 

Issue 


Whether the dismissal of Shri Sanaton Ghosh 
is justifed ১ What relief including the nature 
of work is he entitled to ? 


Usual notices were served upon the parties direc- 
ting them to appear on 6th September 1967 and the 
Union to file its written statement by that date. The 
Union filed its written statement on 6th September 
1967. The O.P.-Company filed an authority autho- 
rising Shri S. C. Sen, Advocate, and 9177 B. 


Sarma, Chief Personnel Officer, to ‘conduct its case. 


10 


অর 
— سے سے۔”٭إ”‌ —— ہے‎ 


- 
موچ‎ সপ ৩০ oe Es Ge ee leit سے‎ = 


By my order No. 2, dated 6th September 1967, the 
O.P.-Company was directed to file its written state- 
ment by 21st September 1967. The O.P.-Company 
oan time on several occasions and ultimately filed 
its ‘written statement on 27th October 1967. | 


و 


{ 
The Union’s case is that O.P.-Company employs 


about 5,000 workmen in its various departments. The ‘ 


petitioner-workman was a Turner of the Lathe 
Machine in the Company and served the Company 
for long 13 years. He was an active worker of the 
Bengal Chatkal Mazdoor Union and played an 
effective role in bringing the workers of the Company 
under the banner of the said Union, much to the dis- 
comfort of the Company. The O.P.-Company issu- 
ed a charge-sheet upon the petitioner-workman on 
30th October 1965, to which the petitioner-workman 
replied by his explanation, dated 1st November 1969. 
The Company invited the petitioner-workman to an 
enquiry on 4th November 1965, when the petitioner- 
workman by his letter, dated 4th November 1965, 
wanted assistance of a competent person to help him 
at the time of the domestic enquiry and also made cer- 
tain other enquiries. The O.P.-Company replied by 
a letter, dated 4th November 1965, virtually denied 
everything and refused the prayer of the petitioner- 
workman. Under the circumstances, the petitioner- 
workman did not appear at the time of the domestic 
enquiry, which was held ex parte. The domestic 
enquiry ‘was mala fide and was in violation of the 
principles of natural justice. The petitioner-workman 
was found guilty at the time of the ex parte domes- 
tic enquiry and he was dismissed from his service 
by a letter, dated 13th November 1965. The find- 
ing of the domestic enquiry was erroneous, perverse 
and otherwise illegal and void. The Union made 
a‘ representation to the Assistant Labour Commissioner, 
Howrah, by its letter, dated 23rd November 1965, 
when after several conciliation meetings the Concilia- 
tion Officer asked the O.P.Company to reinstate the 
petitioner-workman in his original post and the peti- 
tioner-workman was also told to write a letter for sof- 
tening the feelings of the management. As such, the 
petitioner-workman wrote a letter to the O.P.-Company 
on 10th June 1966, accordingly, but the petitioner- 
workman was betrayed and the Company tried to 
outwit him in a mala fide manner as would be evident 
from the Union's’ representation, dated 16th June 
1966, to the Assistant Labour Commissioner, Howrah.

the present case. He does not speak of this letter 
of complaint Ext. I. Thus there is no evidence on

Enquiring Officer at the time of the domestic enquiry. 
Q. P. W. 2 goes further as he states that Mr. Sen

On the above discussions I am bound to hold that 
the complaint Ext. I was never in existence on 30th 
October 1965, or at any time before the commence- 
ment of the domestic enquiry on 4th November 1965, 
and is thus clearly a manufactured document. Even 
conceding that the complaint Ext. I was written on the 
date as it shows, 1.6.) on 30th October 1965, there is 
no evidence, whatsoever, that it was handed over to 
any one else by the complainant Shri S. Sen Gupta. 
I have already indicated that there is no evidence that 
Shri S. Sen Gupta acted as prosecutor at the time of 
the domestic enquiry and I have already disbelieved 
that he was the first witness to depose at. the time of 
the domestic enquiry. Even if this be a fact, there 
is no evidence that Shri S. Sen Gupta received back 
the complaint from the Labour Officer, to whom it 
was addressed for filing at the time of the domestic 
enquiry and the absence of this evidence is a clear 
suggestion that Shri 5 Sen Gupta all along had the 
custody of the document since its creation. This 
apart, the petitioner-workman never had any chance 
of knowing the complaint against him by Shri Sen 
Gupta and a domestic enquiry without allowing the 
delinquent-workman to know the nature of the allega- 
tions on the basis of which the charges were frame 
is clearly another violation of the principles of natu- 
ral justice. The learned lawyer for the petitioner- 
workman relies upon the decision reported in 1963 
(11) LLJ. 371 which, however, does not exactly 
relate to this point, but relates to oral statement made 
at the back of the delinquent-workman at the time of 
the domestic enquiry. 


The duty of an Enquiring Officer at the time of the 
domestic enquiry is to allow the prosecutor to examine 
the prosecution witnesses and the delinquent-workman 
or his representative to cross-examine the prosecution 
witnesses. The Enquiring Officer himself may very 
well examine the prosecution witnesses, but this task 
cannot be delegated to someone else. It has trans- 
pired in cross-examination of O.P.W. 3 and O.P.W. 4 
who *were both examined at the time of the domestic 
enquiry, that 0.۲۰.۷۰. 2 put the questions to them at 
the time of the domestic enquiry. The learned lawyer 
for the Union rightly urges that this also makes the 
domestic enquiry defective. 


O.P.W. 3 has stated in his cross-examination that 
at the time of his deposition Shri Sen Gupta was 
present. O.P.W. 4 has also admitted in his cross- 
examination that Shri Sen Gupta was present at the 
time of his deposition. I have already referred to: the 
reply of the Enquiring Officer O.P.W. 1 in his cross- 
examination to show that Shri Sen Gupta deposed as 
prosecution witness No. 8 at the time of the domestic 
enquiry, whereas 0.P.W. 3 and O.P.W. 2 deposed as 
prosecution witnessé& Nos. 1 and 2 respectively. Thus 
it transpires that Shri Sen Gupta was present at the 
time of the domestic enquiry even before he was exa- 
mined and at the time of examination of the other 
prosecution witnesses. This also vitiates the domestic 
enquiry.

The learned Jawyer for the Union next urges that 
in awarding the punishment by way of dismissal sub- 
clause (g) of clause 14 of the Standing Orders has 
not been complied with. Clause 14(g) of the Stand- 
ing Orders of the O.P.-Company, as is evident from 
Ext. J, provides for taking into account the gravity 
of the misconduct, the previous record, if any, of the 
workman and any other extenuating or aggravating 
circumstances that may exist at the time of awarding 
the punishment under the Standing Orders. Ext. 5 is 
a copy of the letter of dismissal, dated 13th Novem- 
ber 1965. Ext. E is another copy of this letter of 
dismissal. The O.P.-Company has not produced any 
document to show that at the time of passing the order 
of dismissal the punishing authority took into conside- 
ration any of the matters provided under clause 14(p) 
of the Standing Orders. 


The order of dismissal, therefore, has not been 
passed in accordance with the Standing Orders. 


I have already found above that the domestic en- 
quiry is vitiated because of consideration of extra- 
neous matters violation of the principles of natural 
justice, non-allowing a representative of the petitioner- 
workman to participate at the domestic enquiry, non- 
disclosure of the complaint against the delinquent 
workman to him, brushing of the powers of the 
Enquiring Officer by the scribe of the enquiry pro- 
ceedings, allowing a prosecution witness examined 
later to be present at the time of examination of the 
former prosecution witnesses, non-recording of the 
enquiry proceedings properly and lack of proper rea- 
soning in his findings by the Enquiring Officer and 
also non-compliance with the provisions of the Stand- 
ing Orders at the time of passing the order of dismis- 
sal against the petitioner-workman. 


The O.P.-Company has however examined witnesses 
in support of the charges framed against O.P.-work- 
man at the time of hearing of the present case. It is 
well-settled law that if the domestic enquiry is found 
to be defective, either party may adduce evidence in 
support or against the charges framed against the 
delinquent workman and the Industrial Tribunal 
Labour Court must come to a finding of its own on the 
basis of appreciation of the evidence adduced at the 
time of the domestic enquiry as also at the time of 
hearing of the industrial dispute itself. So I now 
propose to consider the evidence in the present case 
as well as at the time of the domestic enquiry, on 
merits, 


The O. P.-Company has examined 6 witnesses in 
support of its case at the time of hearing. Of these 
the Engquiring Officer O. P. 1, the scribe 
O.P.W. 2 and th. Assistant Labour Officer 
O.P.W. 5 did not at all depose in support of the 
charges framed. O.P.W. 6 15 the complainant 
Shri S. Sen Gupta himself. O.P.Ws. 3 and 4 are 
the only independent witnesses rs to the charges 
framed. Both of them however deposed as to the 
incident in the machine shop and not as to the 
incident in the Labour Officer. Thus at the time 
of hearing of the present case, there is no eviclence 
against the petitioner-workman as to his behaviour 
in the Labour Office towards the Labour Officer. 
O.P.W 3 is the Head Mistry of the departmént in 


which the  petitioner-workrnan served and is the

most material witness. Even in his examination-in- 
chief he never states that the petitioner-workman ever 
behaved in any rude and insolent manner towards 
Shri Sen Gupta. In his cross-examination he states 


that he has’ never seen the petitioner-workman to 


evade his duty and there is no reason for the peti- 
tioner-workman to evade his duty on the relevant 
date. He next states that he does not say that the 
petitioner-workman evaded his work on that date. 
He also states that the altercation between Shri Sen 


Gupta and the petitioner-workman was overtime that 


would cover the pending work to be completed. 
Shri Sen Gupta got angry with — such altercations. 
On his evidence I do not find that the charge of 
rude and insolent behaviour towards Shri Sen Gupta 
has been proved against the petitioner-workman. 
O.P.W. 4 also serves as a Turner under the O. P.- 
Company and his seat of work is at a distance of 
15 cubits from the seat of work of the petitioner- 
workman. He also does not depose as to any rude 
and insolent behaviour of the petitioner-workmar 
towards Shri Sen Gupte. There is evidence on 
record at the time of the domestic enaviry as to some 
taunting manner of speaking against the petitioner- 
workman and also using harsh words azainst Shri S. 
Sen Gupta. I have already indicated above that 
these statements never had the test of cross-examina- 
tion because of the denial of reasonable opportuni- 
ties ما‎ the petitioner-workman by the enquiring 
officer himself and what these persons deposed at 
the time of the domestic enquiry does not rebut what 
O.P.Ws. 3 and 4 state at the time of hearing of the 
case. ] am unwilling to rely upon the statements 
made at the time of the domestic enquiry in the 
absence of the  petitioner-workman and that too 
recorded in an irregular manner as ] have already 
indicated above. The O. P.-Company was examin- 
ed as many as 20 witnesses at the time of the domes- 
tic enquiry. There is no reason, whatsoever, for 


their examining only 4 witnesses out of the list of 
witnesses examined at the time of the domestic 
enquiry at the time of hearing of the present case. 


I am rather willing to accept that withholding of the 
witnesses examined at the time of the domestic 
enquiry along with absence of cross-examination of 
these witnesses and defective recording of evidence, 
as I have already found out, is another ground for 
not relying upon the prosecution evidence as adduced 
at the time of the domestic enquiry. 


On the above discussions, I hold that the O. P.- 
Company has failed to establish the charges framed 
against the petitioner-workman at the time of hearing 
of the present case by way of independent evidence. 


The learned lawyer for the'O. P.-Company has 


relied upon the decision reported in 1961(II) LLJ. 


417 to urge that the workman against whom the 
enquiry was held was not entitled to be represented 
at such enquiry by a representative of his Union. 
This decision is of no help to the O. P.-Company as 
the Enquiring Officer O.P.W. 1 has admitted that 


there is a system of representation at the time of 


the domestic enquiry in the O. P.-Company. He 
next relies upon the decision reported in 1965(1) 
LI.J. 426 as to the non-existence of the right of ' 
representation at the time of the domestic enquiry, 
but that decision also is of no avail because of the

specific admission of the Enquiring Officer O.P.W. 
1. The learned lawyer for the O. P.-Company then 
relies upon the decisions reported in 1951 (II) LJ. 
314, 1963 (II) LLJ. 78, (1961-1962) XXI F.J.R. 347 
and 1964 (II) LLJ. 113 to urge that the findings of the 
domestic enquiry should not be disturbed by the Indus- 
trial Tribunal or Labour Court except under specified 
circumstances. I have already discussed above how 
and why I have come to the conclusion that the 
domestic enquiry was held in violation of the principles 
of natural justice and is defective in nature, and there- 
fore a fresh appreciation of evidence on record and as 
adduced in this case by the parties is necessary. 


So I hold that the dismissal of the petitioner- 


workman is not justified and he is entitled to rein- . 


statement along with back wages as if his service 
was never terminated as such. Parties have not pro- 
duced the appointment letter or the order of the peti- 
tioner-workman. Normally it would be accepted 
that the employer O. P.-Company has a right or trans- 
fer of the petitioner-workman to similar types of jobs. 
So I hold that the petitioner-workman cannot refuse to 
work in a particular capacity if that work be allotted 
to him and is ہ٤‎ similar nature in which he was 
appointed. If, however, the particular work allotted 
to him required a specific training. the employer 0, P.- 
Company must arrange for such training, if necessary. 


The first part of this issue is so answered in the 
negative. The petitioner-workman is entitled to rein- 
statement as well as back wages since 5th November 
1965 till the date of reinstatement as such at his usual 
rate of emoluments. The petitioner-workman however 
is not entitled to reinstatement in a particular job and 
may be allotted jobs of similar nature after under- 
going required training for which the 0. P.-Company 
would arrange, if necessary. 


The second part of this issue is so disposed of. 


An award be passed accordingly holding that the 
dismissal of the petitioner-workman from his service 
is not justified and the O.P.-Company shall reinstate 
the petitioner-workman within one month from the 
date of publication of this award in the “Calcutta 
Gazette” and shall also pay the back wages since 5th 
November 1965, till the date of reinstatement as such, 
as if his service was never terminated. The petitioner- 
workman, however, is not entitled to reinstatement in 
a particular post and may be allotted jobs of | similar 
nature after undergoing required training for which 
the 0.P.-Company would arrange, if necessary. 


This is my award.

Two relevant factors are to be kept in mind by the 
Tribunal when fixing a wage structure. Those are: ہے‎ 


(1) The financial capacity of the employer to 
bear the additional burden imposed by the, 
scheme ; and 


(2) Wages Scales fixed in other comparable con- 
cerns in the region. 


In this connection I may mention that neither party 
has produced any wage structure of similar employees 
of similar concerns. According to Shri A. L. Roy 
for the Union, no such comparable unit is necessary ' 
in the matter of revising the wage and the D.A. of the 
employees of the roofing department because the wage 
structure and the D.A. were enjoyed by the employees 
of other departments of the .Company are better than 
those of the roofing department. According to Shri 
A. L. Roy, we are to revise the wages and D.A. of 
the roofing department employees only on a considera- 
tion of this fact. The financial position of the em- 
ployer is a primary consideration when awarding a 
a revision of the wage scalws. The contention of Shri 
A. L. Roy, in my opinion, cannot be accepted in toto. 
The type of work performed by the aforesaid diffe- 
rent categories of employees of the roofing depart 
ment is quite different from the type of work perform- 
ed by the employees of the other departments of the 
Company and also by the Head Office staff. But in 
this case on behalf of thé employer, it has not also 
been shown that the rates of wages in his concern are 
higher than those prevailing in similar ‘concerns in 
the region. Also in this case, we find that the exist- 
ing wages of the different categories of employees of 
the roofing department of the' Company were fixed 
so far back in the year 1957. There cannot be any 
doubt in this case that since after 1957 till today, there 
has been much increase in the cost of living index. 
Now, if it is found that the financial capacity of the 
employer is such that the employer would be able to 
bear the extra financial burden for increase of wages 
and D.A., then the wages and D.A. of the different 
categories of employees of the roofing department of 
of the Company, should be enhanced suitably. The 
Company has. produced the Report of the Directors 
and the Profit and Loss Accounts from the year 1961, 
" till the year 1967. The financial year of the Com- 
pany is from Ist November of a_ year till the 31st 
October of the next year. Though several entries in 
the balance sheets of all the years have been challeng- 
ed on behalf of the Union by Shri A. L. Roy, 
specially for the year ending 31st October 1964, I 
cannot but accept the correctness of these audited 
balance sheets. According to Shri Roy, the expenses 
under the Heading ‘“Miscellanequs” amounting 10 
Rs. 7,96.015 at page 2] of that year's balance sheet 
supports his contention that the Company did actually 
employ a large number of Goondas to evict the 
roofing departinent employees from the K. P. Godown 
in the year 1964. I cannot and should not consider this

such to bear any additional burden for  incréase of 
wages and D.A. of the roofing department employees. 
Thus the overall picture of the financial capacity of 
the Company is not bright and that the Company is 
now a losing concern and I hold as such. But even 
then it is to be remembered that it is an admitted fact 
that sometime in the year 1964, on the basis of a 
settlement between the Company authorities and the 
previous Union, the wages, D.A., tiffin allowance of 
the Head Office employees and,the employees of other 
department of the Company have all been increased. 
As the Company could actually increase the wages of 
its employees in respect of other departments, I think, 
though the Company’s financial position is not bright, 
the wage structure of the different categories of the 
employees of the roofing department, should also be 
increased.

Next coming to issue No. 7 regarding fixation 
of duty hours of the employees of the roofing 
department, we find that the present working 
hours of the roofiing department workers are 48 
hours in a week i.e. 8 hours per day, excluding 
one hours recess for rest. According to the 
union, as the weekly hours of duty of the sub- 
staff in the Head Office is about 42 hours per 
week ; the daily working hours of the roofing 
workmen should also be fixed at 6 hours.a day, 
But in my opinion the existing working hours of 


roofing department workers at 48 hours in a- 


week or 8 hours per day excluding one hour's 
recess, are not excessive. In fact these working 
hours are sanctioned by the provisions of West 
Bengal Shops and Establishment Act. Though 
5 working days in a week system was introduced 
in the Head Office, the same cannot be introduced 
in the roofing § section because of the special 
nature of their work. Accordingly I reject the 


Union's claim on this point and I hold that the 
present existing working hours of the roofing de- 
partment shall continue. 


I now take up issue No. 4 regarding payment 
of overtime allowance and fixation of the rate 
of overtime. Admittedly the Company is paying 
overtime allowance at the rate of 1) times, for 
working beyond the scheduled working hours. 
The Union claims that overtime should be gran- 
ted at double the rate, as paid to the factory 
workers covered under the Factories Act. But 
this claim cannot be supported in any way. The 
roofing workers ‘can by no stretch of imagina- 
tion be said to be covered under the Factories 
Act. West Bengal Shops and Establishment Act 
provides payment of overtime allowance at the 


‘rate of 18 times and as such the existing rate of 


overtime allowance, I am of opinion, is quite 
justified and reasonable and ] hold that the 
workers of the roofing department shall contig 
nue to get their overtime allowance at this exist- 
ing rate. 


According to the union, the roofing department 
workers are to attend K. P. Godown at Kidder- 
pore first, daily before their work starts and after 
completion of their day's work, they are to give 
attendance at the K. P. Godown to hand over. 
the implements. On the othgr hand, the Com- 
pany's case is that the workers are not required 
to ‘attend K. P. Godown after day’s work and 
that they are not to attend K. P. Godown first, 
before going to the site, where the work is being 
done. There is only oath against oath on this 
point. Now if the workers are 10 
attend .کا‎ P. Godown or the Head Office, 
before start of their working hours and 
if they are also to attend cither K. P. Godown 
or Head Office, after working till the end of the 
working hours, then certainly such labourers are 
entitled to overtime allowance at the aforesaid 
existing rate, and I hold as such. This issue No. 
4 is thus decided.

is the Company’s_ case that even the factory 
workers of the company also do not enjoy the 
same holidays as enjoyed by the head office staff. 
The number of holidays enjoyed by the roofing 
department workers in a year with wages, in my 
opinion, is quite sufficient and I do nol find any

As regards the last issue No. 8, regarding per-

prays that the 56 employees as mentioned in

be made permanent at once. Now, the case of 
the Company is that the permanency of the 
workmen, depends not only on the vacancies ‘in 
the permanent posts but also on the requirements 
on the volume of business and work. It is in 
evidence that the roofing business of the Com- 
pany has been reduced during the year 1968. A 
Jarge number of permanent workers are sitting 
idle. The Company has given a chart of such 
idle workers of the roofing department: from

there’ are surplus staff of permanent’ workers. 
But the nature of business of the roofing depart- 
ment is such that during the.year, certain months, 
can be called the season inthe roofing depart- 
ment. During that time, the workload increases. 
The number of workmen required by the Com- 
pany during those seasonal months, cannot be 
called the standard requirement of total number 
of workmen, throughout the year on the required 
basis. There are many months during the year, 
when a suitable number of workmen constantly 
remain idle, and during that period, the Com: 
pany has, of course, to pay idle wages to them. 


LL 


' This is an extra financial burden of the Com- 


pany. So, the Company cannot, in my opinion, 
maintain a large number of permanent emplo- 
yees who could only be fully utilised during the

got no written rules of permanency. This must 
be due to casual nature of work in the roofing 
department ite. ‘contract execution job. The

Foremen are not recruited directly. It is in evi- 
dence that the workers are made permanent, 
whenever vacancy in the permanent post occurs.

Schedule to the said Act, to the industrial establish- 
ments may affect the employers سا‎ relation thereto 
so prejudicially that such application may cause 
Serious repercussion on the industries concerned and 
that public interest so requires; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred 
by section 9B of the said Act, the Governor is 
pleased hereby to direct that the provisions of sec- 
tion 9A of the said Act shall apply to the industrial 
establishments, subject to the condition that, for 
a period of seven days from the 3rd February 1969 
to the 9th February 1969, no notice referred to in 
the said section 9A shall be required in respect of 
the matters specified in items Nos. 4 and 6 of the 
Fourth Schedule to the said Act. 


By order of the Governor, 


A. K, MITRA, 
Jt. Secy. to the Govt. of West Bengal.

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 


DEVELOPMENT AND PLANNING (T. & C.P.) DEPARTMENT 


RESOLUTION 


No. T.&CP. اہ او‎ 67.—30th January 1969.—-Whereas the area describ- 
ed in Schedule [ to this Resolution (hereinafter referred to as the Haldia Region) 
is rapidly developing into a major urban centre, and has assumed great 
commercial, industrial and economic importance due to the construction of 
a subsidiary Port and the proposed establishment of major industrial projects; 


And whereas at present the Haldia region is confronted with many 
problems relating to acquisition and distribution of land needed for various 
uses like industries, commerce, and residence, promotion of industrialisation, 
control of use and development of land, rehabilitation of displaced persons, 
housing, water-supply, public health, transport and communication, and civic 
amenities, all of which require an integrated approach for their solution, and 
the preparation of a comprehensive Development Plan for the development of 
the Haldia region in social, civic, economic and other aspects; 


And whereas an iaterim Development Plan for the Haldia region has 
already been prepared with financial assistance proyided by the Government 
of India in the Ministry of Health, Family Planning and Urban Development; 


And whereas it is considered expedient in the larger interest of the Haldia 
region developing into an important industrial complex and integrated urban 
centre to establish a unified State agency for practical and operational 
planning and development and to co-ordinate activities of all public and 
private agencies engaged or to be engaged in development of the Haldia 
region; 

Now, therefore, the Governor is pleased hereby to order as follows: 

(1) An organisation to be named as the Haldia Development Authority, 
with Commissioner, Town and Country Planning, Government of 
West Bengal, as Chairman and the following as Members, be 
established with immediate effect: 


(i) A representative of the Calcutta Port Commissioners. 
(ii) A representative of the South Eastern Railways. 


603 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, EXTRAORDINARY, JANUARY 30, 1969 


সপ আআ سس سو‎ RS ATE 5 
সস wade EE ET کک ے۔ ھےہ‎  ۔ے‎ 


(iii) Director of Industries, West Bengal. 


(iv) Director of Cottage and Small-Scale Industries, Government of West 
Bengal. 


(v) A representative of Land and Land Revenue Department, Govern- 
ment of West Bengal. 


(vi) District Magistrate, Midnapur. 


(vii) Chief Engineer, Housing Directorate under the Government of 
West Bengal. 


The Authority shall have a Chief Executive Officer to be appointed by the 
State Government who shall also be its Member-Secretary. The Authority 
shall have jurisdiction over the Haldia region. 


(2) The Authority shall function as a Directorate under the Town and 
Country Planning Branch of the Development and Planning Depart- 
ment of the State Government which will sanction such staff for the 
Authority as may be considered necessary from time to time in 
consultation with the Finance Department. 


(3) The headquarters of the Authority shall be at Calcutta, but it may 
maintain a subsidiary office within the Haldia region; but the State 
Government may, at such appropriate time as it may think fit, 
transfer the headquarters of the Authority to the Haldia region. 


(4) The functions, duties and powers of the Authority shall be as stated 
in Schedule II to this Resolution. 


(5) The Chief Executive Officer shall have the powers specified in 


Schedule III to this Resolution. 


(6) Such sums as the State Government may decide shall be placed at the. 
disposal of the Authority from time to time for meeting 105 
expenditure. . 


(7) The Authority shall have the powers to incur such expenses as may 
be necessary out of its budget provision with the approval of the 
State Government which may delegate such financial and other 
powers to the Authority as it may consider desirable. 


(8) The Authority shall have its own administrative and technical estab- 
lishment consisting of such posts as may be created by the State 
Government, Initially the sanctioned establishment of the Haldia 
Planning Cell under the Development and Planning (T&CP) 
Department shall be placed under the Authority, and such other 
Officers and staff from existing State Government agencies as 
decided by State Government may also be placed under the 
Authority. The State Government may also appoint any officer 
already in service of the Government to be the Chief Executive 
Officer and Member-Secretary of the Authority in addition to his 
own duties, or on a full-time basis. 


2. The Governor is pleased to order further that this Resolution be 
published in “Calcutta Gazette” and copies thereof be sent to the Accountant- 
General, West Bengal, all departments of the State Government and others 
concerned.
