SCHEDULE II 
The functions, duties and powers of the Haldia Development Authority 
1. The functions of the Authority are: 


(1-1) To secure and promote the integrated development of the Haldia 
region according to plan. 


(1-2) To prepare a comprehensive Development Plan for the Haldia 
region and implement development projects within the framework 
of the comprehensive Development Plan including water-supply, 
roads, sewerage and drainage, markets, parks, industrial and 
residential areas and housing. 


-.-(1-3) To set up adequate organisational machinery and take other 

necessary steps for control of land used in the Haldia region, 

- under the provisions of the Calcutta Metropolitan Planning Area 

(Use and Development of Land) Control Act, 1965, and any other 
relevant statute. 


(1-4) To promote activities in the area by offering land and _ infrastruc- 
ture at attractive terms for location of public and private sector 
industrial projects. 1... 


(1-5) To advise State Government on all future land acquisition and 
development activities in the Haldia region. 


(1-6) To execute land development projects in the Haldia region. , 


(1-7) To draw up projects for rehabilitation of people who have been 
displaced or are likely to be displaced from their avocations by 
land acquisition in the Haldia region and secure their implemen- 
tation, to fulfil which function the Committee set up by the Land 
and Land Revenue Department of Government of West Bengal 
under Memo. No. 5412(16)-LA(?W), dated 25th April 1968, shall 
remain attached to the Authority as an advisory body. 


- (1-8) To execute ancillary development projects and take other action 
outside the Haldia region as may be required for the discharge of 
the above functions. 


(1-9) To co-ordinate activities of public and private agencies executing 
development projects in the Haldia region. 


(1-10) To advise the State Government and other public authorities, 
agencies and organisations on all matters relating to integrated 
development of the Haldia region. 


2. The duties of the Authority shall be as follows: 


(2-1) To prepare its annual budget in such form as may be prescribed by 
the State Government and to submit the same to the State 
Government for approval. 


(2-2) To keep and maintain proper accounts of money received and 
expended by it and publish an annual statement of accounts in the 
manner prescribed by the State (Government. 


(2-3) To submit to the State Government such reports at such intervals 
as may be determined by the State Government and to publish 
an annual report embracing its activities. 


(2-4) The account of the Authority shall be audited by the competent 
authority every year and report thereof submitted to Government. 


(2-5) To maintain close contact with the Calcutta Metropolitan Planning 
Organisation, the Durgapur Development Authority and such other 
authorities. or organisations. as -may.be. determined by the State. 
Government and to receive such advicé arid’ guidancé as‘ may! be 
necessary to fulfil the objectives of the Authority. 


606 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, EXTRAORDINARY, JANUARY 30, 1960 [Part I 


3. The powers of the Authority shal) be as follows: 


(3-1) To conduct such civic, social, economic and other surveys and 
investigations 95 are required in the performance of its functions 
for which purpose it shall have appropriate access to information 
already available with the various organisations in the private and 
public settors and departments of the Government. 


(3-2) To exercise disciplinary control over its employees and to demand 
security from its employees according to the rules of the State 
Government. 


2 
(3-3) To administer and disburse the funds placed at its disposal to 
discharge the functions for which the Authority is constituted in 

the manner to be prescribed by the State Government. 


(3-4) To receive the plans of other public and private agencies, authorities 
and organisations and after due consultation with them revise and 
amend their plans, if necessary, in order to ensure an integrated 
and efficient utilisation of resources within its jurisdiction for 
which purpose the State Government may appoint co-ordinating 
or special Committees and invest them with such powers as may, 
be necessary. 


(3-5) To do such other things as may be necessary and proper in order 
to achieve its objectives, 


SCHEDULE III 
4. The powers of the Chief Executive Officer shall be as follows: 


(4-1) The Chief Executive Officer of the Authority and/or such other 
officer as may be authorised by the State Government according 
to the rutes in force in this behalf shall sign bills, receipts, 
acceptances, endorsements and charges and all documents on 
behalf of the Authority. 


(4-2) The Chief Executive Officer may grant such advances and/or 
allowances including travelling allowances as may be deemed 
proper to its employees and others in connection with the affairs 
of the Authority subject to recoupment according to the rules of 
the State Government. 


(4-3) The Chief Executive Officer may be given, with the concurrence of 
the Finance Department, such powers as may enable him to 
conduct efficiently the work of the Authority.

PART I.—Orders and Notifications by the Governor of West Bengal, the High Court, Government 
Treasury, etc. 


GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
HOME (TRANSPORT) DEPARTMENT 


RESOLUTION 


No. 768-W.T.—27th January 1969.—Government of West Bengal set up on 
12th June 1967 under section 3 of the Commission of Inquiry Act, 1952, a 
Commission of Inquiry under the Chairmanship of Shri P. C. Mallik, retired 
Judge, Calcutta High Court, to inquire into certain matters relating to the 
affairs of the Calcutta Tramways Co. Ltd. The composition of the Commis- 
sion was as follows:-— 


(1) Shri P. C. Mallick, retired Judge, Calcutta High Court—Chairman. 
(2) Shri N. K. Roy, retired Additional Member, Railway Board—Member. 
(3) Shri A. K. Biswas, M. Com., F.1L.C.A., F.C.C.S., F.F.1..1.—-Member. 


2. The matters to be inquired by the Commission were— 


(a) whether the revenues of the Company derived from its existing rates 
of fare are adequate for it to discharge its obligations under the 
Calcutta Tramways Act, 1951 and the Agreement in the First 
Schedule thereto; 


(b) if the revenues are inadequate, whether the inadequacy can be made 
up— 
(i) by improving collection of fares from passengers using the tram 
cars. 


(ii) by better utilisation of tram cars, 


(iii) by effecting economy in expenditure without affecting the efficiency 
of the services carried on by the Company; 


(c) whether the Company has maintained the tramway tracks in proper 
condition with due regard to the safety of the tram cars as also of 
other vehicles using the roads on which the tracks are laid; and if 
the maintenance has not been proper, whether the reason is that 
the Company has not applied its revenue in the order indicated in 
clause 4 of the Agreement in the First Schedule to the Calcutta 
Tramways Act, 1951, but has diverted its resources to matters 
occupying a lower priority than the maintenance of.tram tracks: 


607 


608 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, EXTRAORDINARY, JANUARY 30, 1969 [Part I 
, 54-32-4228 


(0) whether the financial transactions entered into by the Company in the 
past were in accordance with the provisions of the Calcutta Tram- 
ways Act, 1951; and 


(e) what is the general financial condition of the Company at present. 


3. The Commission arrived at unanimous conclusions on the _ matters 
mentioned above and submitted its report on the 30th January 1968. The 
Commission also made a number of recommentations and observations and has 
given statistical and technical diagrams with the report. The major recom- 
mendations and observations are given in the annexure to this Resolution. 


4. The Commission has come to the conclusion that with the existing rate 
of fare structure, the revenue of the Company is not adequate to discharge its 
obligations under the Calcutta Tramways Act of 1951 and the Agreement in 
the First Schedule. It is not sufficient even to cover the operational expenses 
of the Undertaking. 


Government accepted this view of the Commission. 


5. The Commision was unable to accept that large numbers of passengers, 
deliberately cheat the Company by not paying proper fares even though the 
standard of honesty has declined in recent years. The Commission, however, 
felt that some improvement in collection of fares could be effected by posting: 
some of the existing surplus conductors as inspectors at suitable points. 
According to the Commission it is desirable to introduce and gradually con- 
vert all the cars into the type of: PAYE (Pay as you enter) cars. By such 
introduction gradually the number of ticketless travellers will be reduced and 
the revenue of the Tramways will increase. One should not however expect 
that anything more than a small portion of the shortfall between income and 
expenditure can be covered by gradual introduction of PAYE cars. 


The Commission is of opinion that there is undoubtedly scope for improve- 
ment in the management of the Company which is likely to result in an 
increase of income. The Commission holds the view that there is considerable 
loss of trips due to rigid adherence to the old time-table and duty charts of the 
employees. The existing time-table according to the Commission has been! 
outdated with the traffic conditions having undergone considerable changes. 
It is imperative to change the time-table in response to the changed conditions, 
Some improvement in the revenue may be obtained if the time-table 15 
changed. 


The Commission has suggested close scrutiny in the matter of printing and 
issuing tickets. The Commission has also suggested economies in the purchase 
of stores and sundries and the exercising of scientific control over storage, 
issue and ultimate consumption of stores. The Commission however finally 
came to the conclusion that the gap between the income and expenditure being 
so heavy it is not possible to bridge the gap between expenditure and revenue 
only by taking recourse to the methods indicated in the terms of reference. 


6. On a careful consideration of all the facts the Commission has come 
to the conclusion that the tramway track has not been properly maintained 
and the company is guilty of breach of clause 2(4) of the Agreement. The' 
Commission further holds that there has been improper application of revenue 
and there has been a breach of clause 4 of the Agreement also. The Commis- 
sion also records that the Company has failed to discharge its obligation ta 
maintain the track in a proper condition mainly by not properly applying its 
revenue both for maintenance and repairs as well as for renewals and replace- 
ments. Appropriation have been made to Accounts referred to in clauses 
4(1)(d) and (e) without proper maintenance of the physical assets of the 
undertaking which obligation the Commission holds is absolute. 


Government agree with these views of the Commission. 


After the taking over of the management of the Company by Government 
a five-year programme of work (1968-73) for phased replacement and renewal 
to clear backlog of repairs, renewal and maintenance of the physical assets 
and to restore the operational efficiency, has been drawn up more or less in 
line with the recommendations made by the Commission. 


PART I] 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, EXTRAORDINARY, JANUARY 30, 1969 


ee ہم‎ 


oe eo eee 


সস Saute ee ও আজ ے‎ 


The Calcutta Tramways Advisory Committee (Statutory Committee under 
the Calcutta Tramways Act, 1951) has also been reconstituted with members 
expert in cost-benefit and industrial problems to guide the management of the 
undertaking in fulfilling its work programme by making valuable 
recommendations. 


7. The terms of reference being not more specific the Commission 
considered three transactions, namely:— 


(i) transfer of considerable sums from the Special Reserve Account to 
the Shareholders’ Account; 


(11) raising a loan of Rs. 16 lacs, the object of raising such loan and its 
application; and 


(iii) transfer of considerable sums to London. 


Regarding (i)—The Commission holds the view that loss of undertaking 
only is liable to be recouped from the Special Reserve Account and the Special 
Reserve Account could be drawn for such losses in subsequent years also 
where this would be necessary to meet the expenses referred to in sub-clause 
4(1)(a) of the Agreement. The Special Reserve Account could not, however, 
be utilised to make appreciation to the Shareholders Account in any account- 
ing year where no profits had accrued and the failure on account of lack of 
profits did not entitle the Company to provide for the Shareholders’ Account 
from the Special Reserve Account in any year. 


Regarding (ii)}—-The Commission has discussed at length the procedure 
adopted by the Company to obtain the loan. The object of taking this loan 
was for purchasing of Tram Cars from Bombay. Six Bombay Cars were 
purchased in 1964. The application for loan was made in April 1965 and 
the Government sanction to the loan was granted in May 1965. The loan 
was actually taken from the United Bank in 1967. The Commission has held 
this transaction to be irregular. 


Regarding (iii)—The Commission refers to two remittances of the Co. to 
its London Head Office in March 1967 and May 1967. In the opinion of the 
Commission these are questionable when the financial condition of the 
Company was so bad that it had not sufficient money to maintain its physical 
assets and to pay wages to its workers. The considered view of the Com- 
mission is, therefore, that the transfer of such a big sum to London at the 
time was most inopportune and totally uncalled for and cannot be condoned. 


With regard to items (c) and (d) of the Commission’s terms of reference 
and its findings as recorded Government are of the view that the observa- 
tions of the Commission with regard to the specific transactions mentioned 
in paragraph 7 above and the Commission’s general observations in the 
matter of the Company’s failure or neglect to maintain in due and proper 
order its physical assets should be taken into due and fullest consideration 
at the time negotiations are conducted and finalised for the acquiring of the 
undertaking of the Calcutta Tramways Company by the State Government 
as provided for in the Calcutta Tramways Act, 1951. 


8. The Commission has examined the financial position of the Company 
from the following two aspects— 


(i) If the real value of the Company’s assets can meet its liabilities, and 
(ii) What is the profitability potential of the Company? 


The Commission has commented on the absence of a regular Depreciation 
Account as contemplated in the Companies Act under individual heads of 
assets by the Company which makes it difficult to assess the present value 
of the fixed assets at the end of each year. 


The Commission has found that at the end of 1951, 1956 and 1965, the 
residual book value of the fixed assets indicated a shortage of about 
£1.30, £1.80 and £2.00 million respectively, and to that extent the assets 
failed to meet the liabilities in the years mentioned. 


The Commission has, found that the Company is very unsound and that 


it had become so shortly’ after 1951.

ANNEXURE 


The contention that fall in the number of passengers کا‎ directly 
attributable to the competition from the private buses allowed to ply in 
Calcutta is difficult to accept. (Page 16.) 


It is surprising to find that between 1951 and 1965, both years inclusive, 
the Company set apart £1,027,349 to the Shareholders’ Account and the 
Renewals and Replacements Reserve Accounts showed a credit balance of 
£2,94,964 at the end of 1965 allowing almost all the assets, specially the track 
roadway and rolling stock to deteriorate to the present condition. (Page 38.) 


It is unfortunate that the Board of Directors in London became extra- 
sensitive to the issues raised by the Commission, which it had to raise to 
do full justice to the terms of reference and refused to co-operate with it in 
supplying information even on matters of fact, not to speak of matters of 
opinion. (Page 53.) 


The fixed assets have not been in proper condition nor the worn-out 
assets renewed and replaced as and when necessary. Had the works been 
carried out from year to year as they become necessary the cost would have 
been less than what it is to day. (Page 55.) 


The traffic potential of the Calcutta Tramways Co. after reaching the 
Saturation point has taken a downward trend. By increasing the fares very 
substantially the budget may be balanced for some years but not for all time 
to come. (Page 62.) 


According to the Commission to run the Tramways with the existing fare 
structure means that the Undertaking will have to be subsidised to the extent 
of more than a crore of rupees annually. This to the mind of the Com- 
mission is not proper, the Tramways being a Commercial undertaking. The 
Commission has therefore suggested that there should be a revision of fare so 
that the burden on the public exchequer may be minimised. (Pages 62-63.) 


The Commission strongly recommends that a Board of Management 
should be set up to assist the Administrator. In the Board there should be 
one superannuated Railway Officer and one who should have special 
knowledge of labour problems. (Pages 63-64.) 


Government was not justified in not taking adequate care سا‎ the proper 
maintenance of the physical assets of the Company. (Page 65.) 


The Commission holds that the present position of ownership being with the 
Tramways Co. and the management with the Government is not at all desir- 
able. The present arrangement is bound to lead to innumerable complications 
not the least of them being legal. It is imperative that the question of buying 
up the Undertaking is taken up in right earnest. Negotiation should proceed 
forthwith and if for any reason the parties are unable to agree to a reasonable 
price, the machinery of arbitration should be taken recourse to for the purpose 
of determining the price (The Commission thinks that the seller will not insist 
on the price fixed on 1951 agreement). (Pages 68-69.)

Careful watch should be kept over the consumption of current as well as 
expenditure per unit. (Page 83.) 


The Commission has discussed at length expenditure regarding renewals 
and replacements, and maintenance and repairs of the Undertaking. It has 


also suggested programme year by year for five years at pages 98, 99 and 100 
of the Report. 


The Commission holds that to increase the efficiency in materials usage it 
is essential to introduce a perpetual system of proper checks at different points 
of material flows for measuring the quantum as well as the quality of materials 
and the performances they offer while actually being consumed. (Page 105.) 


In order to reduce the cost, a responsibility accounting (individualwise and 
groupwise) should be introduced for the employees, particularly those in 
higher levels of management. (Page 107.) 


A thorough job analysis of the Mechanical, Traffic and Permanent way staff 
should be made to find out their work load so that the maximum output can 
be had from the existing staff. (Page 122.) 


The Commission suggests that if the trams are to run in the streets of 
Calcutta all resources like “Contract” labour, “Temporary” labour and even 
Contract” work must be tapped. (Page 122.) 


A thorough study of the stores procedure right from purchase to final 
utilisation should be made. Main lines of investigation have also been suggested 
by the Commission. (Pages 122-123.) 


Vigorous search should be made to locate indigenous source and to evolve 
substitutes for track materials vital parts of rolling stock including electric 
motor which are now imported. Indian Railways, Bhopal Heavy Electricals, 
Hindusthan Machine Tools and other public and private manufacturing 
concerns should be contacted. (Page 123.) 


Passenger-concentration at different part of the day should be studied and 
accordingly frequency of service in different zones should follow the same 


pattern. Investigation into the possibility of a skeleton night service in some 
selected routes should be made. (Page 197.) 


Attempt should be made to run the tram cars in reserved centre track of 
the roads. There is enormous economy in this system since standard rails 
(instead of grooved rails—imported item) and only one R.C.C. Pole can be used. 
Investigation should also be made for running tram cars in newly developed 
areas with wide roads having reserved centre—tracks instead of running in 
congested and water-logged routes. (Page 198.) 


Existing Rotary Convertors should be replaced by Silicon Power Rectifiers. 
This would minimise cost in the long run. (Page 201.)

ORDER 


No. 784-FS / FS/CG/14R-5/67.—30th January 1969.—In exercise of the powers 
conferred by section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 (Act 10 of 1955), 
read with the Government of India, Ministry of Commerce, S.O. No. 26(11)- 
Com-Genl1/66, dated the 18th June 1966, the Governor is pleased hereby to make 
the following amendments in the West Bengal Lubricating Oil Licensing Order, 
1967, published at pages 109-117 of Part I of the “Calcutta Gazette, 
Extraordinary”, of the 20th January 1967 (hereinafter referred to as the said 
order), namely:— 

Amendments 

In paragraph 11 of the said order,— 


(1) for sub-paragraph (1), substitute the following sub-paragraph, 
namely:— 


“(1) Any person aggrieved by an order refusing to grant or renew a 
licence or cancelling or suspending a licence under the provisions 
of this order may, within thirty days of the receipt by him of 
such order, prefer an appeal— 


(a) where the order is passed by the Director of Consumer Goods, 
Department of Food and Supplies, Government of West Bengal, 
or the District Magistrate or the Deputy Commissioner of a 
district, to the State Government; and 

(b) in any other case, to the said Director of Consumer Goods.”; 


(2) in sub-paragraph (3), for the words, brackets and figure “the appellate 
authority appointed under sub-paragraph (1)”, substitute the words 
“the Director of Consumer Goods, Department of Food and 
Supplies, Government of West Bengal,”. 


By order of the Governor,

Organisers of Saraswati Pujas are requested ٥ 
restrict use of loud-speakers and msicrophanes for 
broadcasting music from Puja  Pandals. Local 
officers have been instructed to keep im touch with 
the organisers of the Pujas and enlist their co- 
operstion for implementation of those instructions. 
No permission is being given to the installation of 
micropnones outside the Puja Pandals. The Deputy 
Commissioners of the Divisions are authorised to 
permit, on receipt applications, use of loud-speakers 
inside the Pandals hetween 6 a.m. and 10 a.m, and 
6 p.m. and 10 p.m. on the 22nd January 1969 
(Saraswati Puja Day). Use of loud-speakers الا‎ 
also be permitted between 6 a.m. and 10 a.m. on the 
23rd January 1969 and 24th January 1969 (Immersion 
Days). Persons so permitted will be expected to 
use loud-speakers during this period at reasonable 
intervals and not continuously and at a low pitch. 
Organisers are requested to submit applications for 
such permission to the Officer-in-charge ot the 
"0 0 concerned not later than 17th January

No. 7.—l6th January 1969.-- In exercise of the

and Waterways, Government of West  Bengal,.

ant Store-Keeper in the River Research _ Institute,

and Waterways, Government of West Bengal, shall 
be as detailed below:

(1) Method of recruitment: 


Direct by interview and selection, or by promo- 
tion of an Assistant Store-Keeper with ten 
years’ experience in the River Research 
Institute, West Bengal. ۱

rience of running workshop

Land Acquisition 


NOTIFICATIONS 


BURDWAN.—No. 632-L.A.—9th January 1969. — 
Whereas it appears to the Governor that land is 
likely to be needed for a public purpose, namely, for 
construction of Railway Siding in connections with 
the development of Industries at Durgapur in the 
village of Gopinathpur, jurisdiction list No. 85, 
police-station Faridpur, district Burdwan, it is hereby 
notified that a piece of land comprising part of 
cadastral survey plot No. 6552 (northern porticn), 
and measuring, more or less, 0.0567 hectare (0.14 
acre), is likely to be needed for the aforesaid public 
purpose at the public expense within the aforesaid 
village of Gopinathpur; 


This notification is made under the provisions of 
section 4 of Act I of 1894, to all whom it may 
concern. 


A plan of the land may be inspected in the office 
of the Special Land Acquisition Officer, Burdwan. 


In exercise of the powers conferred by the afore- 
said section, the Governor is pleased to authorise 
the officers for the time being engaged in the under- 
taking, with their servants and workmen, to enter 
upon and survey the land and ہ4‎ all other acts 
required or permitted by that section. 


Any person interested in the above land, who has 
any objection to the acquisition thereof, may, within 
thirty days after the date on which public notice of 
the substance of this notification is given in the 
locality, file an objection in writing before the 
Collector, Burdwan.

No. 17L.S.-G.—6th January 1969.—Whereas by 
Notification No. 843M, dated 8th April 1922, issued 
under clause 2 of section 30 of the Bengal Municipal 
Act, 1884 (Act III of 1884), the Commissioner, 
Rajshahi Division, excluded the six roads specified 
in the said notification along with side ditches and 
drains and all side lands lying along side thereot on 
cither side lying within the limits of the Jalpaiguri 
Municipality from the operation of the Bengal 
Municipal Act, 1884; 


Whereas it is necessary to withdraw the said 
notification; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers con- 
ferred by section 22 of the Bengal General Clauses 
Act, 1899 (Bengal Act I of 1899), read with Noti- 
fication No, 7908M, dated 3rd November 1936, I, 
Commissioner, Jalpaiguri Division, hereby rescind 
the said notification. This cancels this office Noti- 
fication No. 498L.S.-G., dated 28th June 1968.

MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 


New Delhi, the 18th December 1968 
The All India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1968 


G. S. R. 3.—In exercise of the powerg conferred by sub-section (1) of 
section 3 of the All-India Services Act, 1951 (61 of 1951), the Central 
Governinent after consultation with the Governments of the States con 
cerned, hereby makes the following rules, namely :— 


1. Short title and commenoement.---(1) These rules may he called the 
All-India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1968. 


(2) ‘They shall come into force on the date of their publication in the 
Official Gazette. 


2. Wefinitions.—In these rules, unless the context otherwise requires,— 


(a) ‘‘Government”? means— 


(i) in the case of a member of the Service serving in connection with 
the affairs of the Union, the Central, Government; or 


(ii) in the case of a member of the Service serving under a Foreign 
Government or outside India (whether on duty or on leave), 
the Central Government; or 


(iii) in the case of a member of the Service serving in connection with 
the affairs of a State, the Government of that State; 


Explanation.—A member of the Service whose services are placed at 
the disposal of a company, corporation or other organisation or a local 
authority by the Central Government or the Government of a State shall, 
for the purposes of these rules, be deemed to be a member of the Service 
serving In connection with the affairs of the Union or in connection 
with the affairs of that State, as the case may be, notwithstanding that his 
salary is drawn from sources other than the Cousolidated Fund of India or 
the Consolidated Fund of that State;

(c) ‘‘member of the Service’? means a member of an All-India Service 
as defined in section 2 of the All India Services Act, 1951 (61 
of 1951). 


. General.—(1) Every member of the Service shall at all times 
۰ maintain absolute integrity and devotion to duty and shall do nothing which 
| is unbecoming of a member of the Service. 


(2) Every member of the Service shall take all possible steps to ensure 
integrity, of, and devotion to duty, by all Government servants for 
the time being under his control and authority. 


(3) No member of the Service shall, in the performance of his official 
duties or in the exercise of powers conferred on him— 


(1) act otherwise than in his best judgement except when he is acting 

under the direction of his official superior and he shall obtain 

such direction in writing, wherever practicable, and where it 18 

not practicable, he shall obtain written confirmation as soon 
thereafter us possible; 


Qi) evade the responsibility devolving legitimately on him and seek 
instruction from, or approval of, a superior authority when such 
instruction or امم‎ Is not necessary in the scheme of distri- 
bution of powers and responsibilities. 


4. Employment of near relatives in companies or firms.—(1) No mem- 
ber of the Service shall use bis position or influence directly or indirectly to 
secure employment for any member of his family with any company or firm. 


(2) (a) No member of the Service shall, except with the previous sanc- 
tion of the Government, permit his son, daughter or dependent to accept 
employment with any company or firm having oflicia] dealings with the 
Government: 


Provided that where the acceptance of such employment cannot await 
the sanction of the Government or is otherwise considered urgent, 
the matter shall be reported to the Government; and the em- 
ployment may be accepted provisionally subject to the sanction 
of the Government. 


(b) A member of the Service shall, as soon as he becomes aware of the 
fact of acceptance by a member of his family of an employment with any 
company or firm, report to the Government the fact of such acceptance and 
also whether he has or has had any official dealings with that company or 
firm ; 


Provided that no such report shall be necessary if the member of the 
Service has already obtained sanction of, or 89800 a report to. the Government 
under clause (a).

(3) (a) No member of the Service shall in the discharge of his official 
duties, deal with any matter relating to, or award any contract in favour 
of, 1 company or firm or any other person, if any member of his family is 
employed in that company or firm or under that person or if he or any 
member of his family is interested in such company or firm or other person 
In any other manner, 


.. (b) In any case referred to iv clause (a), the member of the Service 
shall refer the matter to his official superior and the case shall there 
after be disposed of according to the instructions of the otheial superior. 


Taking part in politics and elections.—(1) No member of the Service‏ .ہ5 
shall be a member of, or be otherwise associated with, any political party‏ 
or any organisation which takes part in polities, nor shall he take part in,‏ 
or subscribe in aid of, or assist in any other manner, any politica] movement‏ 
jor political activity.‏ 


(2) It shall he the duty of every member of the Service to endeavour to 
prevent any member of his family from taking part in or subscribing in aid 
of or assisting in any other manner, any movement or activity which is, 
or tends directly or indirectly to be, subversive of the Government 88 
by luw established and where a member of the Service is unable to prevent 
a member of his family from taking part in or subseribing in aid of, 
or assisting in any other manner any such movement or activity, he 
shall make a report to that effect to the Government. 


(3) 11 any question arises whether any movement or activity falls within 
the scope of this rule, the question shall be referred to the Government for 
its decision. 


(4) No member of the Service shal] canvass or otherwise interfere with, or 
use his influence in connection with, or take part in, an election to any 
Legislature or local authority: 


Provided that— 


(1) a member of the Service qualified to vote at any 81101) election may 
exercise his right to vote but where he does so, he shall give no 
indication of the manner in which he proposes to vote or has 
voted; and 


(11) a member of the Service shall not be deemed to have contravened 
the provisions of this sub-rule by reason only that he has assisted 
in the conduct of an election in the due performance of a duty 
imposed on him by or under any law for the time being in force. 


Explanation.—The display by a member of the Service on his person, 
vehicle or residence of any electoral symbol shall amount to using = his 
influence in connection with an election, within the meaning of this 
sub-rule. 

6. Connection with press or radio.—(1) No member of the Service shall, 
except with the previous sanction of the Government, own wholly or in 
part, or conduct or participate in the editing or management of 
any newspaper or other periodical publication. 


(2) No member of the Service shall except with the previous sanction 
of the Government or any other authority empowered by it in this behalf, 
or except in the bona fide discharge of his duties. 


(a) publish a book himself or through a publisher, or contribute 
un article to a book or a compilation of articles, or 


(b) participate in a radio broadcast or contribute an article or write 
a letter to a newspaper 08 periodical, 
either in his own name of anonymously, or pseudonymously or in the name 
of any other person: 
Provided that no such sanction shal] he required— 
رں‎ if such publication is through a publisher and is of a purely 
literary, artistic or scientific character; or 
(Gi) 11 such contribution, broadcast or writing is of a purely literary, 
artistic or scientific character.

8. Evidence before committees, etc.—(1) Save as provided in sub-rule 
(3), no member of thie Service shall except with the previous sanction of 
the Government, give evidence in connection with any inquiry con- 
ducted by any person, committee or other authority. 


(4) Where any sanction has been accorded under sub-rule (1) 
no member of the Service giving such evidence shall criticise the policy 
or any action of the Centra] Government or of a State Government. 


(3) Nothing in this rule shall apply to— 


(a) evidence given at any inquiry before an authority appointed 
by the Government, or by Parliament or by a State Legislature; 
028 


(hb) evidence given in any judicial inquiry; or 


(9) evidence given oat departmental inquiry ordered by any 
authority subordinate to the Government. 


(4) No member of the Service giving any evidence referred to حز‎ sub- 
rule (3) shall give publicity to such evidence. 


9, Unauthorised communication of information.—No member of the 
Service shall except in accordance with any general or special order of 
the Government or in the performance in good faith of the duties assigned 
to him, communicate directly or indirectly any official document or part 
thereof or information to any Government servant or any other person to 
whom he is not authorised to communicate such document or information. 


Explanation.— Quotation by a member of the Service (in his representa- 
tions to the Head of Office or Head of Department or President) of, 
or from, any letter, circular or office memorandum or from the notes 
on any file to which he is not authorised to have access, or which 
he is not authorised to keepin his personal custody or for personal 
purposes, shall amount to unauthori communication of information 
within the meaning of this rule. 


10. Subscriptions.—No member of the Service shall, except with the 
previous sanction of the Government or of such ganic as may be 
empowered by it in this behalf, ask for, or accept, contributions to or 
otherwise associate himself with the raising of, any fund or other collec- 
tions in cash or in kind in pursuance of any object whatsoever. 


1l. Gifts.—(1)Save ag provided in those rules no member of the 
Service shall accept, or permit his wife or any other member of his 
family or any other person acting on his behalf to accept, any gift exceeding 
weventy-five rupees in value without the previous sanction of the Covern- 
ment.

Provided further that nothing in this sub-rule shall apply in respect of

(11) When a member of the Service is appointed or transferred to a post 
of such nature as would involve him in the চিন of any of the provisions 
of sub-rule (2) or sub-rule (4), he shall forthwith report the circumstances 
to the Government and shall thereafter act in accordance with such order 
as may be made by the Government. 


15. Insolvency and habitual indebtedness.—(1) A “member of the 
Service shall so manage his private affairs as to avoid habitual indebtedness 
or insolvency. 


2) A member of the Service against whom any legal proceeding is 
instituted for recovery of any debt due from him or for adjudging him as an 
insolvent, shall forthwith report the full facts of such legal proceeding to 
the Government. 


(3) The burden of proving that indebtedness or insolvency is the result 
of circumstances which, with the exercise of ordinary diligence, the member 
of the Service could not have foreseen or over which he had no control, and 
has not proceeded from extravagant or dissipated habits, shall be upon him,

17. Vindication of acts and character of members of the Service.—No 
member of the Service shall, except with the previous sanction of the Gov- 
ernment, have recourse to any court or to the press for the vindication of 
any official act which hns been the subject mutter of adverse criticism or 
any attack of a defamatory character. 


Explanation.—Nothing in this rule shall be deemed to prohibit a member 
of the Service from vindicating his private character or any act done by: 
him in his private capacity, provided that he shall submit a report to the 
Government regarding such action. 


18. Canvassing.—No member of the Service shall bring or attempt to 
bring any political or other influence to bear upon any superior authority 
to further his interests in respect of matters pertaining to his service under 
the Government. 


19. Bigamous Marriages.—(1) No member of the Service shall enter 
into, or contract, @ marriage with a person having a spouse living; and 

(2) No member of the Service, having a spouse living, shall enter into, 
or contract, a marriage with any person: 


“ Provided that the Government may permit a member of the Service to 
vnter inty or agptract, any such marriage as is referred to in clause (1) 
or Clause (2), if it is satisfied that— oH 

(a) such marriage is permissible under the personal law applicable to 
such inember of the ‘Service and the other party to the marriuge ). 
and 


(b) there are other grounds for so doing. 


20. Consumption of intoxicating drinks and drugs.—A member of the 
Service shall— 

(a) strictly abide. by any law relating to intoxicating drinks or drugs 
in foype in any area in which he may happen to be for the time 
being; 

(b) take due care that the performance of his duties is not prejudiced 
or affected in any way by influence of such drinks or drugs; 


(c) not appear in a public place in a state of intoxication; 
(d) not habitually use such drinks or drugs to excess. 


21. Interpretation.—If any doubt arises as to the interpretation of 
(ese rules, the Central Government shall decide the same. 


22. Delegation of powers.—The Government may, by general or special 
order, direct that any power exercisable by it under these rules (except 
the power under rule 21 or the power under this rule) shall, subject to such 
conditions, if any, as may be specified in the order, be exercisable also by 
such officer or authority as may be specified in the order. 


23. Cesser and saving.—The All-India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1954 
(hereinafter referred to as the said rules), shall cease to be in force: 
Provided that the cesser shall not affect— 


(a) the previous operation of, or anything duly done or suffered under, 
the said rules; or 

(b) any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired accrued or in- 
curred under the said rules; or | 

(০) any penalty or punishment incurred under the said rules; or 

(d) any investigation, legal proceeding or remedy in respect of any 
such right, privilege, obligation, liability, penalty or punishment 
as aforesaid ; 


and any such investigation, legal proceeding or remedy may be instituted, 
continued or enforced and any such penalty or punishment may be imposed 
ay if the said rules had not ceased to be in force.

of an industrial dispute relating to the undermentioned

service of ‘Shri K. D. 
To what relief, if any,

Banerjce is justified ? 
is he entitled ? 


On receipt of the reference notices were sent to both 
parties by this Tribunal and they appeared on 3rd June 
1968. The Union filed its written statement on 20th 
June 1968, and the Company filed’ statement on 26th 
July 1968. The case was taken up for hearing on 10th 
December 1968. The concerned workman, namely, Shri 
K. D. Banerjee himself deposed and the Company 
examined one witness, namely, Shri K. Natarajan, the 
Commercial Manager of the Company. Some docu- 


ments were admitted in evidence . by both sides and | 


they were marked exhibits. O.P.W. 1 Shri Natarajan 
was cross-examined on 20th December 1968 and both 
parties advanced their argument at length on that date. 


The case of the Union, inter alia, is that Shri K. D. 
Banerjee was appointed by the Company on 15th April 
1965, as General Assistant with specified duties relating 
to Shipping and Stores of the Company, at their Site 
Office in the Durgapur Steel Plant and he was con- 
firmed in service .on 26th October 1965. .On 11th 


August 1965 the Company guaranteed Mr. K. D. . 


Banerjee continuance of service till the completion of 
the Company's contract with Hindusthan Steel Ltd. On 


‘its part of the 


14001) April 1967, the Company issued a letter desiring 
(0 terminate his service from. the end of May 1967, on 
the plea that the contract of the Company with Hin- 
dusthan Steel Ltd. was coming to successful conclusion 
and the Company offered to pay one month's salary in 
advance to Mr. Banerjee. The latter took payment ٠ 
the pay in good faith trusting the statement of the Com- 
pany to be genuine. Mr. Banerjee, however, raised . 
his claim regarding payments towards privilege leave 
salary and other dues but this claim was not paid heed 
to. Thereafter it came to light that the Company had 
played a trick upon Mr. Banerjee under the plea of 
completion of the contract with Hindusthan Steel Ltd. 
as the Company not only continued to function but also 
gave fresh appointment. It is alleged that one Shri B. 
Banerjee was appointed on 8th September 1966 as 


‘Stores Glerk to assist Mr. K. D. Banerjee and is still 


continuing in service and he has _ subsequently been 
awarded increment of Rs. 50. The Union. therefore, 
alleges that the termination of the service of Shri K. 
D. Banerjee is unjustified and violates the principle 
“Come last go first” and it prays for his reinstatement 
and other benefits. 


In the written statement the case of the Company in 
brief is that Shri K. D. Banerjee was employed on a 
temporary basis for a period of 3 months only with 
effect from 19th April 1965 at a monthly salary of 
Rs. 400 and he agreed to serve the Company upon such 
terms and conditions. Thereafter on 17th July 1965, 
the Company extended the service of Shri Banerjee 
as General Assistant for a further period of 3 months 
from 19th July 1965, on the same terms and conditions . 
on a temporary basis. Next, by letter, dated 26th 
October 1965, the Company confirmed his appointment 
as General Assistant with effect from 19th October 
1965 at a monthly salary of Rs. 400 consolidated and 
with the express stipulation that the service was liable 
to be terminated by one month's notice on either side, 
or one month’s salary in lieu of notice. Shri K. D. 
Banerjee accepted the terms of this employment. 
Afterwards on or about the month of August 1966, the 
Company informed Shri Banerjee that his employment 
as a Genera] Assistant made on a temporary basis 
could !وہ‎ be extended any further after the completion 
of a contract whereunder the Company had agreed to 
erect a Skelp Mill Plant at Durgapur for Messrs. Hin- 
dusthan Steel Ltd. and which construction was then 
well under way. The contract between the Company 
and Shri Banerjee regarding the terms of his employ- 
ment under the Company was subsequently recorded in 
a letter, dated 11th August 1966, sent by the Company 
to Shri Banerjee who received and accepted the same 
withont protest. Meanwhile the Company was busy 
erecting the said Skelp Mill Plant under the said con- 
tract with Hindusthan Steel Ltd. and by the beginnin 
of February 1967, the Company had all! but fulfille 
obligation thereunder by erecting the 
same in accordance with agreed specifications. In the 
beginning of April 1967, on seeing that the completion 
of the said contract was near at hand, the Company 
duly served a notice in writing, dated 10th April 1967, 
on Shri Banerjee communicating its intention to termi- 
nate his service with effect from the end of May 1967. 
The Company asserts that the service of Shri Banerjee 
was terminated by this notice in good faith and in full 
compliance with the terms and conditions of service. 
Shri Banerjée himself accepted this termination without 
protest and on or about’! ]th April 1967, he received 
115. 800 in cash from the Company in full and final 
settlement of his salary up to 3lst May 1967. The

I may also point out that one Shri B. C. Banerjee 
was appointed to help Shri K. D. Banerjee in his work 
and this B. C. Banerjee is still continuing in his service 
under the present Company at Durgapur. Shri K.

and in evidence that Shri B. C. Banerjee was appointed

“Store Clerk”. It is admitted that Shri .ظط‎ C. Banerjee 
has been retained even after the termination of the 
service of Shri K. D. Banerjee, though both of them 
were appointed in’ general service and Shri K. D. 
Banerjec was appointed earlier than Shri B. C. 
Banerjee. It is said by the Company in its written 
statement that because Shri B.C. Banerjee has a 
“mechanical bend of mind” so he was retained to help 
the Installation Engineer of the Company in the work 
of commissioning the Skelp Mill Plant. I cannot under- 
stand what this company wants to mean by the word 
mechanical bend of mind. There is nothing to show 
that Shri B. C. Banerjee has any technical knowledge. 
‘Shri K. Natarajan also admits in cross-examination 
that Shri S. C. Dutta was appointed as a clerk subse- 
quent to the appointment of Shri B. C. Banerjee and

violated the principle of .“last come first go” rule in 
terminating the service of Shri K. D. Banerjce before 
the termination of the services of Shri S. C. Dutta and 
Shri B. C. Banerjee. 


Under clause (b) of section 25F of the Industrial 
Disputes Act no workman employed in any industry 
who has been in continuous service for not less than 
one year shall be retrenched unless he has been paid 
retrenchment compensation as provided in that clause. 
But in this case the Company did not pay any retrench- 
ment compensation to Shri Banerjee. Again under 
clause (c) of section 25F notice in the prescribed 
manner is to be served on the appropriate Government 
by 119, Company before retrenchment of such a work- 
man. But there.is no evidence that any such notice 
was served by the Company on the Government. 


On a consideration of these facts and’ circumstances 
it appears that the Company wrongfully terminated the 
service of Shri K. D. Banerjee. Shri Banerjee has 
prayed for reinstatement but I do: not like to’ pass an 
order for reinstatement as the work of the construc- 
tion and commission of the Skelp Mill Piant is almost 
complete if not already completed by this time. Shri 
Banerjee is no doubt entitled to some compensation for 
wrongful retrenchment. The Union has produced a 
letter from the Deputy Labour Commissioner to the 
Company (Ext. 6, dated 24th February 1968) from 
which it appears that conciliation preceeding was held 
before him and the’ Company admitted in that proceed- 
ing that erection of the’ plant was not completed till 
December 1967. The Deputy Labour Commissioner, 
therefore, suggested that the Company should pay Shri 
Banerjee 7 months’ pay from June to December 1967. 
Of course, he has 81909 suggested payment for some 
additional benefits like salary in lieu of unclaimed 
leave, bonus, etc.; but I have already shown that under 
the letter of confirmation of service Shri Banerjee was 
net entitled 10 these benefits. It was argued by the 
learned Counsel for the Company that Shri Banerjee 
did not raise any claim before the Company imme- 
diately after the termination of his service. But it was 
elucidated from him in cross’-examination that he wrote 
a letter-on 25th June 1967 to the Local Administrative 
Manager of the Company at Calcutta making his claim. 
Shri Banerjee says that he waited for some time and 
then he wrote this letter. In the Industrial Disputes 
At there is no provision for limitation in making 
claim. I, therefore, find that the Company should pay 
Shri K. D. Banerjee Rs. 2,800 by way of wages for 
7 months as suggested by the Deputy Labour Commis- 
sioner within one month from the date of publication 
of this award in the official gazette.

the Governor of West Bengal under Government of 
West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 2590- 
1.R./IR/11L-223/67, dated the 16th June 1967. On 
the issue mentioned hereunder there having existed 
an industrial dispute between Messrs. Bharat Dyers 
and Dry Cleaners (hereinafter called the Company) 
and their workmen represented by Laundry Workers’ 
Union (hereinafter called the Union), the Governor 
was pleased to make the aforesaid reference to this 
Tribunal for adjudicating the dispute. 


Issue 
Payment of Gratuity to Shri Rose Mohammad. 


On the receipt of the order of reference this case 
was started on 181 July 1967 and parties were called 
upon to appear before this Tribunal and to file their 
written -statements. The parties duly filed their 
written statements and the case became a contested 
one. The Tribunal fixed various dates for taking 
preliminary steps in the case preparatory to the final 
hearing of the case. Shri S. R. Ghose, Advocate, 
appeared for the Union and Shri .ظط‎ Ash, Advocate, 
appeared for the Company on 24th July 1968 which 
was a date for final hearing of the case, and they 
fled a joint petition praying for an adjournment on 
the ground that a talk of settlement was ‘going on 
between the parties. Afer hearing the learned 
Advocates of both sides, the Tribunal adjourned the 
hearing so that the parties may come to a negotiated 
settlement regarding the dispute. On 19th Septem- 
ber 1968 Shri B. Biswas, Advocate, appeared for 
the Union with a petition for adjournment on the 
ground that Shri S. R. Ghosh, authorised lawyer 
for the Union, was taken suddenly ill. The Union 
was directed to serve a copy of the petition on the 
other side and 24th September 1968 was fixed for 
hearing of the case. “Fhen the case was fixed for 
hearing on 11th November 1968. On that date Shri 
S. R. Ghosh, Advocate, appeared for the Union 
and Shri B. Ash, Advocate, appeared for the Com- 
pany and filed a joint petition of compromise. The 
Tribunal then reserved its order. 


I have perused the joint petition of compromise 
hled by the parties. For the Union the joint 
petition of compromise has been signed by Shri Sib- 
nath Chatterjee, Vive-President. and another. For 
the Company one of the partners has signed the joint 
petition of compromise. On perusal of the petition 
of compromise filed by the parties I find that the 
terms of compromise are fair and_ reasonable. 
Therefore, accepting the petition of compromise, | 
hereby pass this compromise award and dispose of 
this case. As prayed for by the parties, the joint 
petition of compromise is made hereby a part of 
this award and it will be published as annexure ‘A’ 
to this award. 


Usual number of copies of, this award be sent to 
the State Government for necessary action.

The O. P.-Company’s case is that there was a

Decisions 


The O. P.-Company filed a petition for preli- 
minary hearing on 6th February 1968 urging for a 
preliminary hearing on the point whether there was 
a lock-out of the factory with effect from 7th April 
1967, or there was a stay-in-strike. By my order 
No. 11, dated 6th February 1968, I rejected the 
petition for preliminary hearing as the point raised 
was a clear question of fact and could very well 
be taken up for hearing at the time of final hearing 
on merits. 


The learned lawyer for the O. P.-Company urges 
that there was no lock-out of the factory with effect 
from 7th April 1967 and in fact there was a stay- 
in-strike by the workers, He has also urged _ that 
the sponsori::g Union is a stranger Union and the 
order of reference is not proper as the stranger 
Union has not observed the formalities in espousing 
the present industrial dispute. I take up the second 
point first. 


The learned lawyer for the O. P.-Company relie 
upon the decisions reported in 1963(1) LL.-J., 16 
and 1965-1, LLJ., 95 to urge that when a Union 
unconnected with the employer industry takes up the 
cause of the workmen, the Labour Court must see 
whether the stranger Union has the backing, sym- 
pathy and collaboration of the majority or a large 
section of the workers employed in the particular 
industry. Both these decisions relate to cases where 
individual disputes were espoused by a_ stranger 
Union and the law: has been faid down as to specify 
the circumstances when even a stranger Union can 
espouse the cause of an_ individual ‘workman by 
which the individual dispute transforms itself to an 
industrial dispute. The learned lawyer for the 
Union relies upon the recent decision reported in 
1968(17) F. L. R. Parts 6 and 7 191, wherein it 
has been held that “where the dispute which was 
referred to the Tribunal related to gratuity scheme 
sought to be introduced for the benefits of all the 
workmen employed in a particular Company, it was 
perse an industrial dispute. No espousal or support 
was needed for such a dispute.” It has been also 
held therein that—‘“It would appear that the condi- 
tions of espousal or of a body or a_ considerable 
section of the workmen making a common cause 
with the particular dispute arises when individual 
dispute per se is of the nature of an individual dis- 
pute concerning a particular workman as opposed 
to collective dispute involving all the workmen.” 


The present dispute relating to lock-out of the 
factory by the O. P.-Company is clearly per se an 
industrial dispute and no question of backing of

So I find that though the espousing Union of the

present dispute is per se an industrial dispute and 
has been supported by a substantial number of 
workmen serving under the O. P.-Company and so 
the order of reference is quite legal and valid, the 
stranger Union having a locus standi to sponsor the 
present industrial dispute.

The learned lawyer for the O.P.-Company has

227 to urge the distinction between a strike and a

hand, there is no competent evidence that the 
O. P.-Company really declared a lock-out of their

On the above descussion, I am bound to hold that 
the Union has failed to establish by competent 
evidence that there was any lock-out of the factory 
and its stand conclusively proved that the workmen 
resorted to a stay-in-strike since 7th April 1967. 


It is true that there is ample evidence on record 
that the management did not furnish work to the 
workmen on 7th April 1967, but that itself does 
not amount to declaring a lock-out of the factory. 
What is a lock-out has been categorically stated in 


the decision reported in 1962-II, LL.J. 227. 


On the discussions above, ] accept that there was 
no lock-out of the factory with effect from 7th April 
1967 and there was a stay-in-strike. Whether the 
stay-in-strike was justihed because of refusal of 
work to the workmen by the management does not 
lie within the scope of the present reference. 


As I find that there was no lock-out of the factory 
with effect from 7th April 1967, there is no question 
of justification ‘or otherwise of the alleged lock-out. 
The first part of this issue is so dispose of. 


On my findings above, the workmen cannot be 
entitled to any benefits and so the second part of 
the issue is answered in the negative. 


An award be passed accordingly holding that 
there was no lock-out of the factory with effect 
from 7th April 1967 and so no question arises as 
to the justification of the alleged lock-out or other- 
wise. It is also hold that the workmen are not 
entitled to any benehts. 


This is my award.

above. 


I shall now proceed to discuss the evidence 
adduced by the respective parties and the merits 
thereof regarding each issue seperately. 


Issue No. 1: 


It is submitted on behalf of the Union that the 
workmen concerned in the present dispute are 
paid very low wages, and that they are entitled 
to fair wages, i.e., a fair margin over the minimum 
wages in view of the stable financial condition of 
the Company. It is submitted further that their 
scales of pay have not been revised since the 
award of 1950 (Ext. B) although the paying capa- 
city of the Company: has improved much since 
then, and the circumstances, 90101) as, rise in price 
index, increase in national income, increase in 
wages in the Dalhousie Square area 1820 
changed. In support of its claim the Union has 
relied on the Consumer Price Index Number for 
working class in Calcutta area, Exts. 4, 4/a and 
5/a. It is true that revision of pay scales and 
wages of workers covered by an award cannot 
be entertained without proof of change in 
circumstances. In the instant case the Com- 
pany, which is a reputed jewellery firm in the 
city of Calcutta, has not seriously challenged that 
the circumstances have now changed since the 
passings of the award in 1950. It is contended 
on behalf of the Company that in view of its 
present financial condition and gloomy future of 
the industry as a whole, it is unable to pay the 
workers moré than what they have already 
offered by their letter, dated 30th August 1965, 
Ext. E (same as Ext. 2). In support of _ their 
case the Company have produced their Balance- 
Sheets for the financial years 1962-63, to 1965-66 
(Ext. A to Ext. A/3). They have 8150 produced 
two awards, Exts. B and B/1, in respect of the 
instant Company. Another award, Ext. B/2, in 
respect of an industrial dispute between Messrs. 
Cooke and Kelvey Ltd. and their employees has 
also been produced on behalf of the Company; 
and it has been urged that it should be taken as 
only comparative unit only in fixing wages of 
the instant Company. 


In Annexure ‘A’ to its written statement the 
Union has given in a tabular form the existing 
scales of pay, since 1950, of the different cate- 
gories of workmen concerned in this dispute, the 
Union's demands and the Company's offer. 
There is no dispute regarding the correctness of 
this chart. The law is well-settled that to deter- 
mine’ fair wages, the important factors are the 
capacity of the industries to pay and the prevail- 
ing rates of wages, and that these are to be 
appraised on the ‘footing of industry-cum-region 
basis. In reply fo the Company’s plea of their 
financial incapacity to meet the Union’s demand, 
the Union has drawn my attention to the case 
reported in 1958, I, L.L.J. p. 1 (Messrs. Crown 
Aluminium Works Vs. their workmen) in which 
their Lordship of the Hon‘ble Supreme Court have 
held that no industry has right to exist unless it 
is able to pay its workmen at least bare minimum 
wages. Their Lordship have further observed 
that the employment of labour جہ‎ starvation 
wage cannot be encouraged or favoured in a 


116 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 30, 1969 


ogee موھد‎ 


modern domecratic Welfare State, and that if 
an employer cannot maintain his’ enterprise 
without cutting down the wages of their em- 
ployees below even a bare subsistance or mini- 
mum wage, he would have no right to conduct 
his enterprise on such terms. On behalf of the 
Company my attention has been drawn to a 
subsequent decision of the Hon'ble Supreme 
Court reported in 1961, I, L.L.J. p. 339 [Express 
Newspaper (P) Ltd. and another Vs. Union of 
India and others] in which the principles of fixa- 
tion of rates of wages have been clearly laid 
down. Regarding the principles to be followed 
in the instant case, there is practically no dispute 
between the parties. The only dispute is over 
choice of the comparable unit. It is contended 
on behalf of the Company that Ext. B/2 namely, 
the award in the case of Messrs. Cooke and 
Kelvey Ltd. made in 1953 should be taken as the 
comparative unit inasmuch as it is in respect of 
a similar industry and also in the same area. 
The Union, on the other hand, claims that the 
wages are to be fixed according to the stable 
financial condition of the Company. 


On the materials of the records I am however 
not inclined to accept the award, Ext. B/2, as 
comparable unit in the instant case inasmuch as 
wages of the workers of Messrs. Cooke & Kelvey 
Ltd. was fixed thereunder in 1953 on the basis 
of the financial capacity of that particular com- 
pany prevailing at that time, within which I have 
no materials before me nor do I know regarding 
the categories of workers concerned therein are 
the same. Moreover, the circumstances have also 
changed much since 1953. I shall therefore pro- 
ceed mainly on the basis of the financial capa- 
city or otherwise of the company and consider 
whether the same is sufficient or not to meet the 
financial demands of the workmen as made or 
at all. Regarding the financial condition of the

company the most important documents produ- 
ced before me are the Balance-Shects for the 
years 1962-63 to 1965-66 (Exts. A to A/3). It is

has been making steady profit and that in each 
of these years their profit exceeded Rupees Four 
Lakhs. In the Profit and Loss Accounts for the 
year ending with 3151 October 1966, as shown in 
the Balance Sheet, Ext. A/3, the profit is shown 
to be Rs. 4,89,759.60 Paise as against Rs.4,05,002.34 
Paise made in the previous year. P.W. 2, Bankim 
Chandra Pandit, the Accounts Assistant Clerk of 
the company, has deposed that the employees of 
the company received bonus for the Jast three 
years at the maximum rate, viz., 20 per cent. 
O.P.W. 1, P. N. Coping, one of the Directors of 
the company, has also admitted that they have 
paid 20 per cent of their annual earning as bonus 
out of profit. In appreciating the financial capa- 
city of the company I cannot also overlook the 
fact that the company being manufacturer of 
silver, gold and diamond setting has been hit by 
the abolition of Raja, Maharaja and Princes who 
are their main customers. In view of the pre- 
sent day high cost of living. it is not possible 
even for the higher middle class to purchase arti- 
cles of gold and silver. They have to purchase 
such articles under pressure, such as, occasion of 
daughters’ marriage ; but that also within very 
limited means. In this background I appreciate 
that the future of this industry is not as bright 
as it was in the past. However, the Balance 
Sheets of the company show that they are making 
steady profit inspite of these hard days and their 
profit for the year 1965-66 almost reached Rs 5 
lakhs. In these circumstances, I think that the 
financial condition of the company is certainly 
sufficient to meet part of the financial demand 
of the workmen concerned, After considering 
the facts and circumstances of the present case 
and in view of what I have stated above, I revise 
the existing grades and scales of pay in the follow-

Regarding fittings of the workmen into these 
revised grade and scales of pay, their present 
pay will be the guiding factor. Where the pre- 
sent pay is less than the minimum of a grade or 


a slab in a grade, that should be pulled up to the - 


next higher pay point. Where the present pay 
is just below a particular slab in a particular 
group, that should be pulled up to the next. higher 
point of pay, and then increments’ will follow. 
This revised scales of pay will be operative from 
Ist Januagy 1968, and the next increment will be 
on 151 January 1969. 


Issue No. 2: 


The Union has claimed dearness allowance at 
the rate allowed by the Bengal Chamber of Com- 
merce in the offices situated at Dalhousie Square 
area. P.W. 1, Satindra Nath Roy Chowdhury, 
the Secretary of the Union and an employee of 
Messrs. Karam Chand Thapar & Bros. Ltd., has 
deposed that Messrs. Hamilton & Co. (P) Ltd. 
and Messrs. Karam Chand Thapar & Bros. Pvt. 
Ltd. are carrying on business in the Dalhousie 
Square area. It is submitted on behalf of the 
Union that both these companies should pay dear- 
ness allowance at the same rate. P.W. 1 has 
stated further that mostly in the offices of the 
Dalhousie Square area Bengal Chamber of Com- 
merce Scheme is followed for dearness allowance. 
But I am not inclined to accept this contention 
of the union. P.W. I has admitted in ‘cross-exa- 
mination that Messrs. Hamilton & Co. (P) Ltd. 
does not carry on business of the same nature 
as done by Messrs. Karam Chand Thapar & Bros. 
*Pvt. Ltd., and that there is no definite demarca- 
tion of Dalhousie Square area. In my opinion, 
the offices like Messrs. Karam Chand Thapar & 
Bros. Pvt. Ltd. situated in the Dalhousie Square 
area and allowing dearness allowance at the rate 
of Bengal Chamber of Commerce are in respect 
of different types of business and cannot be com- 
pared with the business in which the present 
company is engaged. Their scope, financial ca- 
pacity and future prospect are also different. In 
these circumstances, I think, I should not allow 
dearness allowance to the workers of this com- 
pany at the rate of Bengal Chamber of Commerce 
but at the same time I am satisfled that they are 
entitled to some more dearness allowance than 
what they have been getting at present. From 
the materials produced before me, _ I find that 
there has been adjustment from time to time re- 
garding payment of dearness§ allowance to the 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JANUARY 30, 1969 117 


Soe‏ آمے 


workers of this company. Under the award of 
the Industrial Tribunal of 1950 (Ext. B.), the 
dearness allowance was fixed at Rs 30 per month 
at a flat rate. On 3rd December 1951 by an 
agreement between the parties the dearness allo- 
wance was raised to Rs 35 per month with effect 
from 151 December 1951. Under the award of 
1959 (Ext. B/1), the dearness allowance was 
raised from Ra 35 to Rs 40 per month. There- 
after by an agreement, dated 27th August 1964 
(Ext. D), the: dearness allowance was raised to 
Rs 47.50 per month; and regarding those who 
were receiving on percentage basis, dearness 
allowance was raised from 70 per cent. to 75 
per cent. Thereafter during pendency of this 
reference before this Tribunal the workers placed 
a joint petition before the management (Ext. H), 
on 3rd August 1967 praying for an ‘emergency 
allowance’ at any rate the management thinks fit 
so that the poor employees may be saved from 
starvation. In reply, the company issued a notice 
on 10th August 1967 (Ext. 1), and granted an 
emergency food allowance of Rs 12.50 for four 
months, namely August, September, October and 
November, to all clerical staff, durwans, peons, 
sub-staff and salaried employees of workshop. 
On that very day, i.e., 10th August 1967, the 
workers thanked the management by their letter, 
Ext. J, for granting the emergency allowance to 
them. On 9th November 1967 the workmen 
filed a petition before this Tribunal praying that 
the company might be directed to pay the interim 
relief to the extent of Rs. 12.50 till the disposal 
of this case and also praying that an additional 
interim relief of Rs 25 per month might be gran- 
ted to each employee till the disposal of this case. 
Shri R. Bhattacherjee, my predecessor in office, 
by his order, dated 16th November 1967, refused 
to grant the interim relief to the extent of Rs 25 
at that stage but directed the company not to dis- 
continue the payment of Rs 12.50 per month to 
each employee due to rise in price of commodities 
before the disposal of this case. It follows, 
therefore, that each worker is now getting Rs 60, 
in all, per month as dearness allowance at a flat 
rate including the interim relief of Rs. 12.50 Paise. 
It appears from the Middle Class Cost of Living 
Index Number for Calcutta area (Ext. 4/a), that 
in July 1967, i.e., just before the granting of in- 
terim relief the price index number was 618, 
taking August 1939, as the base year, Ext. 5/a 
shows that in January 1963 the price index num- 
ber ‘has gone up to 710. On the materials in the 
record and in the facts and circumstances of the

CALCUTTA IMPROVEMENT TRUST 


THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES FOR THE

Notice under section 43 of the Calcutta Improvement 
Act, 1911 (Bengal Act V of 1911) 


Calcutta, the 315 December 1968. 


Scheme No. XV-M (Supplementary) 


It is hereby notified under section 43 of the Calcutta 
Improvement Act, 1911, that a Rehousing Scheme for 
the construction of flats and shops for providing alter- 
native accommodation mainly to the bustee-dwellers 
and shop-keepers to be displaced due to execution of 
Scheme No. XV-M (Widening of Manicktala Main 
Road between Scheme No. I-M and western flank of 
Railway Bridge) on a block of land in Scheme No. 
VI-M (Narkeldanga Main Road to Manicktala Main 
Road) and Scheme No. VII-M (Manicktala Main 
Road to Ultadanga Main Road), to be hereinafter 
known as Scheme No. XV-M (Supplementary), has 
been framed by the Board of Trustees for the Im- 
provement of Calcutta in constituency No. 32 of the 
Calcutta Corporation. 


2. The area comprised within and +۳ for the 
execution of the scheme (shown in yellow verge in 


the plan) measures 1.71 acres, more or less, and is 
more particularly described below:— 


Boundaries of the land 


On the North: Calcutta Improvement Trust 
acquired land in Scheme No. VII-M. 


On the East: 40 feet wide Calcutta Improvement 
Trust Road in Scheme Nos. VI-M and VII-M. 


On the South: 120 feet wide Manicktala Main 
Road. 


On the West: Eastern Railway permanent way 
embankment. 


3. Particulars of the scheme and a map of 106 
area comprised in the scheme may be seen at the 
office of the Calcutta Improvement Trust at 10 Netaji 
Subhas Road, Calcutta-1, on week days between 11 
a.m. and 3 p.m. and on Saturdays between 11 a.m. 
and 12 noon. All the lands required for the execu- 
tion of the scheme have already been acquired in 
connection with Calcutta Improvement Trust Scheme 
Nos. VI-M and VII-M. 


Copies of the above documents will be available on 
payment of the following fees:— 


Particulars of the scheme—Re. 0.25P. 
Plan of the scheme area—Re. 1.00P. 
4. Objection will be received by the Chairman up 
to the 17th March 1969.

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 


OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF POLICE, 
‘ CALCUTTA 


ORDERS 
Dated Calcutta, the 31st January 1969. 


WHEREAS rioting, affrays and other disturbances of 
_the public tranquillity have already taken place in 
Certain arcas within the town of Calcutta; 


AND WHEREAS there is apprehension of such 
rioting, affrays and other disturbances of the public 
tranquillity spreading out to areas within the suburbs 
of the town of Calcutta; 


AND WHEREAS, I, P. K. Sen, Commissioncr of 
Police, Calcutta, being a Magistrate of the First Class, 
have been specially empowered by the State Govern- 
ment under notification No. 2737-G.A., dated the 6th 
May 1968, to act under section 144 of the Code of 
Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act 5 of 1898); 


AND WHEREAS, in my opinion, there 15 sufficient 
ground for proceeding under the said section for the 
immediate prevention of disturbances of the public 
tranquillity within the said suburbs of the town of 
Calcutta; 


Now, THEREFORE, in exercise of the power con- 
ferred by sub-section (1) of section 144 of the Code 
of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act 5 of 1898), read 
with sub-section (3) of the said section, I, the said 
P. K. Sen, Commissioner of Police, Calcutta, do 
hereby prohibit )٣جہ‎ the 31st January 1969, until 
further orders, any assembly of five or more persons, 
or any procession within the entire suburbs of the town 
of Calcutta, or the carrying of any lathis or other 
dangerous weapons, or the doing of any act which 19 
likely to cause a disturbance of the public tranquillity 
within the said suburbs of the town of Calcutta.

of such rioting, affrays and other disturbances of the

out to other areas of the town of Calcutta;

Police, Calcutta, being a Presidency Magistrate, have 
been specially cmpowered by the State Government - 
under Notification No. S061-G.A., dated the 
Sth September 1968, to act under section 144 of the

AND WHEREAS, in my opinion, there in sufficient 
ground for proceeding under the said section for the 
immediate prevention of disturbances of the public 
tranquillity within the said areas;

conferred by sub-section (1) of section 144 of the

I —Orders and Notifications by the Governor of W>st Bengal, the High Court, Government‏ "ا ."ا

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 


HOME DEPARTMENT 
General Administration 


RESOLUTION 


No. 233-G.A.C.—3lst January 1969.—Government have received with deep 
regret the news of the sudden and untimely death on the night of the 30th 
January 1969 of Shri B. K. Chatterjee, I.A.S., Labour Commissioner, West 
Bengal, at the age of 49 years only. 


Shri Chatterjee was a senior member of the Indian Administrative Service 
and was borne on the cadre of West Bengal. He worked in the districts 
as Additional District Magistrate in Hooghly and 24-Parganas and as District 
Magistrate in West Dinajpur and Burdwan. He also held other responsible 
posts, ৮127 Director, National Employment Service and Controller af Civil 


Defence, 24-Parganas, and was lastly posted as Labour Commissioner in 
June 1967. 


Ever since his assumption of the office of Labour Commissioner at a critical 
time he set himself tirelessly to promote industrial peace and labour welfare 
in this State, and by his earnest and untiring efforts he recently Succeeded in 
securing an agreement between different employers’ and employees’ 
organisations regarding the setting up.of a tripartite machinery for screening 
proposals of mass retrenchment. His sudden and untimely death has caused an 
irreparable lass to the Government and to the Labour Directorate in particular. 


Throughout his service, Shri Chatterjee upheld the highest traditions of 
integrity and devotion to duty expected of the members of the service to which 
he belonged. His sense of fairness and his pleasant personality earned him the 
esteem and affection of all those who came in contact with him. 


The Government of West Bengal desire to record their profound regret at 
the untimely loss of an able and zealous officer and to convey to his family the 
sincere expression of their sympathy. 


By order of the Governor, 
M. M. BASU, 
Chief Secy. to the Govt. of West Bengal.

at the West Bengal Government Press, Alipore.
